name: Java Memory & JVM

beginner.content:
What is a Class Loader?

Before Java code can run, the JVM must load your .class files into memory. The Class Loader is the part of the JVM responsible for finding those .class files, reading their bytecode, and making them usable by the running program.

Without a class loader, the JVM would have no way to turn a compiled .class file sitting on disk into an actual, usable class inside a running program.

The Three Built-in Class Loaders

Java ships with three class loaders, arranged in a hierarchy:

• Bootstrap Class Loader - loads core Java classes like java.lang.String and java.lang.Object from the JDK's own libraries. Written in native code, not Java.
• Extension (Platform) Class Loader - loads classes from Java's extension/platform libraries.
• Application (System) Class Loader - loads the classes you write, from your project's classpath. This is the one that loads your own Main.class, for example.

A Simple Example

When you run a Java program, the Application Class Loader is the one that loads your class first.

Loading, Linking, and Initialization

Getting a class ready to use is not a single step - the JVM does three things in order:

• Loading - the class loader reads the .class file bytes and creates a Class object in memory.
• Linking - the JVM verifies the bytecode is valid, allocates memory for static fields, and resolves references to other classes.
• Initialization - static initializer blocks and static variable assignments actually run.

The Delegation Model (Simple View)

When a class needs to be loaded, the Application Class Loader does not just load it immediately - it first asks its parent (Extension Class Loader), which in turn asks its parent (Bootstrap Class Loader).

Only if none of the parents can find the class does the child actually load it itself. This is called the parent delegation model, and it stops you from accidentally overriding core classes like java.lang.String with your own version.

ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError

These two errors sound similar but happen for different reasons:

• ClassNotFoundException - thrown when code explicitly asks to load a class by name (e.g. Class.forName("com.example.Foo")) and it cannot be found on the classpath.
• NoClassDefFoundError - thrown when a class was available at compile time, but is missing at runtime when the JVM tries to use it (for example, a JAR was removed after compiling).

Fresher Notes

  • Class loader: the JVM component that finds a .class file and turns its bytes into a Class object, lazily, on first use.
  • Three built-in loaders: bootstrap (core java.base), platform (other JDK modules) and application (your classpath).
  • Loading steps: loading, linking (verify, prepare, resolve) and initialization (static blocks run).

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Loading a class goes through fixed phases.

  • Loading: loadClass(name) asks the parent first, then findClass reads the bytes and defineClass creates the Class object.
  • Verification: the bytecode is checked for type safety and stack correctness.
  • Preparation: static fields get default values (0, null).
  • Resolution: symbolic references become direct ones, often lazily.
  • Initialization: static initializers run once, under a lock, in textual order.
  • Cache: each loader records the classes it defined, so a name is defined once per loader.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to load classes and the options around them:

  • Implicit: a reference in bytecode (new, static call) loads the class.
  • Explicit: Class.forName(name) (initializes) or loader.loadClass(name) (does not initialize).
  • URLClassLoader: load from jar or directory URLs, closeable.
  • ServiceLoader: discover implementations through META-INF/services or module-info.
  • Lookup.defineClass: define a class from bytes inside an existing package.
  • Flags: -cp, --module-path, -Xlog:class+load.

expert.content:
Custom Class Loaders

Beyond the three built-in loaders, Java lets you write your own by extending ClassLoader and overriding findClass(). Custom class loaders are used to:
• Load classes from non-standard sources (a database, a network location, an encrypted JAR).
• Implement plugin systems where each plugin gets its own isolated loader (used by application servers and IDEs like Eclipse's OSGi).
• Enable hot-reloading of classes without restarting the JVM.

The Delegation Model, In Detail

        Bootstrap ClassLoader   (loads java.lang.*, native, no parent)
                 ^
                 | parent
        Extension/Platform ClassLoader   (loads javax.*, JDK extensions)
                 ^
                 | parent
        Application/System ClassLoader   (loads your classpath, e.g. com.myapp.*)
                 ^
                 | parent
        Custom ClassLoader (optional, e.g. a plugin loader)
Request flow for loading a class: the request always travels up to Bootstrap first, and only if every ancestor fails to find the class does control fall back down to the loader that was originally asked. This is why it's called delegation - each loader delegates upward before trying itself.

Why Delegation Matters: Preventing Class Spoofing

Imagine an attacker packages their own java.lang.String class inside a malicious JAR, hoping to replace the trusted one and intercept string operations. Because of parent delegation, when anything asks for java.lang.String, the request bubbles up to the Bootstrap Class Loader first - which always finds the genuine JDK version before the Application Class Loader ever gets a chance to load the fake one.

This protection is why user code cannot easily shadow java.* packages - it's a core part of the JVM's security model, not an accident.

Namespace Isolation and "Same Class, Different Loader" Problem

A class is uniquely identified in the JVM not just by its fully qualified name, but by the combination of (class name, class loader). This means the exact same .class file, loaded by two different class loaders, produces two distinct Class objects that are not equal and cannot be cast to each other - even though the source code is identical.

This is a common cause of confusing ClassCastException errors in application servers and plugin systems, where the same library gets loaded twice by different loaders (e.g. once by the app server, once by a deployed application's own loader).

What Happens When a Class Cannot Be Loaded

ScenarioResultWhen it typically happens
Class requested explicitly by name, not found anywhere on classpathClassNotFoundException (checked)Class.forName(), reflection, JDBC driver loading
Class was present at compile time but its .class/JAR is missing at runtimeNoClassDefFoundError (unchecked, extends Error)A dependency JAR was removed/misconfigured after build
Static initializer of a class throws an exception during initExceptionInInitializerError, then NoClassDefFoundError on later attemptsBuggy static block or static field initializer
Custom loader's classpath/source becomes unavailable at load timeNoClassDefFoundError or LinkageErrorPlugin JAR deleted while the app is running

Common Misconceptions

• "ClassLoader loads the whole application at startup." Wrong - classes are loaded lazily, on first use, not all upfront.
• "There are only 3 class loaders." Wrong - there are 3 built-in loaders, but frameworks (Tomcat, Spring Boot's fat-JAR launcher, OSGi) commonly add many more custom loaders for isolation.
• "NoClassDefFoundError means the class was never compiled." Wrong - it usually means the class compiled fine but its JAR/classpath entry is missing or broken at runtime.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What are the three built-in class loaders in order?Bootstrap, Extension/Platform, Application/System
What is the parent delegation model?A class loader delegates the load request to its parent first, only loading it itself if no ancestor can find the class
Why does delegation prevent core class spoofing?Because the Bootstrap loader is asked first and always resolves java.lang.* classes from the trusted JDK before any user loader gets a chance
What's the difference between ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError?ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception from explicitly requesting a missing class (e.g. Class.forName); NoClassDefFoundError is an unchecked Error thrown when a class available at compile time is missing at runtime
Can the same class be loaded twice in one JVM?Yes, if loaded by two different class loaders - they produce two distinct, incompatible Class objects
What are the three phases a class goes through before use?Loading, Linking (verify, prepare, resolve), and Initialization
Why would you write a custom class loader?To load classes from non-standard sources, achieve plugin isolation, or support hot-reloading
Is the Bootstrap Class Loader written in Java?No, it's implemented natively (in C/C++) as part of the JVM itself

Mid-Level Notes

  • Parent delegation: a loader first asks its parent, so java.lang.String always comes from the bootstrap loader and cannot be faked.
  • Class identity is the class name plus its loader, so the same bytes loaded by two loaders give two different, incompatible types.
  • Failures: ClassNotFoundException comes from an explicit lookup like Class.forName; NoClassDefFoundError means it compiled but is missing or failed to initialize at run time.

Senior Notes

  • Custom loaders power plugin systems, app servers (Tomcat per-webapp loaders) and hot reload, but they can leak: a loader lives as long as any of its classes or instances.
  • Context class loader: Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader() lets framework code (JDBC, ServiceLoader) see application classes.
  • Diagnosis: use -verbose:class or -Xlog:class+load to see where each class came from.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical class loading mistakes:

  • ClassCastException with the same name: the two classes came from different loaders; load the shared type from a common parent.
  • Wrong context loader: a framework cannot see your classes; set the context loader around the call.
  • Duplicate jars: two versions on the classpath, the first one wins; find it with -Xlog:class+load.
  • Unclosed URLClassLoader: keeps jar files locked and classes alive.
  • Static singletons in a shared parent: they hold references to child loader classes and leak them.
  • Catching Throwable around init: a failed static initializer gives NoClassDefFoundError on later uses and hides the first cause.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Class loading costs startup time, so tune it deliberately.

  • Fewer classes: trim dependencies and avoid reflection-heavy startup.
  • AppCDS: -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit and -XX:SharedArchiveFile map pre-parsed classes and cut startup.
  • JDK 19+: -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive creates and refreshes the archive automatically.
  • Parallel loading: loaders that register as parallel capable lock per class name instead of per loader.
  • Lazy init: keep static initializers cheap.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a servlet container redeploys a web app and memory climbs each time.

  • Cause: a library in the shared parent loader keeps a thread or static map pointing at the webapp classes.
  • Symptom: loader count and loaded class count grow after each redeploy.
  • Fix: stop threads and deregister drivers in a shutdown hook (ServletContextListener), and keep such libraries inside the webapp.

What are Runtime Data Areas?

When a Java program runs, the JVM doesn't just execute instructions - it also needs places in memory to store objects, method calls, variables, and class information. These memory regions are collectively called the Runtime Data Areas.

Think of them as different "rooms" inside the JVM's memory, each with a specific job.

The Five Main Areas

• Heap - stores all objects created with new. Shared by the whole application.
• Stack - stores method calls and local variables. Each thread gets its own stack.
• Method Area (Metaspace) - stores class-level information like class structure, method code, and static variables. Shared across the application.
• PC Register - a tiny area that tracks which instruction a thread is currently executing. Each thread gets its own.
• Native Method Stack - similar to the regular Stack, but for native (non-Java) method calls.

Shared vs Per-Thread Areas

This distinction is important and comes up a lot:

AreaShared or Per-Thread?
HeapShared (one per JVM)
Method Area / MetaspaceShared (one per JVM)
StackPer-Thread (one for each thread)
PC RegisterPer-Thread (one for each thread)
Native Method StackPer-Thread (one for each thread)

A Quick Mental Model

When you call a method that creates an object:
• The method call itself (its local variables, parameters) goes on that thread's Stack.
• The object created inside the method goes on the shared Heap.
• The class definition for that object's type lives in the Method Area.

This is why an object can keep existing on the Heap even after the method that created it has finished and its stack frame has been removed - as long as something else still references it.

Fresher Notes

  • Runtime data areas are the memory regions the JVM manages: heap, method area (metaspace), thread stacks, PC registers and native method stacks.
  • Shared versus per-thread: heap and method area are shared by all threads; stack, PC register and native stack belong to one thread each.
  • Objects live on the heap; local variables and call frames live on the stack; class metadata lives in metaspace.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The specification divides memory by lifetime and sharing.

  • Per JVM: heap, method area and run-time constant pools, created at startup.
  • Per thread: PC register, Java stack and native method stack, created with the thread.
  • Frames: pushed on call, popped on return; each has locals, an operand stack and a constant pool reference.
  • Beyond the spec: HotSpot adds code cache, GC bookkeeping, symbol tables and direct memory.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Memory flags per area:

  • Heap: -Xms, -Xmx, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage.
  • Stack: -Xss.
  • Metaspace: -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
  • Code cache: -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize.
  • Direct buffers: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize.
  • Tracking: -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary|detail.

   |   +----------------+   +--------------------------+  |

   |   |                |   |   vars, runtime const pool)|  |

   |                                                       |

Comparison Table: All Five Areas at a Glance

AreaScopeStoresCan it throw OutOfMemoryError?Tuning Flag
HeapSharedObjects, instance variables, arraysYes - java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space-Xms / -Xmx
StackPer-ThreadStack frames, local variables, partial results, call chainStackOverflowError (and OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread)-Xss
Method Area / MetaspaceSharedClass metadata, static variables, runtime constant poolYes - java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace-XX:MetaspaceSize / -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize
PC RegisterPer-ThreadAddress of the currently executing JVM instructionNo - fixed tiny sizeNot tunable
Native Method StackPer-ThreadFrames for native (JNI/C/C++) method callsYes - StackOverflowError or OutOfMemoryError depending on JVM implementationJVM/OS dependent

Why the Shared/Per-Thread Split Matters in Production

This split directly explains real production behavior:
• A memory leak from objects that are never dereferenced grows the Heap and eventually causes a full-application OutOfMemoryError that affects every thread.
• A single runaway recursive method only blows up that one thread's Stack (StackOverflowError) - other threads keep running unaffected.
• Loading thousands of dynamically generated classes (common with heavy reflection/proxy frameworks) pressures the shared Method Area/Metaspace, which can bring down the whole JVM even though the Heap looks perfectly healthy.

Common Misconceptions

• "Local variables live on the Heap." Wrong - primitive local variables and object references live on the Stack; only the actual objects they point to live on the Heap.
• "More threads only cost Heap memory." Wrong - every new thread also claims its own Stack, PC Register, and Native Method Stack, which is why creating unbounded threads can itself cause an OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread, separate from Heap exhaustion.
• "The Method Area is part of the Heap." Historically debated - the JVM spec treats it as a logically distinct area, and since Java 8 it's physically implemented as Metaspace in native (non-heap) memory.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Name the five main JVM runtime data areas.Heap, Stack, Method Area/Metaspace, PC Register, Native Method Stack
Which areas are shared across all threads?Heap and Method Area/Metaspace
Which areas are created per-thread?Stack, PC Register, and Native Method Stack
Where do objects created with 'new' live?On the Heap
Where do local variables and method call frames live?On the thread's Stack
Which area stores static variables and class metadata?The Method Area (Metaspace since Java 8)
Why can one thread's infinite recursion not crash other threads' execution directly?Because each thread has its own independent Stack, so a StackOverflowError is isolated to that thread
What does the PC Register track?The address of the JVM instruction currently being executed by that thread

Mid-Level Notes

  • PC register holds the address of the bytecode instruction the thread executes next.
  • Frame contents: local variable array, operand stack and a reference to the run-time constant pool of the current class.
  • Different errors: StackOverflowError for stacks, OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space for heap, OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace for class metadata.

Senior Notes

  • Beyond the spec: real JVMs also use code cache (JIT output), direct buffers, thread stacks and GC structures that are outside the heap.
  • Footprint of a process is larger than -Xmx; plan container limits with this in mind.
  • Tools: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary shows each area.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Sizing container limit equal to Xmx: leave room for non-heap, often 25 to 50 percent extra.
  • Thinking all objects are on the heap: escape analysis can remove allocations.
  • Mixing up errors: each area has its own error and its own fix.
  • Raising Xmx for a leak: it only delays the failure.
  • Ignoring thread count: every platform thread costs stack memory.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance relevant points:

  • Stack access is very fast; heap allocation is fast but feeds the collector.
  • Reduce allocation in hot paths to cut GC work.
  • Direct memory avoids a copy for I/O but is not managed by the heap collector.
  • Fewer threads or virtual threads reduce stack footprint.
  • Measure with JFR rather than guessing.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a Spring service in Kubernetes is restarted with reason OOMKilled while heap graphs look healthy.

  • Check: heap max, metaspace, thread count, direct memory.
  • Finding: 600 threads at 1 MB stack plus Netty direct buffers filled the gap.
  • Fix: cap thread pools, set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, lower MaxRAMPercentage.

beginner.content:
What is the Heap?

The Heap is the area of JVM memory where all objects live - every time you write new, the object is created on the Heap. Unlike the Stack, the Heap is shared by every thread in the application.

A Simple Example

Every object created here is placed on the Heap, no matter which method or thread creates it.

Young Generation and Old Generation

The Heap isn't one big blob of memory - it's divided into generations, based on the idea that most objects die young:

• Young Generation - where all new objects are created. Further split into:
  • Eden - brand new objects are born here.
  • Survivor 0 (S0) and Survivor 1 (S1) - objects that survive a garbage collection in Eden get moved here.
• Old Generation (Tenured) - objects that survive many garbage collections in the Young Generation get "promoted" here, since they're likely to be long-lived.

Controlling Heap Size with -Xms and -Xmx

You can control how much memory the Heap starts with and how much it can grow to, using JVM startup flags:

• -Xms<size> - the initial Heap size.
• -Xmx<size> - the maximum Heap size the JVM is allowed to use.

Example: java -Xms256m -Xmx1024m MyApp starts with a 256 MB heap and allows it to grow up to 1024 MB.

What Happens When the Heap Runs Out?

If the application keeps creating objects that can't be garbage collected (because something still references them), the Heap eventually fills up completely. When that happens, the JVM throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space and the application typically crashes.

Fresher Notes

  • Heap is the shared area where all objects and arrays are allocated; the garbage collector reclaims unreachable ones.
  • Sizing flags: -Xms sets the initial heap and -Xmx the maximum.
  • Generations: new objects start in the young generation and long-lived ones move to the old generation.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

HotSpot heap layout (G1, the default since Java 9):

  • Regions: the heap is split into equal regions (1 to 32 MB) labeled Eden, Survivor, Old or Humongous.
  • Allocation: each thread allocates in a private buffer (TLAB) inside Eden, which needs no lock.
  • Minor GC: live objects are copied to survivor or old regions; dead ones are dropped with the region.
  • Mixed GC: after concurrent marking, old regions with most garbage are also collected.
  • Humongous: objects over half a region get dedicated regions.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Heap options by purpose:

  • Size: -Xms, -Xmx, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage.
  • Collector: -XX:+UseG1GC (default), -XX:+UseParallelGC (throughput), -XX:+UseZGC (low pause; generational mode with -XX:+ZGenerational in 21), -XX:+UseSerialGC (tiny apps).
  • Pause goal: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 is the G1 default.
  • Diagnostics: -Xlog:gc*, -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, -XX:HeapDumpPath.

expert.content:
Heap Layout in Detail

                              HEAP
   +--------------------------------------------------------+
   |          Young Generation           |   Old Generation  |
   |  +--------+  +------+  +------+     |                   |
   |  |  Eden  |  |  S0  |  |  S1  |     |     Tenured        |
   |  +--------+  +------+  +------+     |   (long-lived      |
   |  new objects  survivor  survivor    |    objects live    |
   |  born here    space 0   space 1     |    here)           |
   +--------------------------------------------------------+
        Minor GC runs here                Major/Full GC runs here
        (fast, frequent)                  (slower, less frequent)

Object Lifecycle Through the Generations

• A new object is allocated in Eden.
• When Eden fills up, a Minor GC runs: live objects in Eden are copied to an empty Survivor space (say S0), and Eden is cleared.
• On the next Minor GC, live objects from Eden AND S0 are copied to S1, and both Eden and S0 are cleared - the Survivor spaces swap roles each cycle.
• Each time an object survives a GC cycle, its age counter increases. Once it crosses a threshold (default is often 15, tunable via -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold), it gets promoted to the Old Generation.
• Objects in the Old Generation are only cleaned up by a Major/Full GC, which is more expensive because it scans a much larger memory region.

Heap Tuning Flags

FlagPurpose
-Xms<size>Initial Heap size at JVM startup
-Xmx<size>Maximum Heap size the JVM may grow to
-Xmn<size>Size of the Young Generation specifically
-XX:NewRatio=<n>Ratio of Old Generation size to Young Generation size
-XX:SurvivorRatio=<n>Ratio of Eden size to each Survivor space size
-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=<n>How many GC cycles an object survives in Young Gen before promotion to Old Gen

Common Pitfall: Setting -Xms and -Xmx Very Far Apart

If -Xms is much smaller than -Xmx, the JVM has to repeatedly resize (grow) the Heap as the application's memory needs increase, which causes pauses and CPU overhead. In production, it's a common best practice to set -Xms and -Xmx to the same value, so the Heap size is fixed upfront and the JVM doesn't spend time resizing it under load.

Common Misconceptions

• "All objects go straight to the Old Generation." Wrong - almost all objects start in Eden; only long-lived objects get promoted after surviving several GC cycles.
• "A larger Heap always means better performance." Wrong - a very large Heap can mean longer Full GC pause times when it does eventually need cleaning, even if it's cleaned less often.
• "Garbage Collection frees memory immediately when an object goes out of scope." Wrong - the object simply becomes eligible for collection; the actual reclaiming happens later, whenever the GC runs.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is stored on the Heap?All objects and arrays created with 'new', shared across all threads
What are the two main generations of the Heap?Young Generation (Eden + S0 + S1) and Old Generation (Tenured)
What triggers a Minor GC vs a Major/Full GC?Minor GC runs when Eden fills up; Major/Full GC runs when the Old Generation needs cleaning, and is much more expensive
What do -Xms and -Xmx control?-Xms sets the initial Heap size, -Xmx sets the maximum Heap size the JVM may grow to
What error is thrown when the Heap is exhausted?java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Why are there two Survivor spaces instead of one?So live objects can be copied between them each GC cycle, always leaving one Survivor space empty to copy into, which keeps memory compact
Why is it recommended to set -Xms equal to -Xmx in production?To avoid runtime Heap resizing overhead and pauses as the application's memory usage grows
What promotes an object from Young Gen to Old Gen?Surviving a configured number of GC cycles (tenuring threshold) without being collected

Mid-Level Notes

  • Young gen holds Eden plus two survivor spaces; a minor GC copies live objects out of Eden.
  • Promotion: objects that survive enough collections (the tenuring threshold) move to the old generation.
  • OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space means live data does not fit in -Xmx even after a full collection.

Senior Notes

  • G1 is the default collector since Java 9; it splits the heap into regions and targets a pause goal with -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis.
  • Set Xms equal to Xmx on servers to avoid resize pauses; in containers prefer -XX:MaxRAMPercentage.
  • Evidence first: use GC logs (-Xlog:gc*) and heap dumps (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError) before changing flags.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical heap problems:

  • Unbounded caches: a static HashMap that only grows; use a size-bounded cache with eviction.
  • Listeners never removed: registered objects stay reachable.
  • ThreadLocal in pools: values stay as long as the pooled thread.
  • Loading whole result sets or files: stream or page instead.
  • Calling System.gc(): remove it, or disable with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning steps that work in practice:

  • Measure the live set after full or mixed GC; heap should be about 2 to 4 times that.
  • Reduce allocation rate before tuning flags.
  • Avoid boxing and temporary strings in hot loops.
  • Set Xms equal to Xmx for stable servers.
  • Change one flag at a time and compare GC logs or JFR.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order service shows steadily growing old generation and a restart every few days.

  • Step 1: dump the heap while it is high.
  • Step 2: open in MAT and check the dominator tree.
  • Finding: a static map of sessions never cleaned.
  • Fix: expire entries and add a test that checks the size stays bounded.

beginner.content:
What is the Stack?

The Stack is the area of JVM memory that keeps track of method calls. Every time a method is called, a new block of memory called a stack frame is pushed onto the Stack; when the method finishes, that frame is popped off.

Unlike the Heap, every thread gets its own private Stack - one thread's Stack is never visible to another thread.

What Lives in a Stack Frame?

Each stack frame holds everything a method needs while it's running:
• Local variables (including method parameters)
• Partial results of expressions being calculated
• Information needed to return control to the calling method

A Simple Example

Watch how methods stack on top of each other as they call one another.

StackOverflowError

The Stack is not unlimited - if too many methods call each other without returning (most commonly from uncontrolled recursion), the Stack runs out of space and the JVM throws a StackOverflowError.

Controlling Stack Size with -Xss

Just like the Heap has -Xmx, the Stack has its own size flag: -Xss<size>. It sets the maximum stack size for each thread. Example: java -Xss512k MyApp gives each thread a 512 KB stack.

Fresher Notes

  • Thread stack: every thread has its own stack made of frames, one frame per method call.
  • Frame holds local variables, the operand stack and return information; it is removed when the method returns.
  • StackOverflowError happens when calls nest too deep, usually from missing base case in recursion.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a call uses the stack:

  • Invoke: the JVM pushes a new frame sized at compile time (max locals plus max operand stack).
  • Arguments become the first local slots; this is slot 0 for instance methods.
  • Return: the result moves to the caller operand stack and the frame is popped.
  • Exceptions: unwinding pops frames until a handler matches.
  • JIT: compiled frames use machine registers and can inline callees, so the visible depth differs from bytecode.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controlling stack size and depth:

  • Global: -Xss512k or -XX:ThreadStackSize=512.
  • Per thread: the stackSize argument of the Thread constructor, a hint the JVM may ignore.
  • Executor threads: pass a custom ThreadFactory to set it.
  • Virtual threads (Java 21): no fixed stack size; limited by heap.
  • Main thread: stack size is set by the launcher, -Xss applies.

expert.content:
Stack Frame Internals

Each stack frame the JVM pushes actually contains three logical parts: 

Thread's Stack (grows downward with each call)
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  Frame: main()                                     |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  Frame: methodA()                                  |
|   - Local Variable Array  (params + local vars)    |
|   - Operand Stack (scratch space for computation)  |
|   - Frame Data (return address, reference to        |
|                 the constant pool of this class)   |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  Frame: methodB()  <-- currently executing          |
+--------------------------------------------------+
The topmost frame always corresponds to the method currently executing; when it returns, its frame is popped and control (and any return value) goes back to the frame below it.

Stack vs Heap - Key Differences

AspectStackHeap
ScopePer-thread (private)Shared by all threads
StoresLocal variables, method call frames, referencesActual objects and arrays
Allocation speedVery fast (just move a pointer)Slower (needs GC bookkeeping)
LifetimeTied to the method call - freed automatically on returnTied to reachability - freed by Garbage Collector whenever it's no longer referenced
Failure modeStackOverflowErrorOutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Tuning flag-Xss-Xms / -Xmx

What Actually Happens on StackOverflowError

When the JVM tries to push a new frame but the thread's Stack has no room left, it throws StackOverflowError immediately - it does not try to grow the Stack automatically (unlike the Heap, which can grow up to -Xmx). Production causes typically fall into two buckets:
• A genuine bug - unbounded or incorrectly-based recursion (missing/broken base case).
• A legitimately deep call chain (e.g. deeply nested JSON/XML parsing, or a very deep object graph being processed recursively) that simply needs more Stack space, tunable via -Xss.

Common Pitfall: Increasing -Xss to "Fix" StackOverflowError

Bumping -Xss can mask a genuine infinite-recursion bug rather than fix it - the program will still eventually overflow, just after more iterations, and each thread now consumes more memory (which matters a lot in high-thread-count applications, since Stack memory is per-thread and multiplies quickly). Always check for a missing/incorrect base case in recursive code first, and only increase -Xss for algorithms that are correctly, intentionally, deeply recursive.

Common Misconceptions

• "Objects created inside a method live on the Stack." Wrong - only the reference variable lives on the Stack; the actual object it points to is always on the Heap.
• "More threads means the Heap runs out faster." Partially wrong - more threads primarily consume more Stack memory (one Stack per thread), which is a separate, common cause of OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread, distinct from Heap exhaustion.
• "StackOverflowError can be safely caught and ignored like a normal exception." Risky - by the time it's thrown, the Stack is nearly exhausted, so the catch block itself may have very little Stack space left to execute safely.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is stored in a stack frame?Local variables, method parameters, the operand stack for expression evaluation, and the return address
Is the Stack shared across threads?No - each thread has its own private Stack
What causes StackOverflowError?Too many nested/recursive method calls exceeding the thread's Stack capacity, most commonly from unbounded recursion
What flag controls the Stack size?-Xss
Does the Stack grow automatically like the Heap?No - if it runs out of space, the JVM throws StackOverflowError immediately rather than growing it
Where does an object created with 'new' inside a method actually live?On the Heap - only its reference variable lives on the Stack
Why might increasing -Xss be the wrong fix for StackOverflowError?It can mask a genuine infinite-recursion bug and increases per-thread memory cost, which adds up quickly with many threads
What happens to a stack frame when its method returns?It is popped off the Stack immediately and its memory is reclaimed

Mid-Level Notes

  • Primitives and references are stored in the frame; the objects behind references are in the heap.
  • Thread safety: locals are private to a thread, so they need no synchronization unless a reference escapes.
  • Stack size is set with -Xss (or new Thread(group, run, name, stackSize)); the default on 64-bit Linux is typically 1 MB.

Senior Notes

  • Escape analysis: the JIT can allocate a non-escaping object in registers or on the stack (scalar replacement), so short-lived objects may cost nothing.
  • Cost of threads: many platform threads reserve many MB of stack; Java 21 virtual threads keep stacks on the heap and grow on demand.
  • Diagnosis: jstack or jcmd Thread.print shows each stack; deep recursion or lock waits are visible there.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common stack mistakes:

  • Missing base case: add it and test with small and large inputs.
  • Mutual recursion: A calls B calls A without progress.
  • Recursive toString or equals on cyclic object graphs.
  • Huge Xss for all threads: memory is reserved per thread.
  • Assuming tail-call optimization: Java does not do it, so deep recursion needs a loop.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Small methods are inlined, so call depth costs little once hot.
  • Smaller Xss lets you run more threads in the same memory.
  • Escape analysis can keep short-lived objects out of the heap.
  • Thread dumps are cheap and safe, take several 5 to 10 seconds apart.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a JSON parser endpoint crashes with StackOverflowError on deeply nested input from clients.

  • Risk: attacker-controlled depth is a denial-of-service vector.
  • Fix: enforce a maximum nesting depth in the parser and reject the request with a 400 response.
  • Backup: catch the error at the request boundary and log the input size only.

What is the Method Area?

The Method Area is the part of JVM memory that stores information about the classes themselves, rather than the objects created from them. It is shared by all threads in the application, just like the Heap.

What is Stored in the Method Area?

• Class structure - the class's name, its parent class, and which interfaces it implements.
• Method code - the actual compiled bytecode for every method in the class.
• Static variables - fields declared with the static keyword, since they belong to the class itself, not to any one object.
• Runtime Constant Pool - a table of constants (literals, references) used by the class, resolved at runtime.

A Simple Example

Static variables are a good example of something stored in the Method Area rather than on the Heap with regular objects.

Method Area vs Heap

It's easy to confuse these two shared areas, but they store different things:

• The Method Area stores information about the class - one copy per class, no matter how many objects of that class exist.
• The Heap stores the actual objects (instances) - a separate copy for every single object created with new.

Fresher Notes

  • Method area is the shared region that stores per-class data: class structure, field and method info, method bytecode and static metadata.
  • Run-time constant pool belongs to each class and holds literals and symbolic references resolved at link time.
  • Logical area: the spec defines it; HotSpot implements it as metaspace in native memory since Java 8.

Worked Example 1

Count loaded classes.

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What the method area holds for each loaded class:

  • Class structure: name, super type, interfaces, modifiers.
  • Members: field and method descriptors, bytecode, exception tables.
  • Run-time constant pool: literals and symbolic references, resolved lazily.
  • Statics: in HotSpot the static reference values sit in the heap inside the Class mirror.
  • Vtables and itables for dispatch.
  • Implementation: metaspace in native memory, allocated per class loader.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to look at method area data:

  • Reflection: getDeclaredFields, getDeclaredMethods.
  • javap: -c code, -v constant pool, -p private members.
  • MXBean: ClassLoadingMXBean for counts.
  • jcmd: VM.classloader_stats, VM.metaspace, GC.class_histogram.
  • Logging: -Xlog:class+unload shows unloading.

expert.content:
Method Area Contents, In Detail

                    Method Area (one region per JVM, shared)
   +------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  For each loaded class:                                     |
   |    - Fully qualified class name, superclass, interfaces      |
   |    - Access modifiers (public/final/abstract/...)            |
   |    - Method bytecode + method signatures                     |
   |    - Field information (names, types, modifiers)             |
   |    - Static variables (class-level, one copy per class)      |
   |    - Runtime Constant Pool (literals, symbolic references     |
   |      to other classes/methods/fields, resolved lazily)       |
   |    - Reference to the ClassLoader that loaded this class      |
   +------------------------------------------------------------+

Runtime Constant Pool Explained

Every compiled .class file has a constant pool - a table of numeric literals, string literals, and symbolic references to classes/fields/methods that the code uses. When the class is loaded, the JVM copies this into the Runtime Constant Pool inside the Method Area, and resolves symbolic references (e.g. "call method X on class Y") into direct memory references as needed.

This is also where interned String literals conceptually tie in - the String Pool is closely related to (and in modern JVMs physically resides in) the Heap, but its entries are referenced from constant pools in the Method Area.

Method Area vs Heap vs Metaspace - Comparison

AspectMethod AreaHeap
What it storesClass metadata, method bytecode, static variables, runtime constant poolObject instances and arrays
Copies per classOne (shared across all instances)Many (one per object created)
Java 7 and earlier implementationPermGen (part of Heap, fixed size)Heap
Java 8+ implementationMetaspace (native memory, not part of Heap)Heap
Garbage collected?Yes, but only when the defining ClassLoader itself becomes unreachableYes, per normal GC rules for unreachable objects

Note: the Method Area is a logical concept defined by the JVM Specification; Metaspace is simply how HotSpot (the mainstream JVM) implements that concept since Java 8. The next topic covers Metaspace specifically.

What Happens When the Method Area Runs Out

Because static variables and class metadata for every loaded class sit in the Method Area, applications that dynamically generate huge numbers of classes at runtime (heavy reflection, dynamic proxies, some ORM/ AOP frameworks, or classes that are loaded but never unloaded by leaking class loaders) can exhaust it. In Java 7 and earlier this surfaced as java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space; from Java 8 onward it surfaces as java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace.

Common Misconceptions

• "Static variables live on the Heap with regular instance fields." Wrong - static variables belong to the class itself and are stored in the Method Area, not per-object. Note that since JDK 7 the static field VALUES live on the heap, attached to the java.lang.Class mirror - the Method Area holds the class metadata and bytecode.
• "The Method Area is never garbage collected." Wrong - class metadata can be collected, but only when its entire defining ClassLoader becomes unreachable, which is much rarer than ordinary object collection on the Heap.
• "Method Area and Metaspace are two different things." Not quite - Method Area is the JVM Specification's logical concept; Metaspace is HotSpot's concrete implementation of it since Java 8.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does the Method Area store?Class-level metadata: class structure, method bytecode, static variables, and the runtime constant pool
How many copies of a static variable exist for a class?Exactly one, shared by all instances of that class
Is the Method Area shared across threads?Yes, like the Heap, it is shared by the entire JVM/application
What is the Runtime Constant Pool?A per-class table of literals and symbolic references, copied from the compiled .class file's constant pool and resolved at runtime
How is the Method Area implemented before vs after Java 8?Before Java 8 it was PermGen, a fixed-size part of the Heap; from Java 8 onward it is Metaspace, allocated from native memory
Is Method Area content ever garbage collected?Yes, but only when the ClassLoader that defined those classes becomes completely unreachable
Why do heavy reflection/proxy frameworks risk Method Area exhaustion?They can dynamically generate very large numbers of classes at runtime, filling up the shared Method Area/Metaspace
Where do instance (non-static) fields live?On the Heap, as part of each individual object, not in the Method Area

Mid-Level Notes

  • Static variables: the static field slot is tied to the class mirror, and in modern HotSpot the static object values live in the heap inside the Class object.
  • String literals are interned in the String table, which is on the heap since Java 7.
  • Per class loader: class metadata is allocated per loader and freed when the loader is collected.

Senior Notes

  • Not the same as PermGen: PermGen was a fixed-size heap-like region removed in Java 8, which also removed -XX:MaxPermSize.
  • Code cache is separate: JIT-compiled native code is not in the method area.
  • Inspect with jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats and jcmd <pid> GC.class_stats style tools, or jmap -clstats.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical confusions and mistakes:

  • Calling it PermGen: PermGen no longer exists; the flag -XX:MaxPermSize is ignored with a warning.
  • Putting strings in the method area: the String table is in the heap.
  • Assuming static means immortal: statics die with their class loader.
  • Creating a class per request with dynamic proxies without caching.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance points:

  • Class Data Sharing keeps JDK class metadata in a shared mapped archive, so startup is faster and memory is shared between JVMs.
  • Fewer classes means less metaspace and quicker startup.
  • Cache generated classes (proxies, lambdas are fine, they are linked via invokedynamic).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a service that uses a scripting engine for rules loads a new script class on every evaluation.

  • Symptom: loaded class count rises steadily.
  • Fix: compile each script once and cache the compiled object by script hash.

What is Metaspace?

Metaspace is the area of memory where the JVM stores class metadata - things like class structure, method bytecode, and static variables. It was introduced in Java 8 to replace an older area called PermGen (Permanent Generation).

Why Did Java Replace PermGen with Metaspace?

Before Java 8, class metadata lived in PermGen, which was part of the Heap and had a fixed maximum size set at JVM startup. Applications that loaded lots of classes at runtime (common with big frameworks like Spring, Hibernate, and application servers) would frequently run out of PermGen space and crash with OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space - even if there was plenty of free Heap memory otherwise.

Metaspace fixed this by moving class metadata out of the Heap entirely, into native memory (memory managed by the operating system, outside the JVM's Heap), which can grow much more flexibly.

A Simple Example

Every class you load, including ones generated dynamically, consumes some Metaspace.

Controlling Metaspace Size

Just like the Heap has -Xms/-Xmx, Metaspace has its own flags:

• -XX:MetaspaceSize=<size> - the initial threshold at which a garbage collection is triggered to clean up unused class metadata.
• -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=<size> - the maximum size Metaspace is allowed to grow to. By default, this is unlimited (only bounded by available system memory), unless you set it explicitly.

Fresher Notes

  • Metaspace stores class metadata in native memory; it replaced PermGen in Java 8.
  • Grows by default: unlike PermGen, metaspace is not capped unless you set -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
  • Error: OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace means too many or too large classes for the limit or for the machine.

Worked Example 1

Exhaust metaspace with generated classes.

Worked Example 2

Watch class count and loaders.

Practice Exercise 1

Read metaspace usage.

Practice Exercise 2

Cap metaspace.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How metaspace manages memory:

  • Native memory: memory is reserved from the OS in virtual space and committed as needed.
  • Per loader arenas: each class loader allocates metadata chunks in its own arena.
  • Release: when a loader is unloaded its arena is returned to the free lists.
  • Compressed class space: a separate region (default 1 GB reserved) for class pointers when compressed class pointers are on.
  • High-water mark: crossing MetaspaceSize triggers a GC to unload classes.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Metaspace flags:

  • -XX:MetaspaceSize: first GC threshold.
  • -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize: hard cap, unlimited by default.
  • -XX:MinMetaspaceFreeRatio and -XX:MaxMetaspaceFreeRatio: how much free space to keep after a collection.
  • -XX:CompressedClassSpaceSize: class space size.
  • -XX:+UseCompressedClassPointers: on by default for heaps under the 32 GB class limit and in general on 64-bit.

expert.content:
PermGen vs Metaspace

AspectPermGen (Java 7 and earlier)Metaspace (Java 8+)
Memory locationPart of the Heap (contiguous JVM-managed memory)Native memory (managed by the OS, outside the Heap)
Default max sizeFixed at startup (small default, e.g. 64-82 MB depending on platform)Unlimited by default - grows until system memory is exhausted
ResizingCannot grow past the fixed max without a restartCan grow/shrink dynamically as classes load/unload
Common failureOutOfMemoryError: PermGen space (very common in app servers)OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace (rarer, but possible if MaxMetaspaceSize is set or system memory runs out)
GC behaviorCollected as part of Full GC, tightly coupled to Heap GC cyclesCollected somewhat independently, triggered by MetaspaceSize threshold

Metaspace Internal Layout

      JVM Process Memory
   +---------------------------------------------------+
   |   Heap (-Xms / -Xmx bounded)                        |
   |     Young Gen | Old Gen                              |
   +---------------------------------------------------+
   |   Native (non-Heap) Memory                           |
   |     +-------------------------------------------+   |
   |     |  Metaspace (-XX:MetaspaceSize /             |   |
   |     |              -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize)          |   |
   |     |    - Class metadata                          |   |
   |     |    - Method bytecode                         |   |
   |     |    - Runtime constant pools                  |   |
   |     +-------------------------------------------+   |
   |     Thread stacks, JIT compiled code cache, etc.     |
   +---------------------------------------------------+
Static variables themselves actually moved to the Heap starting in Java 8 (as part of the corresponding Class object), while the class structure/bytecode metadata moved to Metaspace - a subtlety worth knowing beyond "it's just PermGen renamed."

What Happens When Metaspace Runs Out

If -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize is set and reached (or, without that flag, if the OS itself runs out of available native memory), the JVM throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. Common production causes:
• Classloader leaks - repeatedly redeploying an application (common in application servers) without the old ClassLoader and its classes ever becoming eligible for collection, so metadata accumulates release after release.
• Frameworks that generate huge numbers of dynamic proxy/CGLIB classes at runtime without bound.
• Leaving -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize unset on a shared/constrained host, letting Metaspace silently consume memory that other processes on the machine needed, potentially triggering the OS's own OOM killer instead of a clean JVM error.

Production Tip: Always Set MaxMetaspaceSize in Containers

Because Metaspace defaults to unlimited, it's easy to forget it needs a ceiling - especially in containerized environments (Docker/Kubernetes) with a hard memory limit. Without -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize, a classloader leak can silently grow Metaspace until the container's memory limit is hit, and the container runtime kills the whole JVM process outright (OOMKilled) with no Java-level stack trace to debug from - far worse than a clean OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace that at least leaves a diagnosable log entry.

Common Misconceptions

• "Metaspace is just PermGen renamed." Wrong - it changed memory location entirely (native memory instead of Heap) and its default sizing behavior (unbounded instead of a small fixed cap).
• "Metaspace can never run out of memory." Wrong - it's unbounded by default but still limited by total system memory, and can be explicitly capped with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
• "Static variables are stored in Metaspace." Wrong since Java 8 - static variable values live on the Heap (attached to the Class object); Metaspace holds the class's structural metadata and bytecode.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What replaced PermGen, and in which Java version?Metaspace, introduced in Java 8
Where does Metaspace physically live in memory?In native memory, managed by the OS, outside the JVM Heap
What is the default maximum size of Metaspace?Unlimited by default - bounded only by available system memory, unless -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize is set
Why was PermGen replaced?Its fixed, small default size caused frequent OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space in applications that loaded many classes dynamically
What flags control Metaspace sizing?-XX:MetaspaceSize (GC trigger threshold) and -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize (hard cap)
What commonly causes Metaspace exhaustion in production?ClassLoader leaks from repeated hot redeployments, or frameworks generating unbounded dynamic proxy classes
Why is it risky to leave -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize unset in a Docker container?Metaspace can grow until the container's memory limit is hit, causing an OOMKilled container crash instead of a diagnosable Java OutOfMemoryError
Did static variables also move to Metaspace in Java 8?No - static variable values moved to live on the Heap attached to the Class object; Metaspace holds structural class metadata and bytecode

Mid-Level Notes

  • Flags: -XX:MetaspaceSize is the size at which the first metaspace GC is triggered, not a reservation.
  • Freed per loader: memory comes back only when a class loader and all its classes are unloaded.
  • Typical causes: endless generated classes (proxies, bytecode libraries, scripting) and redeploy leaks.

Senior Notes

  • Always set a cap in containers, for example -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m, so a leak fails fast with a clear error instead of consuming node memory.
  • Compressed class space (-XX:CompressedClassSpaceSize, default 1 GB) holds class pointers separately and can run out first.
  • Monitor with jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace and the MXBean pool named Metaspace.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Metaspace mistakes:

  • No cap in containers: a leak eats node memory instead of failing clearly.
  • Cap too small: large apps with many frameworks need 150 to 400 MB; measure first.
  • Confusing MetaspaceSize with a limit.
  • Generating classes in a loop with CGLIB, ASM or scripting without caching.
  • Leaking loaders through threads, ThreadLocals, JDBC drivers and shutdown hooks.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Operational guidance:

  • Watch the trend of used metaspace and loaded classes, not a single number.
  • Alert when metaspace grows without a plateau after warm-up.
  • Headroom: set the cap about 1.5 to 2 times the steady value.
  • Compare class histogram snapshots to see growing class families.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an app server shows OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace after the fifth redeploy.

  • Investigate: loader stats before and after a redeploy; old webapp loaders remain.
  • Root cause: a library thread started by the webapp still runs.
  • Fix: stop the thread on undeploy, then confirm loaders drop after a GC.

What is the PC Register?

The PC (Program Counter) Register is a very small piece of memory that keeps track of exactly which instruction the JVM is currently executing for a given thread.

Think of it like a bookmark - it remembers "where we are" in the bytecode, so after finishing one instruction the JVM knows exactly which one to execute next.

One PC Register Per Thread

Every thread running inside the JVM gets its own private PC Register. This makes sense - if two threads are running different methods at the same time, each one needs its own separate "bookmark" to track its own progress independently of the other.

A Simple Example

You never interact with the PC Register directly in Java code, but conceptually, it's what lets execution resume correctly after a method call returns.

What About Native Methods?

If the current method being executed is a native method (implemented in C/C++, not Java bytecode), the PC Register's value is undefined - because native code isn't made of JVM bytecode instructions, there's nothing meaningful for the PC Register to point to.

Fresher Notes

  • One per thread: every Java thread has its own program counter, so threads can run different code at the same time.
  • What it holds: the address (bytecode index) of the JVM instruction the thread will run next.
  • Not for you: you cannot read or change it from Java code; the JVM updates it after each instruction.

Worked Example 1

Find the line from a stack trace.

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

See bytecode offsets with javap.

Practice Exercise 2

Two threads, two positions.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The PC register tracks execution per thread.

  • Interpreter: after each bytecode the JVM advances the bytecode index (bci) of the current frame.
  • Frames: each frame also remembers its own return bci, so after a call returns the caller continues where it stopped.
  • JIT code: compiled methods use machine program counters, and the JVM keeps debug maps back to bytecode indexes for stack traces and deoptimization.
  • Exceptions: the exception table maps a bci range to a handler bci.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools that expose the PC / bytecode index:

  • javap -c: bytecode with offsets.
  • javap -l: line and local variable tables.
  • jstack and jcmd Thread.print: show the current line of each thread.
  • -XX:+PrintAssembly: compiled code (needs the hsdis library).
  • Debuggers (JDWP): use the bci to place breakpoints.

expert.content:
Why the PC Register Exists

The JVM is a stack-based, bytecode-interpreting (or JIT-compiling) machine. To execute a method's bytecode correctly, something must track "which bytecode instruction comes next" for each thread - especially since threads can be paused and resumed by the OS scheduler at any point. The PC Register is exactly that per-thread bookkeeping slot, holding the address of the JVM instruction currently being executed.

PC Register vs Other Runtime Data Areas

AspectPC RegisterStack
SizeTiny - holds essentially one address/valueConfigurable, can be sizable (KB to MB)
ScopePer-threadPer-thread
PurposeTracks the current bytecode instruction addressTracks method call frames, local variables
Tunable via JVM flags?NoYes (-Xss)
Can it overflow / cause OutOfMemoryError?No - it's a fixed, tiny slot, not a growable regionYes - StackOverflowError

PC Register During Context Switching

Thread T1:  PC -> instruction #42  (executing, gets paused by OS scheduler)
Thread T2:  PC -> instruction #7   (resumes, continues from its own bookmark)
...later, OS scheduler resumes T1...
Thread T1:  PC -> instruction #42  (still correctly points where T1 left off)
Because each thread has its own isolated PC Register, the JVM (and underlying OS scheduler) can freely pause and resume threads without any thread losing track of its execution position - this is fundamental to how multithreading works correctly at the bytecode-execution level.

Common Misconceptions

• "The PC Register is something developers can read or modify." Wrong - it's entirely internal to the JVM's execution engine; there's no Java API to inspect or change it directly.
• "The PC Register can run out of memory." Wrong - it's a fixed-size, tiny piece of per-thread state (conceptually similar to a CPU's own program counter register), not a growable memory region, so it has no corresponding "out of memory" failure mode.
• "Every JVM instruction execution updates the PC Register the same way for native and Java methods." Wrong - for native methods, the PC Register's value is left undefined, since there's no JVM bytecode instruction sequence being tracked.

Why This Matters for Interviews (Even Though It's Rarely Discussed)

The PC Register is one of the smallest and least "interesting" runtime data areas, but it's frequently used as a quick check of whether a candidate actually understands all five JVM runtime data areas (not just Heap and Stack), and whether they understand the per-thread vs shared distinction correctly across all of them.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does the PC Register store?The address of the JVM instruction currently being executed by that thread
Is the PC Register shared across threads?No - each thread has its own private PC Register
What happens to the PC Register value when executing a native method?Its value is left undefined, since native methods aren't made of JVM bytecode instructions
Can the PC Register be tuned with a JVM flag like -Xss or -Xmx?No - it has a fixed, minimal size that isn't user-configurable
Can the PC Register overflow and throw an error?No - unlike the Stack or Heap, it's not a growable memory region, so it has no corresponding OutOfMemoryError
Why does each thread need its own PC Register?So the OS scheduler can pause and resume threads independently, with each thread resuming exactly where it left off in its own bytecode execution
Is the PC Register part of the Heap or Method Area?No - it's a separate, per-thread runtime data area, distinct from both shared areas
Does application code ever read or write the PC Register directly?No - it's managed entirely internally by the JVM's execution engine

Mid-Level Notes

  • Context switch: when the OS pauses a thread, its PC register value is saved so the thread resumes at the exact instruction.
  • Native methods: while a thread runs native code, the PC value of that thread is undefined.
  • Line numbers: stack traces show source lines because the JVM maps the bytecode index to a line using the LineNumberTable.

Senior Notes

  • No OutOfMemoryError: the specification lists the PC register as the only runtime area with no defined out-of-memory condition.
  • Real hardware: HotSpot keeps the equivalent state in real CPU registers and thread structures, and the JIT-compiled code uses machine addresses.
  • Debugging: debuggers and profilers use bytecode index data (see javap -c -l) to place breakpoints and report lines.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Thinking the PC is shared: it is per thread, which is why code position is never lost on a context switch.
  • Expecting OutOfMemoryError from it: it is fixed size; look at heap, metaspace or thread count instead.
  • Trusting line numbers after obfuscation: stripped debug info shows Unknown Source; keep the mapping file.
  • Reading a thread dump as a snapshot of one instant: threads are stopped at safepoints, so the line is the nearest safepoint.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

The PC register itself is never a tuning target, but its effects are:

  • Context switches: far too many runnable threads waste CPU saving and restoring state.
  • Safepoints: threads must reach a safepoint poll; long counted loops delayed this in old JVMs.
  • JIT: hot loops are compiled so the bytecode PC is no longer stepped one instruction at a time.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a production thread seems stuck. Take three thread dumps a few seconds apart.

  • If the same method and line appear each time, that thread is stuck or looping there.
  • If the line changes, the thread is working and the problem is elsewhere.

beginner.content:
What is the Native Method Stack?

The Native Method Stack is a memory area very similar to the regular Stack, except it's used specifically for native methods - methods that are implemented in a language other than Java, usually C or C++.

Just like the regular Stack, every thread gets its own private Native Method Stack.

What is a Native Method?

A native method is declared in Java using the native keyword, but has no method body in Java - its actual implementation lives in a compiled C/C++ library that the JVM loads and calls into. This mechanism is called JNI (Java Native Interface).

Why Does Java Need Native Methods At All?

Most Java code never touches native methods directly, but they're used under the hood for things like:
• Talking directly to the operating system (file I/O, low-level networking).
• Interfacing with hardware or existing C/C++ libraries that have no Java equivalent.
• Performance-critical operations that benefit from direct native execution.

In fact, many familiar JDK classes (like parts of java.io and java.lang.Thread) rely on native methods behind the scenes.

Native Method Stack vs Regular Stack

The two are conceptually the same idea (tracking method calls for a thread), just for different kinds of code:

• The regular Stack tracks calls to Java methods (bytecode).
• The Native Method Stack tracks calls to native methods (compiled C/C++ code).

Fresher Notes

  • Native method: a method declared with native and implemented in C or C++, such as System.currentTimeMillis().
  • Native stack: the memory a thread uses while it runs native code, separate in concept from the Java stack.
  • Loading: System.loadLibrary("name") loads the library; a missing one throws UnsatisfiedLinkError.

An Important Nuance: The JVM Spec Makes This Optional

The JVM Specification does not strictly mandate a separate Native Method Stack - it explicitly allows an implementation to combine it with the regular Stack. This is exactly what Oracle's HotSpot JVM does in practice: Java frames and native frames for a given thread typically coexist on the same underlying OS thread stack, even though the specification describes them as two conceptually distinct areas. Other JVM implementations are free to keep them fully separate.

Production Relevance: Native Crashes Don't Look Like Java Errors

Because native methods run compiled C/C++ code outside the JVM's normal safety net (bounds checking, garbage collection, exception handling), a bug in native code can crash the entire JVM process with a native crash (segfault) rather than a clean, catchable Java exception - producing an hs_err_pidNNNN.log crash file instead of a normal Java stack trace. This is a key reason JNI usage is treated cautiously in production: a bug three layers deep in a native library can take down the whole application instantly, with no chance for application-level error handling to intervene.

Common real-world native-boundary issues:
• A misbehaving native library causing a JVM segfault under load.
• Memory leaks in native code that don't show up in Java heap dumps at all (since they live outside the Heap entirely).
• JNI reference leaks (native code holding onto Java object references so they can never be garbage collected).

Common Misconceptions

• "Every JVM has a physically separate Native Method Stack." Wrong - the JVM Spec permits combining it with the regular Stack, and HotSpot typically does exactly that.
• "Native method bugs always throw a normal Java exception." Wrong - native code bugs can crash the entire JVM process outright (a native crash/segfault), bypassing Java's exception handling completely.
• "Native methods are rare/exotic and irrelevant to typical Java apps." Wrong - many everyday JDK operations (file I/O, threading, some java.lang.Math operations) are backed by native methods under the hood, even if application developers never write native keywords themselves.

  • JNI (Java Native Interface) is the standard bridge between Java and native code, and it needs a header and a compiled library.
  • Crash risk: a bug in native code can kill the whole JVM with a segmentation fault and an hs_err_pid file, not a Java exception.

Senior Notes

  • Native memory (direct buffers, thread stacks, metaspace, JNI allocations) lies outside the heap, so -Xmx does not limit it.
  • Tracking: use -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.
  • Modern bridge: the Foreign Function and Memory API replaces JNI for many cases; it was preview in JDK 21 and final in JDK 22.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong library name or path: UnsatisfiedLinkError; check -Djava.library.path.
  • Wrong signature: the C function name must match the mangled name exactly.
  • Leaking local references: in long native loops, release them with DeleteLocalRef.
  • Blaming the heap: an OOM with free heap may be native memory.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning points:

  • Call cost: a JNI call costs far more than a normal call, so batch work into one native call.
  • Direct buffers: reuse them; allocation and freeing is expensive.
  • Stack size: keep -Xss small for many threads.
  • Limit: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize caps direct buffers.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a service shows a RSS of 6 GB with an -Xmx of 2 GB.

  • Enable NMT and take a baseline, then a diff after load.
  • If Internal or Other grows, suspect direct buffers or a native library.
  • If Thread grows, suspect thread leaks.

beginner.content:
What Happens When You Write new?

Every time you use the new keyword in Java, the JVM does a small sequence of work behind the scenes to build you a brand-new object in memory.

Think of a class as a blueprint (like a house plan) and an object as the actual house built from that plan. The new keyword is the construction crew that turns the plan into a real house sitting on a real plot of land (memory).

The Object Creation Steps

When the JVM executes new Student(), it roughly performs these steps:

• Step 1: Allocate a block of memory on the Heap large enough for the object.
• Step 2: Set all fields to their default values (0, false, null etc).
• Step 3: Run the constructor code to initialize the fields with real values.
• Step 4: Return a reference (memory address) to the newly created object.

Every Object Has a Little "Header" Too

Besides your own fields (rollNumber, name), every object secretly carries a small amount of extra bookkeeping data called the object header. It stores things like:
• A hash code (used by hashCode()).
• Locking information (used when the object is synchronized).
• A pointer back to the object's class (so the JVM knows "this is a Student").

You never access the header directly - it's managed entirely by the JVM - but it's part of why even an "empty" object still takes up some memory.

Default Values Before the Constructor Runs

A common beginner surprise: fields are NOT left "empty" or garbage before your constructor runs. The JVM zeroes them out first (Step 2 above), then your constructor overwrites them.

Each new Creates a Separate Object

Calling new twice always produces two completely independent objects in memory, even if their field values are identical.

Fresher Notes

  • new allocates memory for the object, sets fields to defaults (0, false, null) and then runs the constructor.
  • Where: the object lives on the heap; the variable that points to it lives on the stack (for a local).
  • Size: an object is its header plus its fields plus padding, so a small object is never zero bytes.

  • Class check: the class must be loaded and initialized.
  • Allocation: the fast path bumps the TLAB pointer; if the TLAB is full, a new one is requested, and if the heap is full, a GC runs.
  • Zeroing: memory is cleared, then the header (mark word, class pointer) is set.
  • Constructor: <init> runs and fields get their values.

Ways an object comes into existence:

  • new: the normal way.
  • Class.newInstance / Constructor.newInstance: reflection.

expert.content:
Deep Dive: JVM-Level Object Allocation

At the bytecode level, new Student(101, "Aisha") actually compiles into two separate bytecode instructions:

• new - allocates raw, zeroed memory on the heap for the object and pushes a reference to it onto the operand stack.
• invokespecial - calls the constructor (<init>) on that freshly allocated memory to actually initialize it.

This two-step split matters: the object technically "exists" on the heap (with all-default field values) for a brief moment before the constructor has even started running.

Where Allocation Actually Happens: TLAB

Modern JVMs rarely allocate directly from a shared, lock-protected heap region for every single object - that would cause heavy thread contention. Instead, each thread gets its own small private chunk of the Young Generation called a TLAB (Thread-Local Allocation Buffer).

• Small, short-lived objects are usually "bump allocated" inside the thread's TLAB - just moving a pointer forward, extremely fast, no locking needed.
• When a TLAB fills up, the thread requests a new TLAB from the shared heap (this does need a small amount of synchronization).
• Very large objects (bigger than a threshold) may bypass TLABs and allocate directly in the shared heap, or even go straight to the Old Generation.

Object Layout in Memory

Heap memory for a Student object (conceptual, HotSpot-style)

+------------------------------+
|  Object Header                |
|   - Mark Word (hash, lock)    |
|   - Klass Pointer (-> Class)  |
+------------------------------+
|  Instance Fields               |
|   - int rollNumber = 101       |
|   - String name  -> "Aisha"    |
+------------------------------+
|  Padding (alignment to 8B)     |
+------------------------------+
The header typically costs 12-16 bytes (depending on JVM/compressed-oops settings) before your own fields even start - this is why a "tiny" object is never truly free.

Allocation Strategies Compared

StrategyWhereSpeedUsed For
TLAB bump allocationThread-local slice of EdenVery fast (pointer bump)Small, short-lived objects (most objects)
Shared Eden allocationEden space, synchronizedSlower (contention)When a thread's TLAB is exhausted
Direct Old Gen / humongousOld GenerationSlowest, triggers GC pressureVery large objects, e.g. big arrays
Escape-analyzed scalar replacementStack / registers (no heap at all)Fastest possibleObjects the JIT proves never "escape" a method

Common Bugs and Misconceptions

• "Object creation is basically free." Not true - even fast TLAB allocation still adds GC pressure later; creating millions of short-lived objects in a hot loop (e.g. boxing primitives, building Strings with + in a loop) is a classic performance bug.
• Believing fields hold garbage before the constructor runs. The JVM guarantees zeroing first - you can never see uninitialized garbage memory in Java, unlike C/C++.
• Assuming new always hits the heap. With escape analysis and scalar replacement, the JIT compiler can sometimes eliminate heap allocation entirely for objects proven to stay local to a method.
• Forgetting that constructors can throw before fully initializing an object, leaving a half-initialized (but already heap-allocated) object referenced by nothing, ready to be garbage collected.

What bytecode instructions does new Foo() compile to?new (allocate memory) followed by invokespecial (call the constructor)
What is a TLAB?Thread-Local Allocation Buffer - a small per-thread slice of Eden space used for fast, lock-free object allocation
What is stored in an object's header?The mark word (hash code, lock state, GC age) and a pointer to the object's class (Klass pointer)

Mid-Level Notes

  • Order: superclass constructor, then instance field initializers and instance blocks, then the rest of the constructor body.
  • Header: with compressed class pointers, the object header is 12 bytes; objects are aligned to 8 bytes.
  • Class loading: the first new Foo() loads, links and initializes class Foo if that has not happened yet.

Senior Notes

  • TLAB: each thread allocates from its own Thread-Local Allocation Buffer, so allocation is usually a pointer bump without locking.
  • Escape analysis: the JIT can remove an allocation (scalar replacement) when the object never escapes the method.
  • Measure: use JOL (ClassLayout.parseClass) to see real object layout instead of guessing.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Calling an overridable method in a constructor: the subclass field is still at its default.
  • Allocating in a hot loop: new Integer or short-lived temp objects; use primitives.
  • Creating an object per call: for expensive objects like Pattern or DateTimeFormatter, make them static final.
  • Assuming zero size: an empty object still takes 16 bytes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Allocation tuning:

  • Reduce garbage: fewer short-lived objects means fewer young collections.
  • Compressed oops: heaps under about 32 GB keep 4-byte references; crossing it makes references 8 bytes.
  • Watch allocation rate: use JFR (jdk.ObjectAllocationSample) or GC logs.
  • Layout: group fields to cut padding; use primitives over wrappers.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an API endpoint is slow under load and GC shows many young collections.

  • Record with JFR and find the top allocation sites.
  • Replace per-request regex compilation and string formatting with cached objects and StringBuilder.

beginner.content:
A Reference Is Not the Object

In Java, when you write Student s1 = new Student();, the variable s1 does NOT hold the actual Student object. It holds a reference - basically an address that tells the JVM "the real object lives over there in the Heap."

Think of a reference like a house's address written on a piece of paper. The paper (variable) is small and easy to carry around; the actual house (object) is the big thing sitting at that address.

Copying a Reference Copies the Address, Not the Object

When you assign one reference variable to another, you are copying the address - both variables now point to the exact same object in memory. No new object is created.

A Reference Can Point to Nothing: null

A reference variable that isn't pointing to any object holds the special value null. Trying to use a null reference to call a method throws a NullPointerException.

Two References, Two Different Objects

If instead you create two separate objects with new, each reference points to its own, independent object - changing one never affects the other.

Reference Equality (==) vs Value Equality (equals())

== on objects checks whether two references point to the SAME object in memory, not whether their contents look equal. Use equals() to compare the actual content.

Fresher Notes

  • Reference: a variable holds the address of an object, not the object itself; a = b copies the reference.
  • Pass by value: Java always passes a copy of the reference, so a method can change the object but cannot re-point your variable.
  • null: a reference to nothing; calling a method on it throws NullPointerException.
