Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the GC treats reference strengths.

  • Strong: the object is a GC root path target and stays.
  • Soft: kept until the GC needs memory; the policy uses -XX:SoftRefLRUPolicyMSPerMB (default 1000 ms per free MB).
  • Weak: cleared when the object is only weakly reachable.
  • Phantom: enqueued after the object is finalized; get() always returns null.
  • Queues: the GC enqueues cleared references on a ReferenceQueue.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Reference types and helpers:

  • SoftReference: memory-sensitive caches.
  • WeakReference / WeakHashMap: canonical maps, listener registries.
  • PhantomReference + Cleaner: run cleanup after unreachable.
  • Optional: a safer holder than null for return values.
  • Objects.requireNonNull: fail fast on null.

expert.content:
References Are Pass-by-Value Too

Java is strictly pass-by-value, even for objects. What gets copied when you pass an object to a method is the reference (the address) itself - not the object it points to. This is a subtle but critical distinction:

• You CAN mutate the object's fields through the copied reference (both point to the same object).
• You CANNOT make the caller's reference point to a different object by reassigning the parameter inside the method - that only rebinds the local copy of the reference.

Reference Layout: Diagram

Stack (or local vars)          Heap
+----------------+             +----------------------+
| account1  ---------------->  | ReferenceCopyDemo obj |
+----------------+             |  balance = 5000       |
| account2  ---------------->  +----------------------+
+----------------+                       ^
                                          |
                    both references point to the SAME heap object
Only the arrows (addresses) live on the stack (for local variables); the object itself always lives on the heap.

Types of References the JVM Recognizes (GC-Relevant)

Beyond ordinary "strong" references, java.lang.ref exposes weaker reference types that change how the Garbage Collector treats the referenced object:

Reference TypeGC BehaviorTypical Use
Strong (normal)Never collected while reachableEveryday variables/fields
Soft (SoftReference)Collected only when memory is lowMemory-sensitive caches
Weak (WeakReference)Collected at the next GC cycle if no strong refs remainWeakHashMap, listener maps, avoiding leaks
Phantom (PhantomReference)Object already finalized; used only for cleanup notificationResource cleanup tracking

Common Bugs and Misconceptions

• "Java is pass-by-reference." False - Java is always pass-by-value; what's passed for objects is a copy of the reference value, not the object, and not a reference-to-the-reference.
• Holding onto references longer than needed causes memory leaks. A static field or a long-lived collection that keeps a strong reference to objects you're "done with" prevents the GC from ever reclaiming them - a very common leak pattern in Java.
• Confusing == with .equals() on wrapper types and Strings is one of the most common real-world bugs, especially since small cached Integers (-128 to 127) make == "accidentally" work sometimes.
• Assuming setting a reference to null immediately frees memory. It only removes one path to the object; the object is reclaimed only when the GC runs AND no other reference exists.

What does a null reference mean?The variable currently points to no object; using it to call a method throws NullPointerException

Mid-Level Notes

  • Strong: a normal reference; the object is never collected while one exists.
  • Soft and weak: SoftReference keeps the object until memory is short; WeakReference lets it go at the next GC.
  • == vs equals: == compares references, equals compares content when overridden.

Senior Notes

  • Four strengths: strong, soft, weak, phantom; they decide when the GC may reclaim an object.
  • ReferenceQueue and Cleaner: get a notification after collection; use Cleaner instead of finalize(), which is deprecated for removal since JDK 18.
  • Leaks: a long-lived map or static field holding strong references is the most common Java memory leak; WeakHashMap can help for caches keyed by identity-like objects.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Using finalize(): slow, unpredictable and deprecated for removal; use try-with-resources and Cleaner.
  • Weak reference to a value you only hold weakly: the cache empties at once.
  • Key referenced by its own value in a WeakHashMap: the entry never goes away.
  • Static collections that only grow: a classic leak.
  • Relying on System.gc(): it is only a hint.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning notes:

  • Soft references make GC behavior harder to predict; prefer a sized cache (Caffeine) for most cases.
  • Many reference objects add reference-processing time to GC pauses.
  • Check logs: -Xlog:gc+ref=debug shows reference processing time.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: heap grows until OOM after a few days. Take a heap dump and look at the dominator tree.

  • Find the biggest retained set, then the path to GC roots.
  • A static map or a listener list holding strong references is the usual cause.

beginner.content:
Two Memory Areas Every Java Program Uses

When a Java program runs, the JVM splits the memory it uses into different areas. The two you'll hear about constantly are the Stack and the Heap.

• Stack - stores method calls and local variables. Very fast, very short-lived.
• Heap - stores all objects (created with new). Larger, longer-lived, shared by the whole program.

What Goes on the Stack

Each time a method is called, the JVM pushes a new stack frame for it. That frame holds the method's local variables and primitive values. When the method finishes, its frame is popped and everything in it disappears automatically.

What Goes on the Heap

Every object you create with new lives on the Heap - not the Stack. Only the reference (address) to that object sits on the Stack.

Primitives vs Objects: Where They Live

A local primitive variable (int, double, boolean, etc.) stores its actual value directly on the Stack. An object always lives on the Heap, and the variable pointing to it (on the Stack) only holds its address.

Why This Matters: Method Calls Are Isolated

Because each method call gets its own fresh stack frame, local variables in one method call can never accidentally clash with local variables of another call - even recursive calls to the same method.

Fresher Notes

  • Stack: each method call pushes a frame with locals and parameters; the frame is removed when the method returns.
  • Heap: all objects and arrays live here and are shared by every thread.
  • Cleanup: stack memory is freed automatically on return; heap memory is freed by the garbage collector.

  • Per thread: created with the thread, reserved by -Xss, and grown by the OS as needed.
  • Heap: shared, split into generations or regions by the collector, and grows between -Xms and -Xmx.

expert.content:
Stack Frame Anatomy

Each thread in Java gets its own private Stack (this is why Stack data is inherently thread-safe - no sharing). Every stack frame pushed onto it typically contains:
• Local variables array (primitives and object references).
• Operand stack (used internally by the JVM to evaluate expressions/bytecode).
• A reference to the runtime constant pool of the current class (for resolving symbols).

The Heap, in contrast, is a single shared area across ALL threads - which is exactly why object access can require synchronization, while purely-local primitive computation never does.

Memory Layout Diagram

Thread-1 Stack        Thread-2 Stack             Shared Heap
+--------------+       +--------------+       +-------------------------+
| main() frame |       | run() frame  |       | Eden | Survivor 0/1     |
|  x = 5       |       |  local vars  |  -->  | Young Generation        |
|  obj -----------------------------------+   +-------------------------+
+--------------+       +--------------+   |   | Old Generation (Tenured)|
                                           +-> |  long-lived objects     |
                                               +-------------------------+
Notice: each thread's stack is private and small; the Heap is shared, larger, and is where the Garbage Collector does all of its work - the Stack is never garbage collected, it just unwinds.

Stack vs Heap: Detailed Comparison

AspectStackHeap
StoresMethod frames, local vars, primitives, referencesAll objects and arrays
ScopePer-thread (private)Shared across all threads
LifetimeTied to method call (LIFO)Tied to reachability (GC-managed)

SizeSmall, fixed per thread (-Xss)Large, configurable (-Xms/-Xmx)

Thread safetyInherently thread-safe (private)Requires synchronization for shared mutable objects

Common Bugs and Misconceptions

• "All local variables are on the stack, always." Mostly true for primitives, but a local object variable only stores a reference on the stack - the object itself is on the heap (unless escape analysis proves it can be scalar-replaced and avoid the heap entirely).
• Deep/unbounded recursion causing StackOverflowError - each call pushes a new frame; without a proper base case, thousands of frames accumulate until the (small, fixed) stack size is exhausted.
• Confusing "heap" (JVM heap) with "Heap" the data structure (priority queue) - same word, completely unrelated concepts.
• Assuming bigger Stack always helps performance. Increasing -Xss only helps avoid StackOverflowError for deep recursion; it does nothing for heap/object performance, and consumes more memory per thread (multiplied by thread count).

Can an object ever avoid the Heap entirely?Yes, via JIT escape analysis and scalar replacement, if the object is proven not to escape the method

Mid-Level Notes

  • Primitives vs objects: a local int sits in the frame; a local String variable holds a reference into the heap.
  • StackOverflowError: too-deep recursion fills the stack; OutOfMemoryError: the heap is full.
  • Sizes: set with -Xss (per thread stack) and -Xms / -Xmx (heap).

Senior Notes

  • Thread safety: locals are private to a thread, so they are safe; heap objects need synchronization when shared.
  • Escape analysis can place non-escaping objects in registers or stack-like storage, so "objects always on the heap" is a model, not a guarantee.
  • Many threads: total stack memory is threads times -Xss, which matters with thousands of platform threads; virtual threads keep stacks on the heap.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Saying "objects are on the stack": only the reference is, unless the JIT scalar-replaces the object.
  • Raising -Xss to hide infinite recursion: fix the base case instead.
  • Large local arrays in recursion: the array is on the heap, but deep recursion still overflows with big frames.
  • Sharing a mutable heap object between threads without a lock.
  • Setting -Xmx equal to container memory: there is no room left for metaspace and thread stacks.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Prefer iteration over deep recursion; the JVM does not eliminate tail calls.
  • Small frames: fewer locals means more depth per MB.
  • Right-size the heap: too small gives frequent GC; too large gives long pauses on some collectors.
  • Many tasks: use virtual threads (JDK 21) instead of thousands of large platform stacks.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a JSON parser fails with StackOverflowError on deeply nested input.

  • Cap nesting depth and reject hostile input.
  • If the depth is legitimate, parse in a thread with a larger stack, or convert to an explicit stack on the heap.

beginner.content:
Strings Are Special in Java

Strings are used so heavily in every Java program that the JVM has a dedicated optimization for them called the String Pool (also called the String Constant Pool or String Intern Pool). It's a special area in memory that stores unique String literals so identical text doesn't get duplicated over and over.

String Literals Share the Same Object

When you create a String using a literal (double quotes), Java checks the pool first. If an identical String already exists there, it reuses it instead of creating a new object.

new String() Skips the Pool

Using the new keyword with String always creates a brand-new object on the Heap, even if an identical literal already exists in the pool.

Bringing a String Into the Pool with intern()

The intern() method looks up the String's content in the pool. If found, it returns the pooled reference; if not, it adds the String's content to the pool and returns that reference.

Why This Saves Memory

Imagine an application that stores "India" as a city/country name a million times across different objects. Without pooling, that could mean a million separate String objects holding identical text. With the pool, all million literal usages share ONE object.

Fresher Notes

  • String pool: a shared table of unique string literals, so "hi" used twice is one object.
  • Literal vs new: "hi" reuses a pooled object; new String("hi") always makes a new one.
  • intern(): returns the pooled copy of a string, adding it if missing.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the pool works.

  • Literals: a string literal sits in the class constant pool; the first time it is resolved, the JVM looks it up in the StringTable or adds it.
  • ldc: the bytecode that loads a constant, giving the same object each time.
  • Storage: the String objects are on the heap; the table holds weak references so unused entries can be collected.
  • Representation: since JDK 9 a String stores bytes with a coder (Latin-1 or UTF-16).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to get a String and what each does:

  • Literal: pooled.
  • new String(s): new object, rarely needed.
  • intern(): pooled copy.
  • + with constants: folded and pooled.
  • StringBuilder.toString(): new object.
  • String.valueOf / concat: new object.
  • Text block: a literal, pooled.

expert.content:
Where the Pool Actually Lives

Historically (Java 6 and earlier), the String Pool lived in PermGen, a fixed-size area prone to OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space if too many Strings were interned. Since Java 7, the pool was moved into the main Heap itself, which lets it grow dynamically and be garbage collected like any other heap data, drastically reducing intern-related OutOfMemoryErrors in practice.

Compile-Time Constant Folding

The pool doesn't just apply to simple literals - the compiler also folds constant expressions at compile time, so they resolve to the same pooled String even though the source doesn't look identical.

String Pool: Key Facts Compared

AspectString literal "x"new String("x")
LocationString Pool (in Heap since Java 7)General Heap (outside pool)
Reused if content matches?Yes, automaticallyNo, always a new object
== with identical literaltruefalse
Eligible for GCOnly if unreferenced pool-wide (rare)As soon as unreachable, like any object
Can be added to pool manually?N/A (already there)Yes, via .intern()

Common Bugs and Misconceptions

• Comparing Strings with == instead of .equals() - works "by accident" for literals due to pooling, then silently breaks in production once a String comes from user input, a database, or new String(...). Always use .equals() for content comparison.
• "Interning everything improves performance." Over-interning large numbers of unique runtime Strings can bloat the pool and increase lookup/GC cost - only intern Strings you know will repeat often.
• Assuming the pool still causes PermGen OutOfMemoryError in modern Java - since Java 7 the pool lives in the regular Heap, so this specific historical failure mode mostly no longer applies.
• Forgetting that StringBuilder.toString() never returns a pooled String, even if the resulting text matches an existing literal exactly - it's a fresh Heap object unless you call .intern() on it.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the String Pool?A special memory area that stores unique String literals so identical text is shared instead of duplicated
Where does the String Pool live in modern Java?Inside the main Heap, since Java 7 (previously in PermGen before that)
Does new String("x") use the pool?No - it always creates a new object on the general heap, bypassing the pool
What does String.intern() do?Returns the pooled reference for that content, adding it to the pool first if not already present
Why is == risky for comparing Strings?It compares references, not content; it may accidentally work for pooled literals but fail for equal-content Strings from new, user input, or concatenation at runtime
Are compile-time constant expressions like "hel" + "lo" pooled?Yes, the compiler folds them into a single literal at compile time, so they resolve to the pooled instance
Is runtime concatenation like prefix + "lo" pooled automatically?No, it's built via StringBuilder at runtime and produces a new, non-pooled object unless .intern() is called

Mid-Level Notes

  • Compile-time constants: "a" + "b" is folded to "ab" and pooled; a runtime concatenation is not.
  • Location: since JDK 7 the pool lives in the heap, so pooled strings can be garbage collected when unreachable.
  • Why immutable: sharing is only safe because a String cannot change.

Senior Notes

  • StringTable is a native hash table; its size is -XX:StringTableSize (default 65536 since JDK 11).
  • Statistics: -XX:+PrintStringTableStatistics or jcmd <pid> VM.stringtable show size and buckets.
  • Deduplication: with G1, -XX:+UseStringDeduplication shares the char data of equal strings that are not interned.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Comparing with ==: works by accident for literals and fails for runtime strings; use equals.
  • Interning every input string: it grows the table and slows lookups.
  • Using new String(literal): it only wastes memory.
  • Concatenating in a loop: creates many temporary Strings; use StringBuilder.
  • Storing secrets as Strings: they stay in memory until collected; prefer char[] that you clear.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Table size: if you intern many strings, raise -XX:StringTableSize to a prime near the expected count to keep buckets short.
  • Dedup: try -XX:+UseStringDeduplication with G1 when heap dumps show many duplicate strings.
  • Compact strings: on by default; -XX:-CompactStrings disables them.
  • Concatenation: since JDK 9 javac uses invokedynamic (StringConcatFactory), which is fast for simple cases.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a heap dump shows 300 MB of duplicate country and status strings read from a database.

  • Intern the small, fixed set at read time, or use an enum.
  • Or enable G1 deduplication with no code change.

beginner.content:
What Does static Mean?

Normally, every object gets its own copy of a class's fields. But mark a field static and something different happens: instead of belonging to each object, it belongs to the class itself. There is only ONE copy of it, no matter how many objects you create.

Static Variables Are Shared Across All Objects

Every instance of the class sees and shares the exact same static variable. Changing it through one object is visible through every other object too.

You Don't Need an Object to Access a Static Variable

Because a static variable belongs to the class, not to any object, you can access it directly through the class name - even before any object has been created.

Static Variables Exist Even With Zero Objects

A static variable is created once when the class is loaded by the JVM, and it keeps its value even if no objects of that class currently exist.

Fresher Notes

  • One copy: a static field belongs to the class, so every object shares the same single value.
  • Where it lives: the value is stored with the class data in the JVM (in the Class object on the heap since Java 8), not inside each instance.
  • Access: use ClassName.field; it works without creating any object.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A static field is part of the class, not of any instance.

  • Linking: fields are allocated during preparation with default values.
  • Initialization: the class initializer <clinit> runs the initializers and static blocks once, in textual order.
  • Location: since Java 8 the values sit in the Class mirror on the heap; class metadata is in Metaspace.
  • Reachability: the loaded class is a GC root path, so static references keep objects alive.
  • Safety: the JVM locks class initialization, so it happens once even with many threads.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Static variants:

  • static: one value per class.
  • static final: a constant; a primitive or String literal is inlined by the compiler.
  • static volatile: a flag visible to all threads.
  • static block: complex one-time setup.
  • Nested holder: lazy initialization.
  • enum: a safe singleton.

expert.content:
Where Static Variables Actually Live

Static variables are stored in an area of memory tied to the Class object's metadata, managed by the Metaspace (Java 8+) or historically PermGen (Java 7 and earlier). Specifically:
• The metadata describing the class layout lives in Metaspace.
• The actual static variable values live as part of the class's representation on the Heap in modern JVMs, conceptually attached to the Class object for that class.
• They are created when the class is first loaded/initialized, and destroyed only when the class is unloaded (which, for normal application classes, is effectively "never" until JVM shutdown).

Class Loading and Static Initialization Order

Static variables are initialized in the exact textual order they appear, interleaved with any static initializer blocks, the very first time the class is loaded (referenced for the first time by the JVM).

Static Memory Layout Diagram

Metaspace                       Heap
+----------------------+        +---------------------------+
| Counter.class layout |        | Counter object #1          |
|  method bytecode      |        |  id = 1                    |
|  field descriptors    |        +---------------------------+
+----------------------+        | Counter object #2          |
          |                      |  id = 2                    |
          |  (Class object)      +---------------------------+
          v
  static totalCount = 3   <-- ONE value, tied to the class,
                               NOT duplicated per object above

Static vs Instance Variables: Storage Comparison

AspectStatic VariableInstance Variable
CopiesOne per classOne per object
Created whenClass is loaded/initializedEach time new runs
Destroyed whenClass unloaded (rare) / JVM shuts downObject becomes unreachable and is GC'd
AccessClassName.field (or via instance, discouraged)instance.field only
Lifetime relative to objectsCan outlive every object of the classTied strictly to its own object

Static Memory Leaks - A Real Production Hazard

Because static fields live for (almost) the entire lifetime of the application, anything you store in a static collection and forget to remove becomes a classic, hard-to-diagnose memory leak:

• A static List or static Map used as a "cache" that only ever grows, never evicting old entries.
• Static references to listeners/callbacks that outlive the objects that registered them, preventing those objects from ever being garbage collected.
• ThreadLocal variables stored statically in thread-pooled environments (e.g. web servers) that are never cleared, silently accumulating request-scoped data across requests.

Because the GC sees a live static reference as a permanent GC root, none of these objects are ever collected, no matter how much memory pressure builds up - eventually leading to OutOfMemoryError.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does the static keyword mean for a variable?The variable belongs to the class itself, with a single shared copy across all instances, instead of one copy per object
Where do static variables live in modern JVMs?Their metadata lives in Metaspace; their values are effectively part of the Class object's representation on the Heap
When are static variables initialized?Once, the first time the class is loaded/initialized by the JVM, in textual order interleaved with static blocks
Can you access a static variable without creating an object?Yes, directly via ClassName.field, since it doesn't belong to any specific instance
Why are static fields a common source of memory leaks?They act as permanent GC roots for the life of the class, so anything referenced from them (e.g. a growing static cache) is never collected
What replaced PermGen for static/class metadata since Java 8?Metaspace, which is allocated from native memory and grows dynamically instead of a fixed-size PermGen
Is a static variable shared across threads?Yes - since it's one copy per class (not per thread), concurrent modification from multiple threads requires synchronization

Mid-Level Notes

  • Initialization: statics are set once, when the class is first initialized, by field initializers and static {} blocks in order.
  • GC roots: a static reference keeps its object alive as long as the class is loaded, so large static collections can leak memory.
  • Thread visibility: a mutable static is shared by all threads, so guard it with volatile, locks or atomics.

Senior Notes

  • Class unloading: statics are freed only when the class loader that loaded the class is collected, which is why redeploys in app servers leak.
  • Design: avoid mutable global state; prefer dependency injection and immutable static final constants.
  • Lazy holder: use a nested holder class for thread-safe lazy singletons, since class initialization is guaranteed once by the JVM.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Static for instance data: all objects overwrite one value; make the field non-static.
  • Unsynchronized mutable static: data races; use atomics or locks.
  • Unbounded static cache: memory leak; use a bounded cache with eviction.
  • Static initialization order cycles: a class sees a default value of another; avoid circular statics.
  • Static holding a Context or request: blocks class loader unload.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and sizing:

  • Bound caches: a size limit or WeakHashMap or soft references.
  • Prefer constants: immutable statics add no GC cost.
  • Heap dumps: look for GC Roots of type "class" to find static retention.
  • Static init cost: heavy work delays first use; consider lazy holders.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: after each redeploy of a web app on Tomcat, Metaspace grows until OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace.

  • A shared library keeps a static reference to a webapp class.
  • The old class loader cannot be collected, so all its classes stay.
  • Fix by clearing the static in a shutdown hook or listener, and upgrading the library.

beginner.content:
What Is an Instance Variable?

An instance variable is a field declared inside a class (without the static keyword) that belongs to each individual object. Every time you create a new object with new, that object gets its own separate copy of every instance variable.

Each Object Gets Its Own Copy

Unlike static variables, instance variables are NOT shared. Two objects of the same class have completely independent values for their instance variables.

Instance Variables Live on the Heap, Inside Their Object

Because instance variables belong to an object, and every object lives on the Heap, instance variables live on the Heap too - as part of the object's memory block.

Instance Variables Get Default Values Automatically

If you don't explicitly assign a value, an instance variable is automatically set to a default (0, false, null, etc.) - never left undefined.

Instance Variables Disappear With Their Object

An instance variable's lifetime is tied entirely to its object. Once nothing refers to the object anymore, the object (and every instance variable inside it) becomes eligible for garbage collection.

Fresher Notes

  • Per object: each object has its own copy of every instance variable, stored inside the object on the heap.
  • Default values: fields get 0, false or null automatically; local variables get none.
  • Lifetime: the fields live as long as the object is reachable, then the garbage collector reclaims them.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Each object is a block on the heap: header plus fields.

  • Header: mark word (8 bytes) and class pointer (4 bytes compressed).
  • Fields: primitives stored inline; object fields store a reference.
  • Alignment: total size rounds up to a multiple of 8 bytes.
  • Allocation: fast pointer bump in a thread-local buffer (TLAB).
  • Escape analysis: the JIT may avoid heap allocation of objects that do not escape.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Field options:

  • Modifiers: private, final, volatile, transient.
  • Initializers: inline, in an instance initializer block, or in the constructor.
  • final fields: safely published after construction.
  • Records: declare components that become private final fields.
  • Inheritance: a subclass object contains the superclass fields too.

expert.content:
Memory Layout of Instance Variables Within an Object

Instance variables are laid out inside the object's memory block on the Heap, right after the object header (mark word + klass pointer). The JVM (HotSpot) doesn't necessarily preserve declaration order - it commonly reorders and groups fields by size (longs/doubles, then ints/floats, then shorts/chars, then booleans/bytes, then references) to minimize padding and improve memory alignment, a technique called field packing.

Instance Variable Layout Diagram

Heap: one Car object

+--------------------------------+
| Object Header (12-16 bytes)     |
|  Mark Word | Klass Pointer      |
+--------------------------------+
| Instance Fields (per-object)    |
|  int speed      = 60            |
|  String color -----------------> "Red" (separate object, own header)
+--------------------------------+
| Padding (align to 8 bytes)      |
+--------------------------------+

Another 'new Car(...)' produces an ENTIRELY separate block like this one,
with its own header and its own copy of speed/color.

Instance vs Static: Where and How Long They Live

AspectInstance VariableStatic Variable
Memory areaHeap (inside the object)Heap, attached to the Class object / Metaspace metadata
CopiesOne per objectOne per class
CreatedOn every new callOnce, at class loading
ReclaimedWhen the object becomes unreachable (GC'd)Only when the class is unloaded (rare)
Thread sharingShared only if the object itself is sharedAlways shared across all threads

Instance Fields and Garbage Collection Reachability

An instance variable's storage is only reclaimable once its owning object is unreachable - but a subtlety often missed: if an instance variable itself references ANOTHER object, that inner object is kept alive too (transitively), for as long as the outer object is reachable. This is why a single long-lived object with a large collection as an instance variable can pin down a huge object graph in memory, even though most of that graph "looks unrelated" to the leak at first glance.

Common Bugs and Misconceptions

• Assuming instance variables are zeroed AFTER the constructor. They're zeroed BEFORE the constructor body runs, as part of allocation - the constructor only overwrites the defaults you explicitly set.
• Believing field declaration order controls memory layout. The JVM is free to reorder fields internally for alignment/packing; only the logical (source-code) view guarantees order, not the physical memory layout.
• Storing large objects as instance fields of a singleton/long-lived object and forgetting they now live "forever" alongside it - a common accidental memory-leak pattern distinct from static leaks, but with a similar root cause: an unexpectedly long-lived reference chain.
• Confusing shadowing: a local variable or parameter with the same name as an instance variable "hides" it inside a method unless accessed via this.fieldName - a frequent source of subtle bugs in constructors.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is an instance variable?A non-static field declared in a class; each object created from that class gets its own independent copy
Where do instance variables live in memory?On the Heap, stored inside the memory block of the object that owns them
When are instance variables created and destroyed?Created each time new runs; destroyed (reclaimed) when the owning object becomes unreachable and is garbage collected
Do instance variables get default values automatically?Yes - the JVM zeroes them during allocation, before the constructor body executes
Does the JVM preserve field declaration order in memory?Not necessarily - HotSpot commonly reorders/packs fields by size to minimize padding, though the source-level view still shows declaration order
How do instance variables differ from static variables in lifetime?Instance variables live and die with their specific object; static variables live for the lifetime of the class, independent of any single object
Can an instance variable cause a memory leak?Yes, if it references a large object graph and the owning object itself is unexpectedly long-lived (e.g. held by a singleton or cache)

Mid-Level Notes

  • Object layout: a header (mark word and class pointer, usually 12 bytes with compressed class pointers) is followed by the fields, padded to 8 bytes.
  • References: an instance field of object type stores only a reference (4 bytes with compressed oops), not the other object.
  • Stack versus heap: the reference variable sits on the stack, while the object and its fields are on the heap.

Senior Notes

  • Field reordering: the JVM groups fields by size to cut padding, so declaration order does not decide the layout.
  • False sharing: hot fields of different threads on the same cache line slow each other; @Contended pads them.
  • Footprint: millions of small objects cost header overhead; use primitives, arrays or records of primitives, and measure with JOL.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Public mutable fields: break encapsulation; use private and accessors.
  • Uninitialized reference: null causes NullPointerException.
  • Shared mutable field across threads: needs synchronization.
  • Calling an overridable method in a constructor: sees defaults of the subclass fields.
  • Wrong equals on == : compare objects with equals.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Footprint tips:

  • Primitives over wrappers: an Integer costs about 16 bytes versus 4.
  • Smaller types: do not use long where int is enough.
  • Lazy fields: allocate rarely used objects on demand.
  • Compressed oops: heaps under about 32 GB keep 4-byte references.
  • Measure: use JOL or a heap dump histogram.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a service keeps 5 million Tick objects with a price and time. Memory is large because of headers and boxed values.

  • Each object costs header plus fields plus padding.
  • Store prices in a double[] and times in a long[] instead.
  • Heap use drops and GC has less to scan.

beginner.content:
What is Garbage Collection?

Garbage Collection (GC) is the process by which the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) automatically finds objects that are no longer being used by your program and reclaims the memory they occupy.

In languages like C or C++, the programmer must manually call free() (or delete) to release memory. Forget to do it, and you get a memory leak. Do it too early or twice, and you get a crash.

Java removes this burden - a background process called the Garbage Collector does this cleanup for you.

Why Doesn't Java Need free()?

When you create an object with new, Java allocates memory for it on the heap. As long as something in your program can still "reach" that object, it stays alive.

Once nothing refers to it anymore, the object becomes unreachable - and the JVM's Garbage Collector will eventually notice this and free the memory automatically, without you writing any cleanup code.

Reachability - How the JVM Decides What's "Alive"

An object is considered reachable if it can be accessed by following references starting from a GC Root - things like:
• Local variables on any thread's stack
• Active static fields of classes
• JNI references

If you can draw an unbroken chain of references from a GC Root to an object, that object is alive. If you can't, it's garbage - eligible for collection.

Mark and Sweep - The Basic Idea

Most Java garbage collectors are built on a simple two-step idea called Mark and Sweep:

• Mark phase - starting from the GC Roots, the collector walks every reference chain and marks every object it can reach as "alive".
• Sweep phase - it then scans the whole heap and reclaims memory for every object that was not marked - those are the unreachable ones.

Think of it like tracing string from a bulletin board (the roots) to every note connected to it. Any note with no string reaching it gets thrown away.

You Can't Force GC, Only Suggest It

Java gives you System.gc() to request garbage collection, but it is only a hint to the JVM - the JVM is free to ignore it entirely. Relying on it in real applications is considered bad practice; the JVM's internal heuristics almost always make better decisions than manual triggers.

Fresher Notes

  • Automatic memory: the garbage collector frees objects that no live code can reach, so you never call free.
  • Reachability: an object is garbage when no chain of references leads to it from a GC root.
  • Not guaranteed: System.gc() is only a hint, and you cannot decide when collection happens.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Tracing collectors find live objects, then free everything else.

  • Mark: walk references from GC roots and flag live objects.
  • Sweep: reclaim unmarked memory.
  • Compact or copy: move live objects together to avoid fragmentation.
  • Safepoints: threads stop at safe points for the stop-the-world phases.
  • Barriers: concurrent collectors use read or write barriers to track changes during marking.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Collectors in JDK 17 and 21:

  • Serial: -XX:+UseSerialGC, single thread, tiny heaps.
  • Parallel: -XX:+UseParallelGC, best throughput for batch jobs.
  • G1: -XX:+UseG1GC, balanced default.
  • ZGC: -XX:+UseZGC, low latency.
  • Shenandoah: -XX:+UseShenandoahGC, low pause, in OpenJDK builds that include it.
  • Epsilon: -XX:+UseEpsilonGC, no collection, for tests.

expert.content:
Reachability States in Detail

The JVM specification (and java.lang.ref package) actually defines several strengths of reachability, not just "reachable" vs "not reachable". This matters for caches, listeners, and memory-sensitive data structures.
ReachabilityReference TypeCollected When
Strongly ReachableOrdinary reference (Object o = new Object())Never, while a strong reference chain exists
Softly ReachableSoftReferenceOnly when the JVM is close to running out of heap memory
Weakly ReachableWeakReferenceAt the next GC cycle, regardless of memory pressure
Phantom ReachablePhantomReferenceAfter finalization, used to schedule cleanup actions
UnreachableNo reference chain from any GC RootImmediately eligible for collection

Mark-and-Sweep Internals

Under the hood, a naive Mark-and-Sweep collector works roughly like this: 

GC Roots
  |-- Thread stacks (local variables, parameters)
  |-- Static fields
  |-- JNI handles
       |
       v
  MARK: traverse every reachable object graph
        set a "marked" bit on each visited object
       |
       v
  SWEEP: scan the entire heap linearly
         unmarked objects  -> reclaim memory, add to free list
         marked objects    -> clear mark bit for next cycle
This basic algorithm has two well-known costs in production:
• Stop-the-World pauses - application threads are typically paused during marking so the object graph doesn't change mid-traversal.
• Fragmentation - plain sweep leaves free memory scattered in small holes rather than one contiguous block, which is why most real collectors add a compaction step afterward.

Mark-Sweep vs Mark-Sweep-Compact vs Copying Collection

StrategyHow it worksFragmentationCost
Mark-SweepMark reachable objects, free the rest in placeHigh - holes left behindFast sweep, but slow future allocation
Mark-Sweep-CompactMark, sweep, then slide live objects togetherNone after compactionExtra compaction pass adds pause time
Copying CollectionCopy all live objects into a second empty space, discard the old space entirelyNone - allocation is always contiguousNeeds 2x space reserved, but very fast for short-lived objects

Java's real-world collectors combine these ideas by generation (see the "Generational GC" topic) - copying collection for the young generation where most objects die quickly, and mark-sweep-compact for the older, longer-lived generation.

Production Note: System.gc() in Real Systems

Calling System.gc() explicitly in application code is almost always an anti-pattern in production services - it can trigger a full, expensive Stop-the-World collection at an unpredictable moment, causing a latency spike for every request being served at that instant.

Some libraries (old RMI implementations, certain NIO direct-buffer cleanup paths) historically called it internally, which surprised teams debugging periodic latency spikes. The fix in modern JVMs is the flag -XX:+DisableExplicitGC, which makes System.gc() a no-op - useful when you can't remove the calls from third-party code but need predictable latency.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is Garbage Collection in Java?The JVM's automatic process of finding and reclaiming memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable from the program
What makes an object eligible for garbage collection?When there is no reference chain from any GC Root (stack variables, static fields, JNI handles) reaching that object
Does System.gc() guarantee an immediate garbage collection?No - it is only a hint/request; the JVM decides whether and when to actually run GC
What are the two basic phases of Mark-and-Sweep?Mark - traverse and flag all reachable objects; Sweep - reclaim memory for everything not marked
Why do collectors add a Compact step after Sweep?Plain sweeping leaves fragmented free memory as scattered holes; compaction slides live objects together for contiguous free space
What is the difference between a WeakReference and a SoftReference?A WeakReference is cleared at the next GC cycle regardless of memory pressure; a SoftReference is cleared only when the JVM is low on memory
What are GC Roots?The starting points of reachability analysis - thread stacks, static fields, and JNI references
Why doesn't Java need a manual free() like C/C++?The JVM's garbage collector automatically tracks reachability and reclaims memory for unreachable objects, removing the risk of manual leaks and double-frees

Mid-Level Notes

  • GC roots: thread stacks, static fields, JNI references and active threads are the starting points of the reachability walk.
  • Mark, sweep, compact: mark live objects, free the rest, and optionally move survivors together to remove fragmentation.
  • Stop-the-world: during some phases all application threads pause; collectors differ in how long and how often.

Senior Notes

  • Trade-offs: throughput, latency and footprint cannot all be optimal; choose the collector by the goal.
  • Collectors: Serial, Parallel (throughput), G1 (default since Java 9), ZGC and Shenandoah (low pause).
  • Observe first: read GC logs with -Xlog:gc* before changing any flag.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Calling System.gc(): triggers a full collection; disable with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC if libraries do it.
  • Relying on finalize: deprecated; use try-with-resources or Cleaner.
  • Tuning blindly: copying flags from the internet; measure first.
  • Heap too small: constant GC; raise -Xmx.
  • Memory leak mistaken for GC problem: more heap only delays the failure.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning workflow:

  • Goal first: latency, throughput or footprint.
  • Log: -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log.
  • Reduce allocation: the cheapest GC is the one that does not run.
  • Set -Xms equal -Xmx for stable servers to avoid resize pauses.
  • Analyze with GCViewer or GCeasy.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an API shows occasional 2 second freezes.

  • The log shows Pause Full events.
  • Heap dump finds an unbounded cache.
  • Bound the cache, then re-check pause times.

beginner.content:
Why Split the Heap into Generations?

Studies of real programs found a simple but powerful pattern: most objects die young. A temporary string built inside a loop, a short-lived request object, a local list used once and discarded - these are created and thrown away within milliseconds.

Very few objects (a cache, a database connection pool, a singleton service) live for the entire lifetime of the application.

Java's Garbage Collector takes advantage of this by dividing the heap into generations and treating young and old objects differently.

The Young Generation

Every new object is first created in the Young Generation (also called the "nursery"). It is usually small and gets garbage collected very often, but each collection is fast because most objects in it are already dead.

This frequent, cheap cleanup of the Young Generation is called a Minor GC.

The Old Generation

Objects that survive several Minor GC cycles are considered long-lived, and get promoted (moved) to the Old Generation (also called Tenured Generation). This area is collected much less often, but a collection here - called a Major GC - takes longer because the Old Generation is larger and has more live data to examine.

Minor GC vs Major GC - Quick Comparison

• Minor GC - cleans the Young Generation only. Fast, frequent, small pause.
• Major GC - cleans the Old Generation (sometimes the whole heap, called a Full GC). Slower, less frequent, bigger pause.

As a beginner, the key takeaway is: creating lots of short-lived objects is cheap in Java precisely because of this design - the Young Generation is built to handle exactly that pattern efficiently.

Promotion in a Nutshell

Think of the Young Generation like a classroom that gets cleared out every day - most students (objects) leave after one day (one GC cycle). A few students who keep showing up for many days in a row (surviving many Minor GCs) eventually get "promoted" to a permanent desk in another room - the Old Generation.

Fresher Notes

  • Weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young, so collecting a small young area often is cheap.
  • Two areas: the young generation (Eden plus two survivor spaces) and the old generation.
  • Promotion: an object that survives several young collections moves to the old generation.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The heap is divided by object age.

  • Eden: new objects are allocated here (TLAB pointer bump).
  • Survivors S0 and S1: live objects are copied between them each minor GC and age increases.
  • Old: objects that reach the tenuring threshold, or do not fit in survivor space.
  • Remembered sets or card table: record old-to-young pointers as extra roots.
  • Young collection is copying, so cost depends on live data, not on garbage.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • -XX:NewRatio=2: old is 2 times young.

expert.content:
The Weak Generational Hypothesis

Generational GC is built entirely on one empirical observation, formally called the Weak Generational Hypothesis:

"Most objects die young, and the ones that survive tend to live a long time."

This is "weak" (as opposed to a hard guarantee) because it's a statistical tendency, not a law - some workloads (e.g. large in-memory caches with high churn, or object pools with unusual lifetimes) violate it and suffer worse GC performance as a result. Understanding this hypothesis is the single most important mental model for reasoning about GC tuning.

Young Generation Internal Layout

The Young Generation itself is subdivided further to implement an efficient copying collector: 

Young Generation
 |-- Eden Space        <-- almost all new objects are allocated here
 |-- Survivor Space S0  <-- "from" space
 |-- Survivor Space S1  <-- "to" space (swaps roles with S0 each Minor GC)

Old Generation
 |-- Tenured Space      <-- objects promoted after surviving enough Minor GCs
Each Minor GC:
• Copies all live objects from Eden into whichever Survivor space is currently empty ("to" space).
• Copies all live objects from the other Survivor space into "to" space as well, aging them by one.
• Clears Eden and the old "from" Survivor space entirely - they become the next "to" space.
• Objects that have survived past a threshold (-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold, default 15) get promoted to Tenured space instead of copied into a Survivor space again.

Minor GC vs Major GC vs Full GC

AspectMinor GCMajor GCFull GC
ScopeYoung Generation onlyOld Generation (implementation-dependent)Entire heap (Young + Old + Metaspace)
FrequencyVery frequentLess frequentRare (ideally)
Typical pauseSub-millisecond to a few msTens to hundreds of msCan be seconds on large heaps
Algorithm usedCopying collectionMark-Sweep-Compact (collector dependent)Mark-Sweep-Compact across the whole heap
Common triggerEden space fills upOld Generation occupancy crosses a thresholdAllocation failure even after Old GC, or explicit System.gc()

Production Scenario: Premature Promotion

A common production issue is premature promotion: if the Young Generation (particularly Eden and Survivor spaces) is undersized relative to the allocation rate, objects that would normally die young get promoted to the Old Generation before they actually die - simply because a Minor GC catches them "in transit" too many times, or Survivor space overflows and forces early tenuring.

Symptom: Old Generation fills up faster than expected, triggering frequent, expensive Major/Full GCs even though the application's true long-lived data set is small.

Fix: increase Young Generation size (-Xmn) or tune the survivor ratio (-XX:SurvivorRatio) so short-lived objects have enough room and time to die inside the Young Generation before being swept along into Old Gen.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the Weak Generational Hypothesis?The observation that most objects die young, while a small fraction survive and live much longer - the basis for splitting the heap into generations
What is the difference between Minor GC and Major/Full GC?Minor GC cleans only the Young Generation (fast, frequent); Major/Full GC cleans the Old Generation or the entire heap (slower, less frequent)
What are Eden and Survivor spaces?Eden is where new objects are allocated; Survivor spaces (S0/S1) hold objects that survived at least one Minor GC, aging them before promotion
What triggers promotion of an object to the Old Generation?Surviving a number of Minor GC cycles beyond the tenuring threshold (-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold), or Survivor space overflow
Why is copying collection used for the Young Generation specifically?Because most objects there are dead, copying only the small number of live survivors is far cheaper than sweeping the whole space
What is premature promotion and why is it a problem?Short-lived objects get promoted to Old Gen too early due to an undersized Young Gen, causing the Old Gen to fill up faster and trigger more expensive Major GCs
Which JVM flag controls Young Generation size directly?-Xmn
Does every collector implement Major GC the same way?No - the exact algorithm and even the definition of "Major GC" varies by collector (e.g. G1's mixed collections behave differently from Parallel GC's Old Gen collection)

Mid-Level Notes

  • Minor GC cleans only the young generation and is fast; major or full GC involves the old generation and costs more.
  • Age threshold: objects get an age per survived collection; -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold caps it (15 maximum).
  • Card table: tracks old-to-young references so a minor GC does not scan the whole old generation.

Senior Notes

  • Sizing: -XX:NewRatio and -Xmn set the young size; too small means premature promotion.
  • Premature promotion: short-lived objects reaching old space fill it and trigger full GCs.
  • Newer collectors: ZGC became generational in JDK 21 with -XX:+ZGenerational; G1 and Parallel were always generational.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Tiny young generation: objects promoted too early; enlarge it.
  • Huge young generation: longer young pauses on Serial or Parallel.
  • Large temporary buffers: allocated straight to old; reuse them.
  • Caches of medium-lived objects: they survive many copies; consider an off-heap or bounded cache.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Target: keep live young survivors small.
  • Reduce allocation rate: avoid needless temporary objects in hot paths.
  • G1: do not set -Xmn; it adapts young size to the pause goal.
  • Watch: promotion rate and old occupancy after each GC.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a session service promotes sessions early.

  • Each request builds 3 MB of temporary JSON.
  • Young space is 20 MB so survivors overflow into old.
  • Raising the young size and streaming the JSON stops the full GCs.

beginner.content:
What is G1?

G1 (short for Garbage-First) is a garbage collector built into the JVM that tries to balance two goals at once: keeping pause times short and predictable, while still collecting garbage efficiently even on large heaps (multiple gigabytes).

Since Java 9, G1 is the default garbage collector for most JVM configurations, replacing the older Parallel GC as the out-of-the-box choice.

Region-Based Heap

Older collectors treat the Young and Old Generations as single large, contiguous blocks of memory. G1 instead splits the entire heap into many small, equal-sized chunks called regions (typically 1MB to 32MB each, chosen automatically).

Each region is dynamically labeled as Eden, Survivor, or Old at any given time - there's no fixed physical wall between generations like in older collectors.

Why "Garbage First"?

G1 gets its name from its core strategy: during a collection, it prioritizes cleaning up the regions that contain the most garbage first, because that gives the biggest memory reclaim for the least amount of work - maximizing efficiency within a limited pause-time budget.

Pause-Time Goals

Unlike older collectors that just run "as needed," G1 lets you specify a target maximum pause time using -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis. G1 then tries to pick how many regions to collect in each cycle so it stays close to that goal, rather than collecting the whole heap in one go.

Mixed Collections - A Quick Preview

G1 doesn't only clean the Young Generation or only the Old Generation in one shot. Once Old Generation regions start filling up, G1 runs mixed collections - a single GC cycle that collects the Young regions plus a chosen subset of Old regions with the most garbage, all within its pause-time goal.

Fresher Notes

  • Default collector: G1 (Garbage-First) has been the default on server-class machines since Java 9.
  • Regions: the heap is split into many equal regions, each acting as Eden, Survivor, Old or Humongous.
  • Pause goal: set a target with -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis (default 200 ms).

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

G1 divides the heap into 1 MB to 32 MB regions (power of two, about 2048 of them).

  • Young pause: evacuates Eden and Survivor regions, copying live objects.
  • Concurrent cycle: snapshot-at-the-beginning marking finds live data in old regions.
  • Mixed pause: adds old regions with the most reclaimable space.
  • Remembered sets per region track incoming references.
  • Full GC: fallback, single or parallel compaction of the heap.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful options:

  • -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=n: soft pause goal.
  • -XX:G1HeapRegionSize: region size for many humongous objects.
  • -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=45: start of marking.
  • -XX:G1ReservePercent: free space reserve (default 10).

  • -XX:+UseStringDeduplication: shares duplicate String arrays.

expert.content:
G1's Region-Based Architecture in Detail

Heap (e.g. 4GB) split into ~2048 regions (region size auto-chosen, e.g. 2MB each)

[E][E][S][O][E][O][O][H][F][O][E][S][O][F][H][O] ...
 E = Eden   S = Survivor   O = Old   H = Humongous   F = Free

Humongous regions: objects larger than 50% of a region size
are allocated directly into one or more contiguous Humongous
regions, bypassing normal Eden allocation.
Because generations are just a logical label on top of physical regions, G1 can resize Young Generation capacity on the fly each cycle - simply by reclassifying more or fewer regions as Eden - which is what lets it adapt toward the pause-time goal dynamically instead of using a fixed generation size.

The G1 Collection Cycle

A full G1 cycle typically involves these phases:

• Young-only collections - repeated Minor-GC-like collections of Eden/Survivor regions using copying collection, evacuating live objects into Survivor or Old regions.
• Initial Mark - piggybacks on a Young collection, marks GC roots.
• Concurrent Marking - runs alongside the application threads, traces the object graph in Old regions to compute how much garbage each Old region holds, without stopping the world.
• Remark - a short Stop-the-World pause to finalize marking.
• Cleanup - reclaims completely empty regions immediately, and identifies the most garbage-dense Old regions as candidates for the next step.
• Mixed Collections - subsequent collections that evacuate both Young regions and the garbage-densest Old region candidates, spread across multiple cycles to respect the pause-time goal.

G1 vs Parallel GC vs CMS - Comparison

Heap layoutContiguous Young/OldContiguous Young/OldRegion-based
GoalMaximum throughputLow pause, no compactionBalanced throughput + predictable pause
CompactionYes, every collectionNo - suffers fragmentation over timeYes, incrementally per region during evacuation
Pause-time goal supportNo direct controlNo direct controlYes - -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis
Default sinceJava 8 and earlierDeprecated Java 9, removed Java 14Java 9+
Best fitBatch jobs, throughput-critical, few pause concernsLegacy low-latency needs (superseded by G1/ZGC)General-purpose default, medium-to-large heaps needing predictable pauses

Production Tuning Scenario

A web service on an 8GB heap was seeing occasional 800ms pauses under load, well above its 200ms SLA. Investigation of GC logs showed large, infrequent mixed collections were pulling in too many Old regions at once.

Tuning applied:
• Lowered -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis from the default 200ms explicitly to reinforce the target.
• Reduced -XX:G1MixedGCCountTarget effect by tuning -XX:G1HeapWastePercent so G1 became more willing to spread mixed collections across more cycles instead of front-loading Old region reclamation.
• Increased heap headroom with -XX:G1ReservePercent to avoid "to-space exhaustion" fallbacks to a Full GC, which is G1's worst-case, most expensive path.

Result: pause times stabilized under the 200ms goal, at the cost of slightly more frequent (but shorter) mixed collections - a classic latency-vs-frequency tradeoff.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does G1 stand for and what is its main goal?Garbage-First - it aims to provide predictable, configurable pause times while efficiently collecting garbage, even on large heaps
Since which Java version is G1 the default collector?Java 9
How does G1's heap layout differ from older collectors?G1 divides the heap into many equal-sized regions dynamically labeled Eden, Survivor, Old, or Humongous, instead of fixed contiguous generations
What is a Humongous region?A region (or set of contiguous regions) used to allocate an object larger than 50% of the standard region size
What is a mixed collection in G1?A GC cycle that collects Young regions together with a chosen subset of the most garbage-dense Old regions, within the pause-time goal

Why is G1 named "Garbage-First"?Because it prioritizes collecting the regions containing the most garbage first, to reclaim the most memory for the least work

Mid-Level Notes

  • Garbage first: G1 evacuates the regions with the most garbage first, to get the most space for the least pause.
  • Concurrent marking: it marks old regions while the app runs, then runs mixed collections that include old regions.
  • Humongous objects: objects of half a region or more get their own regions and can cause fragmentation.

Senior Notes

  • Tuning: keep it simple, set -Xmx and a realistic pause goal; avoid fixing young size, which disables adaptation.
  • IHOP: -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent decides when concurrent marking starts.
  • Failure signs: "To-space exhausted" or Full GC in logs means G1 could not keep up; give it more headroom.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Pause goal too low (like 5 ms): G1 collects too little and falls behind.
  • Fixed -Xmn: removes adaptive sizing.
  • Many humongous allocations: raise region size or split the data.
  • Heap too tight: To-space exhausted; add headroom.
  • Copying old CMS flags: CMS was removed in JDK 14.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning approach:

  • Start with defaults and only set heap size and pause goal.
  • Lower IHOP if marking starts too late and Full GCs appear.
  • Check humongous counts in logs with -Xlog:gc+humongous.
  • Compare throughput against Parallel for batch jobs.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a microservice with a 4 GB heap needs p99 under 300 ms.

  • G1 with a 100 ms pause goal meets this.
  • Pauses of 30 to 80 ms are seen in logs.
  • Bulk imports of 50 MB arrays caused humongous Full GCs, so they are streamed.

beginner.content:
What is ZGC?

ZGC (short for Z Garbage Collector) is a scalable, low-latency garbage collector introduced as an experimental feature in Java 11 and made production-ready in later releases. Its headline promise is sub-millisecond pause times, even on heaps that are hundreds of gigabytes in size.

Where G1 aims for a configurable, "reasonably low" pause, ZGC aims to make Stop-the-World pauses almost disappear entirely, regardless of how large the heap gets.

Why "Ultra-Low-Latency" Matters

Some applications - trading systems, real-time bidding platforms, large in-memory caches, latency-sensitive APIs - cannot tolerate even a 100-200ms pause, because every request being processed at that instant freezes along with it. ZGC is designed specifically for this class of application, where predictable, tiny pauses matter more than maximum raw throughput.

Concurrent Collection - The Big Idea

Traditional collectors stop all application threads ("Stop-the-World") while they trace and move objects, because moving an object while a thread is reading it is unsafe.

ZGC instead does almost all of its work concurrently - while your application threads keep running - including the hardest part: actually relocating (moving) live objects in memory. This is what allows it to keep pauses so short.

How to Enable ZGC

Turning ZGC on is a single JVM flag - no code changes are needed in your application.

When Should You Reach for ZGC?

• Your application has a strict, low latency SLA (e.g. p99 response time under 10ms).
• You run a very large heap (many GB to TB range) and pause times with older collectors scale badly with heap size.
• You can tolerate slightly higher CPU usage and memory overhead in exchange for near-elimination of long pauses.

If your workload is a batch job or offline data pipeline where total throughput matters more than pause time, a throughput-oriented collector (like Parallel GC) is usually a better fit than ZGC.

Fresher Notes

  • Low latency: ZGC keeps pauses very short (typically under a millisecond in modern JDKs), almost independent of heap size.
  • Concurrent: marking, relocation and reference processing run while application threads keep working.
  • Enable: -XX:+UseZGC; since JDK 21 add -XX:+ZGenerational for the generational mode.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

ZGC does almost all work concurrently.

  • Colored pointers: metadata bits in 64-bit references mark state.
  • Load barrier: every reference read checks the color and fixes stale pointers.
  • Phases: short pause mark start, concurrent mark, short pause mark end, concurrent relocate.
  • Pages: small, medium and large pages are relocated to compact memory.
  • Generational (JDK 21): minor cycles for young, major cycles for old.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options (JDK 17 and 21):

  • -XX:+UseZGC: select ZGC.
  • -XX:+ZGenerational: JDK 21 generational mode.
  • -Xmx: leave headroom, ZGC needs free memory to relocate.
  • -XX:SoftMaxHeapSize: soft target below Xmx.
  • -XX:ConcGCThreads: concurrent worker count.
  • -XX:+UseLargePages: may cut TLB misses.

expert.content:
Colored Pointers

ZGC's core trick for enabling concurrent relocation is a technique called colored pointers. On 64-bit systems, object references (pointers) have far more bits than are needed to address memory, so ZGC "steals" a handful of unused high-order bits in every reference and uses them to store metadata about the object's GC state directly in the pointer itself:

• Whether the object has been marked as live in this GC cycle
• Whether the object has already been relocated
• Whether the reference still needs to be "remapped" to the object's new address

Because this metadata lives in the pointer, not in a separate side table, the JVM can inspect and update a reference's GC status extremely cheaply, without needing to stop other threads to keep bookkeeping data consistent.

Load Barriers and Concurrent Relocation

ZGC inserts a lightweight check called a load barrier on every reference read from the heap. When a thread reads a reference, the barrier examines its colored bits: 

Thread reads reference "ref" from the heap
        |
        v
Load barrier inspects ref's color bits
        |
   +----+----------------------+
   |                           |
Good color              Bad color (object relocated / needs remap)
   |                           |
Use ref directly       Slow path: look up new address,
(fast, common case)     fix up the reference on the fly,
                         then continue using it

Result: the application thread never sees a stale
pointer to a moved object, without ever needing a
Stop-the-World pause to fix up references globally.
This is what allows ZGC to relocate (move) objects while application threads keep running - each thread fixes up any reference it happens to touch, one reference at a time, instead of the JVM pausing everyone to fix all references at once.

ZGC vs G1 vs Shenandoah - Comparison

AspectG1ZGCShenandoah
Typical pause targetTens to low hundreds of msSub-millisecondSub-millisecond to low single-digit ms
Core techniqueRegion-based, mostly Stop-the-World evacuationColored pointers + concurrent load barriersBrooks forwarding pointers + concurrent compaction
Scales to very large heaps?Good up to several GB, pauses grow with heapYes - pause time largely independent of heap sizeYes, similar goal to ZGC
CPU / memory overheadLowerHigher (barrier checks, extra metadata)Higher (forwarding pointer per object)
Default sinceJava 9Production-ready Java 15+ (generational ZGC in Java 21+)Not the JDK default (OpenJDK backport, Red Hat-driven)
Best fitGeneral-purpose defaultUltra-low-latency, very large heapsUltra-low-latency, similar use case to ZGC

Production Scenario: Migrating to ZGC

A real-time bidding platform running G1 on a 64GB heap was seeing occasional pauses of 300-500ms during mixed collections, violating a strict 20ms p99 SLA for bid responses.

Steps taken:
• Switched from -XX:+UseG1GC to -XX:+UseZGC (Java 17, then later generational ZGC on Java 21 with -XX:+ZGenerational for better throughput on high-allocation-rate workloads).
• Verified enough spare CPU headroom existed, since ZGC's concurrent work runs alongside application threads and consumes extra CPU cycles that G1's Stop-the-World phases did not.
• Monitored with GC logging (-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log) to confirm pause times dropped into the sub-millisecond range consistently.

Result: p99 pause-related latency dropped from hundreds of ms to effectively negligible, at the cost of roughly 10-15% higher steady-state CPU usage - an acceptable tradeoff given the strict SLA.

What are colored pointers?References that use spare unused bits in a 64-bit pointer to store GC metadata (marked, relocated, remap-needed) directly in the reference itself
What is a load barrier in ZGC?A lightweight check inserted on every heap reference read that inspects the pointer's color bits and fixes up stale references on the fly if needed

  • Colored pointers and load barriers: metadata in pointer bits and a check on each reference load let ZGC move objects concurrently.
  • Heap range: it scales from small heaps to multi-terabyte heaps (up to 16 TB).
  • Cost: it uses more CPU and some extra memory than G1, so throughput can be a little lower.

Senior Notes

  • Generational ZGC: JDK 21 adds young and old generations, cutting allocation stalls and memory overhead; it became the default ZGC mode in JDK 23.
  • Allocation stall: if the app allocates faster than ZGC reclaims, threads wait; add heap or concurrent threads.
  • Alternatives: Shenandoah is another low-pause collector (OpenJDK builds); Parallel suits batch throughput.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Heap sized exactly to live data: allocation stalls; add 20 to 30 percent.
  • Too few CPUs: concurrent threads compete with the app.
  • Expecting best throughput: Parallel is faster for batch jobs.
  • Assuming no pauses: they are tiny but exist.
  • Using non-generational ZGC on JDK 21 for high allocation rates: add -XX:+ZGenerational.

beginner.content:
What is a GC Cycle?

A GC cycle is one complete run of the garbage collector - from deciding it needs to collect, to actually reclaiming memory, to handing control back to your application. Every GC cycle, regardless of which collector is running, generally goes through the same three conceptual phases: Mark, Sweep/Compact, and Promote.

Phase 1: Mark

The collector starts from the GC Roots (stack variables, static fields) and walks every reference it can find, marking each object it reaches as "alive". Anything it never reaches during this walk is garbage.

Phase 2: Sweep / Compact

Once marking is done, the collector reclaims memory from every unmarked (garbage) object. Many collectors then also compact - sliding the remaining live objects together - so that free memory ends up as one large, contiguous block instead of scattered small gaps.

Phase 3: Promote

Objects that have survived several GC cycles in the Young Generation get promoted to the Old Generation, since they've proven they are likely to stick around for a while. This ties directly into the Generational GC design covered in the previous topic.

What is a Stop-the-World Pause?

During key parts of a GC cycle (especially marking), the collector often needs to pause every application thread so the object graph doesn't change while it's being examined. This pause is called a Stop-the-World (STW) event.

This is exactly why GC tuning matters in real systems - a long STW pause means your application literally freezes for that duration, which can cause timeouts, dropped connections, or missed deadlines.

Fresher Notes

  • Young and old: new objects start in the young generation; objects that survive several collections are promoted to the old generation.
  • Minor GC cleans only the young generation and is frequent and short; a major or full GC touches the old generation too and takes longer.
  • Reachability: an object is garbage when no GC root (thread stack, static field, JNI reference) can reach it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A tracing collector finds live objects and reclaims the rest.

  • Roots: thread stacks, statics, JNI handles and loaded classes.
  • Marking: follows references from roots; unmarked objects are garbage.
  • Generational hypothesis: most objects die young, so collecting the young generation is cheap.
  • Copying: survivors move from eden to a survivor space, and their age grows with each cycle until promotion.
  • G1: splits the heap into regions; young-only phases, a concurrent mark and mixed collections form the cycle.
  • Safepoints: pause phases begin when all threads reach a safepoint.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Collection kinds and the log lines you see:

  • Pause Young (Normal): routine young collection.
  • Pause Young (Concurrent Start): a young pause that also starts marking.
  • Concurrent Mark Cycle: runs beside the application.
  • Pause Young (Mixed): young plus old regions.
  • Pause Full: the fallback, single-pass compaction of the whole heap.
  • Parallel GC: generational, stop-the-world, throughput focused.
  • ZGC and Shenandoah: concurrent, short pauses.

Anatomy of a Full GC Cycle

1. Allocation Failure / Threshold Reached
        |
        v
2. Stop-the-World: pause all application ("mutator") threads
        |
        v
3. MARK
   - Traverse from GC Roots, mark every reachable object
   - Modern collectors do this in parallel across GC worker threads
        |
        v
4. SWEEP
   - Reclaim memory occupied by unmarked (dead) objects
        |
        v
5. COMPACT (if used)
   - Slide live objects together to eliminate fragmentation
   - Update all references to point to new object addresses
        |
        v
6. PROMOTE
   - Objects past the tenuring threshold move Young -> Old Generation
        |
        v
7. Resume application threads
Not every cycle runs every step - a Minor GC only performs steps 3-6 scoped to the Young Generation, while a Full GC runs the entire pipeline across the whole heap.

Stop-the-World vs Concurrent Phases

Modern collectors try to move as much work as possible out of the Stop-the-World pause and into concurrent phases that run alongside the application:
PhaseTypically STW?Why
Initial MarkYes (usually brief)Must snapshot GC roots consistently before app threads resume
Concurrent MarkingNoCan tolerate the object graph changing slightly if it re-checks (via write barriers)
RemarkYes (short)Finalizes marking, catches objects that changed during concurrent marking
SweepCollector-dependentReclaiming clearly-dead memory is often safe concurrently
Evacuation / CompactionCollector-dependent (STW in G1, mostly concurrent in ZGC/Shenandoah)Moving live objects while threads read them requires either a pause or a barrier mechanism (e.g. colored pointers)

Write Barriers - Keeping Concurrent Marking Correct

When marking happens concurrently with running application threads, there's a risk: the application could create a new reference from an already-marked "black" object to a not-yet-marked "white" object, and if the collector never revisits the black object, it could wrongly reclaim the white object while it's still in use.

Collectors solve this with a write barrier - a small piece of code the JVM injects on every reference field write, which records ("remembers") that a change happened so the marking phase can re-examine affected objects during Remark. This is what keeps concurrent marking correct.

Production Scenario: Diagnosing a Long GC Cycle

A service running Parallel GC on a 16GB heap saw a 2.5 second Full GC pause during a nightly batch job, causing a cascade of client timeouts. GC log analysis (-Xlog:gc*,gc+heap=debug:file=gc.log) showed:

• Old Generation occupancy climbed steadily during the batch job (a large in-memory sort operation).
• A Full GC was triggered when Old Gen filled completely, forcing a full Mark-Sweep-Compact across the entire heap in one Stop-the-World pause - Parallel GC has no concurrent phases at all.

Fix: switched to G1 (-XX:+UseG1GC) so Old Generation marking could run concurrently, and split the sort operation into smaller batches to reduce peak Old Gen occupancy - cutting the worst observed pause from 2.5s to under 150ms.
