What is a Stop-the-World pause?A pause where all application threads are frozen so the garbage collector can safely examine or move objects without the object graph changing underneath it
Why do some GC phases need to be Stop-the-World while others can be concurrent?Phases that require a globally consistent snapshot (like finalizing marks) need a pause; phases that can tolerate ongoing changes if tracked (like concurrent marking with write barriers) don't
What is a write barrier used for in GC?To record reference field writes during concurrent marking so the collector can revisit and correctly re-mark objects that changed mid-cycle
What's the difference between Sweep and Compact?Sweep reclaims memory from dead objects in place, leaving fragmentation; Compact additionally slides live objects together to eliminate that fragmentation
Why does Parallel GC tend to have longer Full GC pauses than G1?Parallel GC has no concurrent phases - the entire Mark-Sweep-Compact cycle runs Stop-the-World, unlike G1 which does most marking concurrently
What typically triggers a Full GC?The Old Generation (or whole heap) filling up such that a Minor GC or mixed collection alone cannot free enough space, or an explicit System.gc() call
How would you diagnose a long GC pause in production?Enable and analyze GC logs (e.g. -Xlog:gc*) to identify which phase and generation caused the pause, then correlate with allocation patterns or heap sizing

Mid-Level Notes

  • Stop-the-world: all application threads pause at a safepoint while the collector runs its pause phases.
  • Premature promotion: a survivor space that is too small pushes short-lived objects into the old generation and causes more full GCs.
  • Allocation rate drives minor GC frequency, while the live set drives pause time and old generation growth.

Senior Notes

  • G1 cycle: young-only collections, then a concurrent marking cycle, then mixed collections that also reclaim old regions.
  • Concurrent collectors (ZGC, Shenandoah) do marking and relocation while the application runs, so pauses stay short and mostly independent of heap size.
  • Read the log: use -Xlog:gc* and look at pause time, heap before and after, and the cause such as Allocation Failure or Humongous Allocation.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes with GC and the fix for each:

  • Calling System.gc(): triggers a full pause; remove it or set -XX:+DisableExplicitGC if a library calls it.
  • Relying on finalizers: they delay reclamation; use try-with-resources or Cleaner.
  • Static caches that never evict: they stay reachable; use bounded caches.
  • Unremoved listeners: the registry keeps the object alive.
  • Large temporary arrays: in G1 they become humongous allocations; reuse or split them.
  • ThreadLocal in pools: values live as long as the thread; call remove().

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance levers:

  • Lower allocation rate: fewer minor GCs.
  • Smaller live set: shorter marking and copying.
  • Right young size: too small promotes garbage early; too large lengthens pauses on some collectors.
  • Survivor sizing: watch the tenuring threshold in the log.
  • Avoid humongous objects (half a G1 region or larger).
  • Watch: GC time percentage, allocation rate and old generation after-GC occupancy.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order service shows 1.5 second latency spikes every few minutes.

  • Evidence: the GC log shows Pause Full (G1 Humongous Allocation).
  • Cause: a report builder allocates a 40 MB array per request.
  • Fix: stream the data in chunks, then confirm that the full GCs disappear.

What Does "Tuning the GC" Mean?

GC tuning means adjusting JVM startup flags so the garbage collector behaves better for your specific application - fewer pauses, shorter pauses, less memory used, or higher throughput, depending on what you actually need.

You don't change your Java source code to tune GC - you pass extra flags when starting the JVM.

-Xms and -Xmx: Setting Heap Size

The two most fundamental flags control how much heap memory the JVM can use:

• -Xms - the initial heap size when the JVM starts.
• -Xmx - the maximum heap size the JVM is allowed to grow to.

Example: java -Xms512m -Xmx2g MyApp starts with a 512MB heap and allows it to grow up to 2GB as needed.

Choosing a Collector

You can explicitly choose which garbage collector the JVM should use:

• -XX:+UseG1GC - the general-purpose default since Java 9.
• -XX:+UseZGC - for ultra-low-latency needs.
• -XX:+UseParallelGC - for maximum throughput, batch-style workloads.

If you don't specify one, the JVM picks a sensible default automatically (G1 on modern JVMs).

Setting a Pause Time Goal

With G1, you can tell the collector how long you're willing to let a pause be, and it will try its best to honor that target:

java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 MyApp

Turning On GC Logging

Before tuning anything, you need visibility into what the GC is actually doing. The modern unified logging flag is:

-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,level,tags

This writes a detailed log of every GC event - which phase ran, how long it took, and how much memory was reclaimed - to gc.log, which you can then inspect or feed into a GC log analysis tool.

Fresher Notes

  • Measure first: turn on GC logging and tune only when pauses or throughput are a real problem.
  • Heap size is set with -Xms (initial) and -Xmx (maximum); a heap that is too small causes frequent GC.
  • Default collector: since JDK 9 G1 is the default on server-class machines; the default is fine for most applications.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Tuning works by trading three goals against each other.

  • Throughput: the share of time spent running application code.
  • Latency: the length of the longest pauses.
  • Footprint: heap and native memory used.
  • G1 ergonomics: sizes regions and the young generation dynamically to meet the pause goal.
  • Adaptive sizing: fixing the young size with flags disables part of that adaptation.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful flags (JDK 17 and 21):

  • Sizing: -Xms, -Xmx, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, -XX:InitialRAMPercentage.
  • Collector: -XX:+UseG1GC, -XX:+UseParallelGC, -XX:+UseZGC, -XX:+UseSerialGC.
  • G1: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, -XX:G1HeapRegionSize, -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent.
  • ZGC: -XX:+ZGenerational on JDK 21.
  • Threads: -XX:ParallelGCThreads, -XX:ConcGCThreads.
  • Logging: -Xlog:gc*.

Production Tuning Walkthrough: Diagnosing Frequent Full GCs

A microservice on G1 with -Xmx4g was hitting Full GCs every few minutes, each taking 1-2 seconds, and memory usage kept climbing back to near-max after each collection - a classic sign of a memory leak, not just under-tuning.

Diagnostic steps:
• Enabled -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,level,tags and watched Old Gen occupancy after each cycle - it never dropped back to baseline, confirming a leak rather than a sizing issue.
• Added -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps to capture a heap dump automatically when it eventually failed.
• Analyzed the heap dump and found a static Map used as an unbounded cache, growing without eviction.

Fix: replaced the unbounded cache with a bounded, size-limited cache (eviction policy). GC frequency and pause duration returned to normal immediately - illustrating that GC flags cannot fix an actual memory leak, only application-level fixes can; tuning only helps when the underlying object lifetimes are legitimately what they should be.

  • Containers: prefer -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 so the heap follows the container memory limit.

Senior Notes

  • Choose the collector: Parallel for batch throughput, G1 for balanced services, ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC) for very large heaps and tight latency.
  • Change one thing at a time and compare logs under a realistic load test, not a microbenchmark.
  • Fix allocation first: reducing garbage and live data beats any flag.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Huge flag lists copied from blogs: start from defaults and add one flag with evidence.
  • Tiny pause goal: MaxGCPauseMillis=10 on G1 makes young generation tiny and collections too frequent.
  • Heap larger than the container: the OOM killer ends the process; leave room for non-heap memory.
  • Fixing the young size with -Xmn and losing adaptivity.
  • Tuning when the problem is a leak: more heap only delays the failure.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance method:

  • Baseline: record p50, p99 and GC overhead under a realistic load.
  • Change one flag and repeat the same test.
  • Keep a change only if the numbers improve.
  • Prefer code fixes: reduce allocation and live data first.
  • Tools: GC logs with an analyzer, JFR and JMH -prof gc.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a nightly batch of 20 million rows runs 40 percent slower after moving to a container.

  • Finding: the JVM sees 1 CPU and picks Serial GC.
  • Fix: give the container 4 CPUs, or set the collector explicitly, and use a fixed heap.
  • Check: -Xlog:gc shows which collector started.

What is the JIT Compiler?

JIT stands for Just-In-Time compiler. It is a part of the JVM that converts frequently used bytecode into native machine code while the program is running, so it can execute much faster.

Java code goes through two stages before it becomes machine instructions:
• javac compiles .java source files into .class bytecode (platform-independent).
• The JVM then either interprets that bytecode line by line, or JIT-compiles hot parts of it into native code for the actual CPU.

Interpreter vs JIT-Compiled Code

When a Java program starts, the JVM's interpreter begins executing bytecode immediately - this gives fast startup but slower execution, since every instruction is decoded and executed one at a time, every single time.

• Interpreter - starts fast, runs slow, no upfront compilation delay.
• JIT Compiler - takes a moment to compile, but the resulting native code runs dramatically faster on repeated execution.

The JVM combines both: start with the interpreter for quick startup, then JIT-compile the "hot" methods that run over and over.

What Makes a Method "Hot"?

The JVM keeps an invocation counter for every method and loop. Once a method is called (or a loop iterates) more than a threshold number of times, the JVM marks it as hot and schedules it for JIT compilation on a background compiler thread.

This is why the very first few runs of a Java program (or the first few iterations of a loop) are often slower than later ones - this warm-up period is sometimes called the JIT warm-up.

C1 and C2 - The Two JIT Compilers

The HotSpot JVM (the standard Oracle/OpenJDK JVM) actually ships with two different JIT compilers:

• C1 (Client Compiler) - compiles quickly with light optimizations. Good for fast startup and short-lived programs.
• C2 (Server Compiler) - takes longer to compile but produces highly optimized native code. Good for long-running server applications.

Modern JVMs use both together in a strategy called Tiered Compilation, which we cover next.

Why This Matters to You

Understanding the JIT compiler explains real things you will see in production:
• Why a server "feels slow" for the first minute after deploy and then speeds up (JIT warm-up).
• Why microbenchmarks that don't warm up the JVM give misleading numbers.
• Why load-testing tools often run a "warm-up phase" before taking measurements.

Fresher Notes

  • JIT means just-in-time: the JVM compiles hot bytecode to native machine code while the program runs.
  • Interpreter first: code starts interpreted, and methods or loops that run often get compiled.
  • Warm-up: a program is slower at the start, so benchmarks must warm up before measuring.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

HotSpot profiles code while it runs and compiles what is hot.

  • Levels: 0 interpreter, 1 to 3 C1 (3 adds profiling), 4 C2.
  • Counters: method invocation and loop back-edge counters trigger compilation.
  • OSR: on-stack replacement swaps a running loop into compiled code.
  • Speculation: C2 uses profile data, such as the receiver types seen, and adds uncommon traps.
  • Background threads: compilation runs on separate compiler threads.
  • Code cache: stores the compiled code.

  • Compile everything: -Xcomp is for experiments only.

  • Code cache: -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=256m.
  • Log: -XX:+PrintCompilation, or -Xlog:jit+compilation=debug.

expert.content:
Tiered Compilation in Detail

Since Java 8, the default strategy is Tiered Compilation, which uses C1 and C2 together across five compilation levels:

LevelCompilerDescription
0InterpreterPure bytecode interpretation, gathers profiling data
1C1Simple C1 compile, no profiling (for trivial methods)
2C1C1 compile with invocation/backedge counters only
3C1C1 compile with full profiling (branch, type profiling)
4C2Fully optimized C2 compile using profiling data from level 3

A method typically walks 0 -> 3 -> 4: it's interpreted and profiled, quickly C1-compiled with profiling to get fast speedup sooner, and finally recompiled by C2 once it's proven hot enough to justify heavy optimization. This gives Java both fast warm-up (like C1-only) and peak throughput (like C2-only).

Key Optimizations C2 Performs

• Inlining - replacing a method call with the method body itself, eliminating call overhead and opening the door to further optimizations.
• Loop unrolling - duplicating loop bodies to reduce branch overhead.
• Escape analysis - determining an object never leaves a method, enabling stack allocation or elimination entirely (see the dedicated Escape Analysis topic).
• Dead code elimination - removing code paths that profiling shows are never taken.
• Speculative optimization with deoptimization - C2 will optimize aggressively based on assumptions (e.g. "this call site is monomorphic") and fall back ("deoptimize") to the interpreter if that assumption is later violated.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Tiered compilation: C1 compiles quickly with light optimization, then C2 recompiles the hottest code with heavy optimization.
  • Inlining replaces a small method call with its body and is the base for many other optimizations.
  • Deoptimization: if an assumption proves wrong (for example a new subclass is loaded), the JVM falls back to the interpreter.

Senior Notes

  • See it with -XX:+PrintCompilation and, for inlining, -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining.
  • Code cache: compiled code lives in a limited area, sized by -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize.
  • Benchmark with JMH, which handles warm-up, dead-code elimination and forks for you.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Timing code without warm-up: use JMH.
  • Results unused: the JIT removes dead code, so the loop measures nothing.
  • Huge methods: methods over 8000 bytecodes are not compiled by default (HugeMethodLimit); split them.
  • Code cache full: the log says CodeCache is full and compilation stops.
  • Megamorphic call sites: many receiver types stop inlining.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning for startup and peak speed:

  • Warm-up: send synthetic traffic before a node joins the load balancer.
  • Class data sharing (CDS): speeds up startup.
  • AOT and GraalVM native image: remove warm-up at the cost of peak throughput and flexibility.
  • Monitor: JFR events jdk.Compilation and jdk.Deoptimization.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: p99 latency is bad for the first minute after each deploy.

  • Cause: cold code is interpreted.
  • Fix: warm-up requests on start, readiness only after warm-up, and rolling deploys.

beginner.content:
What is Escape Analysis?

Escape Analysis is a technique the JVM's JIT compiler (C2) uses to figure out whether an object created inside a method ever "escapes" - that is, whether it becomes visible or reachable outside that method.

If the JVM proves an object never escapes, it can skip some of the normal, more expensive steps of object creation (like allocating it on the heap), making the code run faster and reducing garbage collection pressure.

What Does "Escaping" Mean?

An object "escapes" a method if it can be accessed from outside that method after the method returns. Examples:
• It is returned from the method.
• It is stored in a field of another object.
• It is passed to another method that itself lets it escape.
• It is stored in a static variable or shared collection.

If none of these happen, the object is said to be non-escaping - it only ever lives and dies inside that one method call.

Why Should a Beginner Care?

You don't need to write any special code to benefit from escape analysis - it happens automatically inside the JIT compiler once a method gets hot enough. But understanding it explains:
• Why creating small, short-lived helper objects (like a Point or a temporary wrapper) is often "free" in modern Java, contrary to older advice to avoid object creation at all costs.
• Why heavily optimized Java code can sometimes perform close to hand-written low-level code, even though Java is "object heavy."

Scalar Replacement - A Quick Preview

When an object doesn't escape, the JIT compiler can go a step further and completely eliminate the object, replacing its fields with individual local variables (like ints or references) that live only in CPU registers or the stack. This is called scalar replacement, and it is one of the most powerful outcomes of escape analysis - we go deeper into it in the expert section.

Fresher Notes

  • Escape analysis is a C2 JIT optimization that checks whether an object can be seen outside the method or thread that created it.
  • Scalar replacement: if the object does not escape, the JVM can drop the allocation and keep its fields in registers.
  • Result: less heap allocation and less GC work, with no change to the program output.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

C2 builds a connection graph of allocations and references.

  • Input: inlined code, so inlining decides how much it can see.
  • Classification: each allocation is NoEscape, ArgEscape or GlobalEscape.
  • NoEscape: eligible for scalar replacement and lock elision.
  • Limits: arrays larger than EliminateAllocationArraySizeLimit and objects used in merges are often skipped.
  • JDK 21: improved handling of objects at control-flow merges is still evolving, so results vary by version.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Flags (all on by default except the printing ones):

  • -XX:+DoEscapeAnalysis
  • -XX:+EliminateAllocations (scalar replacement)
  • -XX:+EliminateLocks
  • -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintEscapeAnalysis (needs a debug build)
  • Use -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis to compare behavior.

expert.content:
Categories of Escape

The JIT compiler's escape analysis classifies every allocation site into one of three categories:

CategoryMeaningOptimization Enabled
NoEscapeObject is only used within the allocating method (and its inlined callees)Scalar replacement, stack allocation, lock elision
ArgEscapeObject is passed as an argument to another method but doesn't escape globallyLimited - depends on callee's own analysis
GlobalEscapeObject is returned, stored in a field, or otherwise reachable after the method exitsNone - must be heap-allocated normally

Scalar Replacement in Depth

When C2 proves an object is NoEscape, it doesn't just "allocate on the stack" (a common misconception) - it can go further and eliminate the object entirely. The object's fields are "unpacked" into separate scalar values (primitives/references) that the compiler tracks independently, often keeping them in CPU registers. No memory allocation happens at all.

This is why the mental model "escape analysis puts objects on the stack instead of the heap" is only partially correct - the more precise statement is: the object may never be materialized as a memory block at all.

Lock Elision (Biased/Redundant Lock Removal)

Escape analysis also enables lock elision: if a synchronized object is proven to be thread-local (never escapes the current thread), the JIT can remove the synchronized block's locking overhead entirely, since no other thread could ever contend for that lock.

This commonly happens with local StringBuilder usage - even though StringBuffer and older synchronized collection wrappers have internal locks, if an instance never escapes a method, those locks are compiled away.

Escape Analysis and Inlining Work Together

Escape analysis is far more effective when combined with method inlining. Consider a helper method that wraps an object creation and passes it to another small method - if C2 inlines both methods into the caller, the object's full lifecycle becomes visible within a single compiled unit, making it much more likely to be classified as NoEscape. This is one reason very large methods (that exceed inlining size limits) can miss out on escape analysis benefits that smaller, decomposed methods get "for free."

Diagnostic Output: JIT Escape Analysis Log

------------ EscapeAnalysis ------------
com.myapp.Vector3::length
  Allocation: new Vector3  -> NoEscape
  Eliminated: true (scalar replaced into x, y, z)

com.myapp.OrderService::createOrder
  Allocation: new Order    -> GlobalEscape (returned to caller)
  Eliminated: false (heap allocated normally)

Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
A hot method allocates heavily according to a profiler, but GC young-gen pressure is lower than expectedEscape analysis is successfully scalar-replacing most allocations - profiler "allocation counts" can be misleading vs actual heap pressureCross-check profiler allocation sampling against actual GC logs / allocation rate metricsNot a bug - confirm with -XX:+PrintEliminateAllocations that eliminations are happening as expected
Refactoring a large method into smaller ones unexpectedly improves throughputSmaller methods enabled inlining, which let escape analysis see full object lifecycles and scalar-replace allocations that previously escaped analysis boundariesCompare -XX:+PrintEscapeAnalysis output before/after refactor for the same allocation siteKeep hot-path methods small and inlinable; avoid unnecessary indirection in performance-critical code
An object expected to be scalar-replaced is not, and GC pressure stays highThe object escapes via a code path the developer didn't notice - e.g. added to a debug log statement or exception message lazilySearch for any place the object reference is stored, logged, or passed to an unfamiliar APIRemove or restructure the escaping reference (e.g. build the log message from primitives instead of passing the object)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is escape analysis?A JIT compiler technique that determines whether an object's lifetime is confined to the allocating method, enabling optimizations like scalar replacement and lock elision
What does it mean for an object to "escape"?The object becomes reachable outside the method that created it - e.g. returned, stored in a field, or assigned to a static/shared variable
What is scalar replacement?Replacing an object's fields with individual scalar values tracked by the compiler (often in registers), avoiding heap allocation of the object entirely
Does escape analysis guarantee stack allocation?No - the more accurate outcome is the object may never be materialized in memory at all via scalar replacement, not simply moved from heap to stack
What is lock elision?Removing synchronization overhead from a lock proven to only ever be accessed by the current thread (thread-local, non-escaping object)
Why does method inlining improve escape analysis effectiveness?Inlining brings an object's full usage into one compiled scope, making it far more likely the compiler can prove NoEscape
Is escape analysis something a developer configures directly?No - it happens automatically in C2 once a method is hot enough; developers influence it indirectly via code structure (method size, avoiding unnecessary escapes)

Mid-Level Notes

  • Escape states: no escape (stays in the method), arg escape (passed to a call) and global escape (stored in a field or returned).
  • Lock elision: a lock on an object that never escapes its thread can be removed.
  • It is automatic: it is on by default (-XX:+DoEscapeAnalysis) and applies only to hot, compiled code.

Senior Notes

  • Not guaranteed: large methods, failed inlining or branches that leak the object can block it.
  • Not stack allocation: HotSpot does not put objects on the stack; it removes the object and keeps scalars.
  • Verify with allocation profiling or JMH -prof gc, not by guessing; do not rewrite code to chase it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Believing objects go on the stack: they are removed, not stacked.
  • Hand-optimizing readable code into arrays or primitives without proof.
  • Leaking in a rare branch (for example logging the object) blocks the optimization for the whole method.
  • Benchmarks in the interpreter: escape analysis needs C2 compiled code.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Measure with JMH.

  • Profiler: -prof gc reports allocated bytes per operation.
  • Target: close to 0 B/op means allocation was removed.
  • Beware: small changes in the code or JDK can change the result.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a parser creates many small tokens per line, and young GC is busy.

  • Check: JFR allocation profile shows Token as the top allocation.
  • Action: keep the construction and use local to a small, inlinable method so C2 can remove it; if the profile does not improve, reuse a mutable cursor.

beginner.content:
What are JVM Arguments?

JVM arguments are command-line options passed to the java launcher that control how the JVM behaves - things like how much memory it can use, which garbage collector to run, and what diagnostic output to print.

You pass them before the main class name:

java [JVM arguments] -jar myapp.jar [program arguments]
codeExamples:
# Example: run with a max heap of 512 MB and a min heap of 128 MB
java -Xms128m -Xmx512m -jar myapp.jar

beginner.content:
-X Flags (Non-Standard but Common)

Flags starting with a single -X are "non-standard" - not guaranteed identical across every JVM vendor, but the most common ones are supported everywhere in practice. These usually control memory and basic runtime behavior:

• -Xms<size> - initial heap size (e.g. -Xms256m)
• -Xmx<size> - maximum heap size (e.g. -Xmx1g)
• -Xss<size> - thread stack size (e.g. -Xss512k)
• -Xint - run in interpreted-only mode (no JIT)
codeExamples:
# Cap the stack size per thread to 256 KB, useful when running many threads
java -Xss256k -jar myapp.jar

beginner.content:
-XX Flags (Advanced/Non-Standard)

Flags starting with -XX: expose deeper JVM internals - garbage collector selection, JIT behavior, diagnostics, and more. They come in a few shapes:

• Boolean flags - toggled with + or -, e.g. -XX:+PrintGCDetails enables it, -XX:-PrintGCDetails disables it.
• Value flags - set with =, e.g. -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m.
codeExamples:
# Turn on detailed GC logging (older JVMs) and choose the G1 collector
java -XX:+PrintGCDetails -XX:+UseG1GC -jar myapp.jar

# Set the max Metaspace size (where class metadata lives)
java -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m -jar myapp.jar

beginner.content:
Frequently Used Flags Cheat-Sheet

• -Xms512m -Xmx512m - set initial = max heap size (recommended in containers to avoid resize pauses).
• -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError - automatically write a heap dump when the app crashes with OutOfMemoryError.
• -XX:+PrintGCDetails -Xlog:gc* - see what the garbage collector is doing.
• -XX:+UseG1GC / -XX:+UseZGC - choose which garbage collector algorithm to use.

Why This Matters

Getting JVM arguments right is often the single biggest lever for application performance and stability in production - more so than most code-level micro-optimizations. Setting the wrong heap size, or leaving diagnostics off, is one of the most common causes of mysterious "it crashed in prod but not in dev" incidents.

Fresher Notes

  • Three families: standard options (-version, -cp), -X options (-Xmx512m) and -XX options (-XX:+UseG1GC).
  • Boolean flags use + to enable and - to disable, as in -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError.
  • Value flags use =, as in -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200; system properties use -Dkey=value.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The launcher parses arguments in a fixed order.

  • Sources: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, the command line, @argfiles, and JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS (JDK 9 and later).
  • Ergonomics: flags you do not set are chosen from CPUs and memory, including container limits.
  • Flag kinds: product, diagnostic, experimental, manageable (changeable at run time).
  • Class path: arguments after the main class or jar go to main(String[]).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common groups:

  • Memory: -Xms, -Xmx, -Xss, -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize, -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize.
  • GC: -XX:+UseG1GC, -Xlog:gc*.
  • Diagnostics: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError, -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary.
  • Modules: --add-opens, --add-modules.
  • Preview: --enable-preview.

expert.content:
Standard vs Non-Standard vs Experimental/Diagnostic Flags

The JVM classifies its flags into tiers of stability, which matters for how safely you can rely on them across versions and vendors:

CategoryPrefixStabilityExample
StandardSingle dash, no XSupported by all JVM implementations, stable across versions-cp, -jar, -D
Non-standard (X)-XHotSpot-specific but widely relied upon; can change without notice-Xms, -Xmx, -Xss
Advanced (XX)-XX:Internal tuning flags, subject to change between releases-XX:+UseG1GC
Diagnostic/Experimental-XX:+Unlock... requiredUnstable, for debugging the JVM itself; requires unlocking-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintCompilation

Discovering All Flags and Their Current Values

You rarely need to memorize every flag - the JVM can tell you what it's using and what's available.
codeExamples:
# Print every flag and its current value (including defaults you didn't set)
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -i heapsize

# Diff flags between two configurations - useful for reproducing a prod incident locally
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -Xmx512m -version > with_512m.txt
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -Xmx2g   -version > with_2g.txt
diff with_512m.txt with_2g.txt

# Inspect a running JVM's actual flags via jcmd (no restart needed)
jcmd <pid> VM.flags

expert.content:
Container-Aware Memory Flags

Before JDK 10, the JVM would read the host machine's total memory/CPU count even when running inside a container with much tighter cgroup limits - a classic cause of containers being OOM-killed even though -Xmx "looked fine." Since JDK 10+ (and backported to 8u191+), the JVM is container-aware by default via -XX:+UseContainerSupport.

Instead of a fixed -Xmx, many teams now use percentage-based flags so the same image scales correctly across different container memory limits:

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 - use up to 75% of the container's memory limit for the heap.
codeExamples:
# Recommended pattern for containerized services (Kubernetes, Docker)
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0 -XX:+UseContainerSupport -jar myapp.jar

The {ergonomic} tag means the JVM chose this value automatically based on detected hardware/container limits, not a value you explicitly set - important to check when diagnosing "why is my heap this size" issues.

Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix

App runs fine locally but fails to start in CI with "Invalid initial heap size"A flag was set with a value larger than available memory in the CI runner, or with inconsistent unitsCheck the exact flags passed by the CI pipeline vs local run scriptsAlign CI resource limits with the flags, or make heap sizing percentage-based instead of hardcoded

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the difference between -X and -XX flags?-X flags are non-standard but common HotSpot options (like -Xmx); -XX flags expose deeper, more volatile internal tuning options, often toggled with +/- or set with =
What does -Xms and -Xmx control?-Xms sets the initial heap size, -Xmx sets the maximum heap size the JVM is allowed to grow to
Why set -Xms equal to -Xmx in production?To avoid runtime heap resizing pauses and ensure predictable memory behavior, especially in containers with fixed memory limits
What does -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError do?Automatically writes a heap dump file to disk when the JVM throws an OutOfMemoryError, useful for post-mortem analysis
What is MaxRAMPercentage used for?Sizing the heap as a percentage of the container's memory limit rather than a fixed value, so the same image scales correctly across different container sizes
How can you see all JVM flags and their actual values, including defaults?Run java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version, or use jcmd <pid> VM.flags on a running process
Why might a container be OOM-killed even though -Xmx is well within the container limit?Because -Xmx only bounds heap memory - Metaspace, thread stacks, JIT code cache, and native/direct memory are separate and add to total RSS

Mid-Level Notes

  • Heap flags: -Xms, -Xmx, -Xss for thread stack size and -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
  • JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS adds flags through an environment variable, which is handy when you cannot edit the start command.
  • Argument files: java @args.txt reads options from a file, useful for long command lines.

Senior Notes

  • Inspect the real values with -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal or jcmd PID VM.flags.
  • Containers: JDK 17 and 21 are container aware; use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage instead of a fixed -Xmx.
  • Unlock carefully: experimental and diagnostic flags need -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions or -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions and may change between releases.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Xmx equal to container memory: no room for metaspace, stacks and buffers; use 60 to 75 percent.
  • Flag after the jar name: it becomes an application argument and is ignored by the JVM.
  • Typo in a flag: an unknown -XX flag stops the JVM; add -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions only deliberately.
  • Obsolete flags such as -XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC, removed in JDK 14.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Xms = Xmx avoids resize pauses.
  • -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch commits memory at start for steadier latency but slows startup.
  • Xss larger stacks cost memory per thread; many threads need a small value.
  • Large pages and NUMA flags only help specific workloads; test them.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a Kubernetes pod is OOMKilled although the heap looks fine.

  • Cause: -Xmx equals the pod limit, and metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers exceed it.
  • Fix: use MaxRAMPercentage=70, and track non-heap with Native Memory Tracking.

beginner.content:
What is a Heap Dump?

A heap dump is a snapshot of every object living in the JVM's heap memory at a single point in time - every object, its fields, and the references between objects. It's saved to a file (usually with a .hprof extension) that you can open later in an analysis tool.

Think of it like a photograph of your application's memory - frozen at the exact moment you took it, so you can study it calmly instead of guessing about a moving target.

Why Do We Need Heap Dumps?

Heap dumps are the primary tool for answering questions like:
• Why is my application running out of memory (OutOfMemoryError)?
• Which objects are consuming the most memory right now?
• Is there a memory leak - are objects piling up that should have been garbage collected?

Without a heap dump, you're mostly guessing from symptoms. With one, you can see exactly what's in memory.

Generating a Heap Dump Automatically on OutOfMemoryError

The easiest way to capture a heap dump exactly when it matters most is to tell the JVM to write one automatically the moment it throws OutOfMemoryError.
codeExamples:
# Automatically dump the heap to a file when OutOfMemoryError occurs
java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps/myapp.hprof -jar myapp.jar

beginner.content:
Generating a Heap Dump On-Demand with jmap

You don't have to wait for a crash - you can trigger a heap dump manually while the application is running, using the jmap command-line tool that ships with the JDK.
codeExamples:
# Find the process ID of your running Java app
jps -l

# Trigger a live heap dump for that process
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=myapp.hprof 12345

beginner.content:
Analyzing a Heap Dump

A raw .hprof file is not human-readable - you open it in a specialized analysis tool:
• Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT) - the most popular free tool, shows the biggest objects, retained size, and suspected leaks.
• VisualVM - bundled with the JDK, simpler but useful for a quick look.
• JMC (Java Mission Control) - can also open heap dumps alongside JFR recordings.

These tools let you browse "who is holding onto this object" (the reference chain), which is usually the key to finding a leak.

Fresher Notes

  • Heap dump: a snapshot of every live object in the heap, saved as an .hprof file.
  • Use it to find memory leaks and see which objects take the most memory.
  • Automatic dump: start the JVM with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError so the evidence is saved when it crashes.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The HPROF file stores heap structure rather than a copy of the live program.

  • Content: classes, instances, field values, arrays and GC roots.
  • Creation: the JVM stops at a safepoint and writes the heap; this pause grows with heap size.
  • live option: runs a full GC first, so the dump holds only reachable objects.
  • Compression: JDK 17 and later can write with jcmd PID GC.heap_dump -gz=5 file.hprof.gz (check your JDK build).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to obtain a dump:

  • On OOM: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps.
  • jcmd: GC.heap_dump.
  • jmap: -dump:live,format=b,file=....
  • JMX: HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean.dumpHeap.
  • Tools: VisualVM or JConsole buttons.
  • Analysis: Eclipse MAT (Leak Suspects report), VisualVM, IntelliJ profiler.

expert.content:
What's Actually Inside a Heap Dump

A .hprof file contains the full object graph at capture time:
• Every object instance, its class, and field values.
• Every array and its contents.
• Class metadata (static fields, class loaders).
• Thread stacks and local variables referencing heap objects (so you can see GC roots).

From this, an analyzer computes two crucial numbers for each object:
• Shallow size - the memory used by the object itself, not counting what it references.
• Retained size - the total memory that would be freed if this object became unreachable, including everything it exclusively keeps alive.

live vs Full Heap Dumps

ModeCommandWhat HappensTrade-off
Live objects onlyjmap -dump:live,...Forces a full GC first, then dumps only reachable objectsSmaller, cleaner dump; but the forced GC causes a pause and can hide short-lived garbage that might be relevant
Full heapjmap -dump:... (no live)Dumps everything currently in the heap, including garbage not yet collectedLarger file; useful for allocation-rate analysis, but noisier for leak-hunting

For leak investigations, live dumps are usually preferred since a real leak means objects survive even a full GC.

Finding a Leak: The "Dominator Tree" Approach

In Eclipse MAT, the most effective workflow for a suspected leak is:
1. Take two heap dumps some time apart (e.g. 30 minutes) under similar load.
2. Run MAT's "Leak Suspects Report," which automatically flags large retained-size clusters.
3. Use the "Dominator Tree" view, sorted by retained size, to find the single object subtree consuming the most memory.
4. Trace "Path to GC Roots" (excluding weak/soft references) on the suspicious object to see exactly what's still holding a reference to it - this is usually the leak's root cause (e.g. a static Map that's never cleared, or a listener never unregistered).
codeExamples:
# Take two dumps 30 minutes apart to compare growth
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap_t1.hprof 12345
# ... wait 30 minutes under load ...
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap_t2.hprof 12345

# In Eclipse MAT: File > Open, then use "Compare Basket" to diff heap_t1 vs heap_t2

expert.content:
Sample MAT Dominator Tree Output

Class                                   Shallow Heap   Retained Heap    %
com.myapp.cache.SessionCache            48             612,458,320    68.2%
  java.util.HashMap$Node[]              1,048,608      612,000,000    68.1%
    com.myapp.model.UserSession x 42000 -              608,100,000    67.7%
java.lang.Thread[]                      312            89,204,112     9.9%
byte[]                                  -               45,120,880    5.0%
Here, SessionCache retains 68% of the entire heap via a HashMap that has grown to 42,000 UserSession entries - a strong signal that sessions are never being evicted, a classic unbounded-cache leak.

Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
Service memory usage climbs steadily over days until it OOMs and restartsUnbounded cache or collection (e.g. static Map) never evicting entriesTake two heap dumps hours apart, diff dominator trees, look for the class growing unboundedAdd eviction policy (TTL/size-bounded cache like Caffeine) or explicitly clear stale entries

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a heap dump?A snapshot file (.hprof) of every object, its fields, and reference graph in the JVM heap at a point in time
How do you automatically capture a heap dump on OutOfMemoryError?Run the JVM with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=<path>

What does the "live" option in jmap do?Forces a full GC before dumping, so only currently reachable objects are included, producing a smaller/cleaner dump
What tool is most commonly used to analyze a heap dump?Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT), which offers a Leak Suspects Report and a Dominator Tree view
How would you confirm a memory leak using two heap dumps?Take dumps at two points in time under similar load, compare dominator trees/retained sizes, and look for a class whose count/retained size grows without bound

Mid-Level Notes

  • Manual dump: jcmd PID GC.heap_dump file.hprof or jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof PID.
  • Analyze with Eclipse MAT, VisualVM or IntelliJ; sort by retained size to find the real owners.
  • Size: the file is about as large as the used heap, so make sure the disk has room.

Senior Notes

  • Shallow vs retained size: retained size is memory freed if the object were collected, and it points to the leak root.
  • Dominator tree and path to GC roots explain why an object stays alive.
  • Security: a dump contains passwords, tokens and personal data, so protect and delete it like a secret.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • No dump path space: the dump fails because the disk is full; point HeapDumpPath to a big volume.
  • Looking at shallow size only: shallow size hides the owner; use retained size.
  • Opening a huge dump on a laptop: raise the MAT memory in MemoryAnalyzer.ini.
  • Dump after restart: the leak evidence is lost; take it before restarting.
  • Sharing dumps over chat or tickets, leaking secrets.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and safety:

  • Pause: expect seconds per few GB, and take the node out of rotation first.
  • Disk: reserve about the heap size.
  • Two dumps: take one early and one later and compare the growth.
  • Lighter option: GC.class_histogram or a JFR old-object sample.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: heap grows until OOM every two days.

  • Dump: taken automatically at the OOM.
  • MAT: the dominator tree shows a static Map holding 300 MB of Session objects.
  • Path to GC roots: leads to a listener registry that is never cleared.
  • Fix: remove the listener on logout and bound the map.

beginner.content:
What is a Thread Dump?

A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread running inside the JVM at a single moment - what each thread is doing right now, and its full call stack. It's a plain text report, not a binary file like a heap dump, so you can read it directly in a terminal or editor.

Thread dumps are the go-to tool when an application seems stuck, hung, or unresponsive - they show you exactly what every thread was doing at the moment things froze.

What Does a Thread Dump Show You?

For every single thread, a thread dump shows:
• The thread's name and ID.
• Its current state (RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, etc).
• Its full stack trace - which method it's currently executing, and the chain of calls that got it there.
• Any locks it holds or is waiting for.
codeExamples:
"http-nio-8080-exec-3" #45 daemon prio=5 os_prio=0 tid=0x00007f cpu=120.50ms
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
        at com.myapp.service.OrderService.calculateTotal(OrderService.java:88)
        at com.myapp.controller.OrderController.checkout(OrderController.java:41)
        at java.base/java.lang.reflect.Method.invoke(Method.java:568)

beginner.content:
Generating a Thread Dump with jstack

The simplest way to get a thread dump is with the jstack command-line tool included in the JDK.
codeExamples:
# Find the process ID
jps -l

# Capture a thread dump to a file
jstack 12345 > thread_dump.txt

beginner.content:
Generating a Thread Dump with kill -3 (Linux/Mac)

On Unix-like systems, you can also send a SIGQUIT signal (signal 3) directly to the Java process. The JVM catches this signal and prints the thread dump to standard output/its log file, rather than terminating the process (despite "kill" being in the command name).
codeExamples:
# Send SIGQUIT to trigger a thread dump - written to the app's stdout/log, not a separate file
kill -3 12345

beginner.content:
Common Thread States You'll See

• RUNNABLE - actively executing code or ready to run on the CPU.
• BLOCKED - waiting to acquire a synchronized lock held by another thread.
• WAITING - waiting indefinitely for another thread's signal (e.g. Object.wait(), Thread.join()).
• TIMED_WAITING - waiting, but with a timeout (e.g. Thread.sleep()).

Seeing many threads stuck in BLOCKED state at the same spot is a strong hint of lock contention or a deadlock.

Fresher Notes

  • Thread dump: a snapshot of every thread with its state, name and stack trace at one moment.
  • How to take one: jcmd <pid> Thread.print, or Ctrl+Break on Windows and kill -3 <pid> on Linux.
  • States: read RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING and TIMED_WAITING first.

Worked Example 1

Read a blocked thread.
codeExamples:
"http-nio-8080-exec-7" #52 prio=5 os_prio=0 nid=0x2f10 waiting for monitor entry
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
        at com.shop.Cart.add(Cart.java:41)
        - waiting to lock <0x000000076b2a1c20> (a com.shop.Cart)
        - locked by "http-nio-8080-exec-3"

// OUTPUT:
// exec-7 waits on a Cart monitor that exec-3 holds: look at exec-3 next

Spot a deadlock.

  which is held by "T2"
"T2": waiting to lock monitor 0x...2 (object 0x...b, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "T1"

// the fix is a single global lock order, or tryLock with a timeout

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A dump is produced at a safepoint, when every thread is paused briefly.

  • Request: attach (jcmd) or SIGQUIT asks the JVM to print.
  • Per thread: name, id, nid (the OS thread id in hex), state and frames.
  • Locks: lines such as - locked and - waiting to lock show monitor ownership.
  • Deadlock check: the JVM looks for cycles in the lock graph and prints them at the end.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to get and format a dump:

  • jcmd Thread.print: add -l for locks.
  • kill -3 / Ctrl+Break: output goes to the process stdout.
  • jstack: older front end.
  • Thread.dump_to_file: text or JSON, includes virtual threads (JDK 21).
  • ThreadMXBean: dumpAllThreads from code or JMX.

expert.content:
Detecting a Deadlock in a Thread Dump

When two or more threads are each waiting for a lock the other one holds, they deadlock permanently. jstack is smart enough to detect this pattern automatically and prints a dedicated section at the end of the dump. 

Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"Thread-1":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f8a1c003f28 (object 0x000000076ac03a70, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "Thread-2"
"Thread-2":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f8a1c001a08 (object 0x000000076ac03a80, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "Thread-1"

Java stack information for the threads listed above:
===================================================
"Thread-1":
        at com.myapp.TransferService.transfer(TransferService.java:22)
        - waiting to lock <0x000000076ac03a70> (a java.lang.Object)
        - locked <0x000000076ac03a80> (a java.lang.Object)
"Thread-2":
        at com.myapp.TransferService.transfer(TransferService.java:22)
        - waiting to lock <0x000000076ac03a80> (a java.lang.Object)
        - locked <0x000000076ac03a70> (a java.lang.Object)
This is the textbook "lock ordering" deadlock: two threads acquire the same two locks in opposite order.

Reading BLOCKED vs Lock-Owner Relationships

When a thread is BLOCKED, its stack trace includes a line like - waiting to lock <0xADDRESS> (a com.myapp.Account). Somewhere else in the same dump, another thread will show - locked <0xADDRESS> for the same address - that's the thread currently holding the lock you need to find.

This lets you manually trace lock-contention chains even when jstack's automatic deadlock detector doesn't fire (e.g. contention without a true cyclic deadlock, just severe serialization on one hot lock).

Thread States - Full Reference

StateMeaningCommon Cause
NEWThread created but not yet startedRare to catch in a dump; thread object exists, start() not called
RUNNABLEExecuting or ready to execute on CPUNormal active work, or busy-spinning/CPU-bound code
BLOCKEDWaiting to enter a synchronized block/methodLock contention, potential deadlock
WAITINGWaiting indefinitely for another threadObject.wait(), Thread.join(), LockSupport.park()
TIMED_WAITINGWaiting with a timeoutThread.sleep(), wait(timeout), a connection-pool checkout with timeout
TERMINATEDThread has finished executingrun() method completed or threw an uncaught exception

Multiple Dumps Over Time - The Real Diagnostic Technique

A single thread dump only shows one instant; the real skill is taking 3-5 dumps a few seconds apart during the incident and comparing them:
• If the same threads are stuck at the exact same stack frame across all dumps -> genuinely stuck (deadlock, infinite loop, or blocked on an external call with no timeout).
• If threads are RUNNABLE but at different stack frames each time -> the app is just slow/CPU-bound, not hung.
• If threads are BLOCKED waiting on the same lock across dumps -> strong lock contention, look at what's holding it and why it's held so long.
codeExamples:
# Capture 5 thread dumps, 5 seconds apart, for comparison
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  jstack 12345 > dump_$i.txt
  sleep 5
done

expert.content:
Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
All request-handling threads eventually go BLOCKED and the app stops responding entirelyTrue deadlock between two locks acquired in inconsistent order (e.g. account transfer logic)jstack's "Found one Java-level deadlock" section identifies the exact threads and locksEnforce a consistent global lock ordering, or replace nested locking with a single lock / lock-free structure
Throughput degrades under load but no deadlock is reportedSevere contention on a single coarse-grained lock (e.g. a synchronized cache) - not cyclic, just serializedMultiple dumps show many threads BLOCKED waiting on the same lock address, held briefly by a rotating single ownerNarrow the synchronized scope, use a concurrent collection (ConcurrentHashMap) or finer-grained locking
App hangs specifically when calling a downstream service, never recoversA thread is TIMED_WAITING/RUNNABLE stuck inside a socket read with no timeout configured on the HTTP clientStack trace shows the thread stuck inside the HTTP client's socket read across all dumpsConfigure explicit connect/read timeouts on all outbound clients so threads never wait forever

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a thread dump?A snapshot of every thread's state and stack trace in a running JVM at a point in time
How do you generate a thread dump?Use jstack <pid>, or send kill -3 <pid> on Unix systems to print it to the process's stdout/log
What thread states indicate a potential problem?BLOCKED (waiting on a lock) most directly; many threads stuck at the same frame across repeated dumps in any waiting state also signals a problem
How does jstack detect a deadlock?It analyzes the lock-wait graph across threads and reports cycles where thread A waits for a lock held by B, which waits for a lock held by A
Why take multiple thread dumps instead of just one?A single dump only shows one instant; comparing several dumps a few seconds apart distinguishes a genuinely stuck thread from one that's just slow/CPU-bound
What's the difference between WAITING and TIMED_WAITING?WAITING blocks indefinitely until another thread signals it; TIMED_WAITING blocks for a bounded time and resumes automatically on timeout
How would you diagnose a hang caused by a downstream call with no timeout?Take a thread dump and look for a thread stuck inside the HTTP/socket client's read call across repeated dumps, then check if a read/connect timeout is configured

Mid-Level Notes

  • Take three dumps a few seconds apart; a thread stuck on the same frame in all of them is the suspect.
  • Deadlock: the dump ends with Found one Java-level deadlock and lists the locks each thread holds and wants.
  • Thread names: give pool threads real names, so a dump shows order-worker-3 and not pool-1-thread-3.

Senior Notes

  • Virtual threads: jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json file.json includes them, while plain Thread.print does not.
  • High CPU: match the hex nid in the dump to the busiest OS thread id from top -H.
  • Automation: capture dumps on a health-check failure, and compare them with a tool such as a dump analyzer.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • One dump only: take three, a few seconds apart.
  • Reading only RUNNABLE: a thread waiting in native socket read is also shown as RUNNABLE.
  • Unnamed pools: use a ThreadFactory with names.
  • Ignoring idle pool threads: parked pool workers are normal, not a problem.
  • Dump to a file that fills the disk: rotate and compress dumps.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

A dump has a small cost, so use it with a plan.

  • Pause: grows with the thread count and stack depth.
  • Many threads: thousands of platform threads signal a pool sizing problem, and virtual threads can replace them for blocking I/O.
  • Pool saturation: all workers in the same frame, such as a JDBC call, means the dependency is slow.
  • JFR alternative: JFR records thread states over time with less manual work.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 Thread.print | grep -c "http-nio-8080-exec"
jcmd 4242 Thread.print | grep -A3 "exec-" | grep -c "SocketInputStream"

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 200
# 187      <- almost all workers wait on a slow downstream call

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a service stops answering but CPU is low.

  • Step 1: take three dumps, 5 seconds apart.
  • Step 2: count threads by state and by top frame.
  • Step 3: find the lock owner for the BLOCKED threads.
  • Step 4: fix the root cause: lock order, a timeout, or a bigger or isolated pool.

beginner.content:
What is JFR?

Java Flight Recorder (JFR) is a profiling and event-collection tool built directly into the JVM itself. It records detailed information about what's happening inside your application - method execution, garbage collection pauses, lock contention, I/O, exceptions - while it runs, with very low overhead (typically under 1-2%).

It's called a "flight recorder" by analogy to an airplane's black box: it continuously records what the JVM is doing, so if something goes wrong, you can go back and see exactly what happened.

Why JFR is Special

Before JFR, most profiling tools attached an external agent that added significant overhead, often changing the very behavior you were trying to measure (the "observer effect"). JFR is different because:
• It's built into the JVM itself - no external agent needed.
• It's designed to run safely in production, continuously, with minimal performance impact.
• It's free and included with every OpenJDK/Oracle JDK since Java 11 (and available via backport in Java 8).

Starting a JFR Recording

You can start a JFR recording right when you launch your application, or attach to one that's already running.
codeExamples:
# Start the app with a JFR recording running for its whole lifetime
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=recording.jfr,duration=60s -jar myapp.jar

# Attach to an already-running JVM and record for 60 seconds
jcmd 12345 JFR.start duration=60s filename=recording.jfr

# Check the status of an active recording
jcmd 12345 JFR.check

# Manually stop and dump a running recording
jcmd 12345 JFR.stop filename=recording.jfr

beginner.content:
What Kind of Events Does JFR Capture?

JFR organizes what it captures into "events" - each one a small, structured record of something that happened. Common categories include:
• CPU / Method profiling - which methods consumed the most CPU time.
• Garbage Collection - every GC pause, its duration and cause.
• Memory allocation - which classes are allocated most frequently.
• Thread activity / lock contention - which locks threads waited on, and for how long.
• I/O - file and socket read/write events.
• Exceptions - thrown exceptions and their frequency.

Viewing a Recording

Once you have a .jfr file, you open it in JMC (Java Mission Control) - a free GUI tool covered in the next topic - to browse the recorded events visually with charts and drill-down views.

Fresher Notes

  • JFR (Java Flight Recorder) records JVM and application events with very low overhead.
  • Start at launch with -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=app.jfr.
  • Open the .jfr file in JDK Mission Control, or print it with the jfr command.

Worked Example 1

Read a recording from the command line.
codeExamples:
jfr summary app.jfr
jfr print --events jdk.GarbageCollection app.jfr

# OUTPUT: (excerpt, varies)
#  Event Type                     Count  Size (bytes)
#  jdk.GarbageCollection             12           480

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

A custom event.

jcmd 4242 JFR.dump name=rec1 filename=C:\temp\rec1.jfr

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

JFR is built into the JVM and writes events into thread-local buffers.

  • Events: JVM (GC, JIT, locks), OS (CPU) and application ones.
  • Sampling: method samples about every 10 or 20 ms, not every call, so overhead stays low.
  • Storage: buffers flush to chunks in a repository, then to a .jfr file on dump.
  • Config: .jfc files choose events and thresholds.
codeExamples:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=app.jfr,settings=default -jar app.jar
jfr configure --help

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# Started recording 1. The result will be written to: app.jfr

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful options:

  • duration / maxage / maxsize: bound the recording.
  • settings: default, profile or a custom .jfc path.
  • dumponexit=true: write the file when the JVM ends.
  • jfr print / summary / view: inspect on the command line.
  • jfr assemble and disassemble: split or join chunk files.
codeExamples:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=maxage=15m,maxsize=250m,dumponexit=true,filename=last.jfr ^
     -jar app.jar
jfr print --events jdk.CPULoad last.jfr

# OUTPUT: (excerpt, varies)
# jdk.CPULoad { jvmUser = 12.4 %  jvmSystem = 1.1 %  machineTotal = 35.0 % }

expert.content:
JFR Architecture: Event Streaming

Internally, JFR events are written to an in-memory circular buffer per thread, then periodically flushed to disk (or consumed live). This design is what keeps overhead so low - most of the work is simple, lock-free buffer writes rather than expensive synchronization or I/O on every event.

Since JDK 14, JFR also supports Event Streaming - reading events in near real-time as they're produced, rather than only after a recording finishes, which enables live dashboards and alerting built directly on top of JFR data.

Recording Configurations: default vs profile

JFR ships with two built-in configuration templates that trade off detail against overhead:

TemplateTypical OverheadUse Case
default< 1%Always-on continuous production monitoring
profile~2%Deep-dive performance investigation, shorter targeted recordings

You can also define a fully custom .jfc configuration file to enable/disable specific event types and their thresholds/stack-depth precisely.
codeExamples:
# Use the deeper "profile" template for a focused investigation
jcmd 12345 JFR.start name=deepdive settings=profile duration=120s filename=deepdive.jfr

# List available/running recordings on a JVM
jcmd 12345 JFR.dump name=deepdive filename=snapshot.jfr

expert.content:
Sample JFR Text Summary (jfr print)

The JDK also ships a jfr CLI tool that can summarize or print recordings without opening a GUI - handy for quick server-side triage or scripting. 
$ jfr summary recording.jfr

 Chunks: 3
 Start: 2026-08-14 10:02:11
 Duration: 60 s

 jdk.SocketRead                       9,822   511,004
 jdk.ObjectAllocationSample            5,672   296,116

Continuous Production Recording Strategy

Because overhead is so low, a common production pattern is to run JFR continuously with the default template and a rolling ring-buffer, so that whenever an incident happens (crash, latency spike, alert), you can dump the last N minutes of recorded data retroactively - even though you didn't know in advance that you'd need it.
codeExamples:
# Start a continuous recording that keeps the last 15 minutes in a ring buffer
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=disk=true,maxage=15m,maxsize=250M,name=continuous -jar myapp.jar

# After an incident is noticed, dump what's currently buffered without stopping the recording
jcmd 12345 JFR.dump name=continuous filename=incident_$(date +%s).jfr

What is JFR?Java Flight Recorder - a low-overhead, built-in JVM profiling and event-recording framework
Why is JFR considered safe for production use?Its default configuration adds well under 1-2% overhead by writing events to lock-free per-thread ring buffers rather than doing expensive instrumentation on every call
How do you start a JFR recording on an already-running JVM?Use jcmd <pid> JFR.start with options like duration and filename
What is the difference between the default and profile JFR templates?default is tuned for near-zero overhead continuous monitoring; profile captures more detail (e.g. more allocation/lock events) at slightly higher (~2%) overhead

Mid-Level Notes

  • Free: JFR is open source and free in OpenJDK 11 and later (it was commercial in Oracle JDK 8).
  • Profiles: settings=default is light, and settings=profile collects more detail with a little more cost.
  • Running JVM: use jcmd <pid> JFR.start, JFR.dump and JFR.stop.

Senior Notes

  • Continuous recording: run with maxage and maxsize and dump on demand, so an incident always has data.
  • CLI: jfr summary, jfr print --events jdk.GCPhasePause and jfr view (JDK 21) work without a GUI.
  • Custom events: extend jdk.jfr.Event to record business timings next to JVM events.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong file path: the file is written on the server, not your laptop.
  • profile in production all day: use default for continuous use.
  • No dump before restart: use dumponexit.
  • Old Java 8 flags: -XX:+UnlockCommercialFeatures is not needed in OpenJDK 11 and later.
  • Reading only CPU: check allocation, locks and GC events too.
codeExamples:
# Java 8 Oracle (old)
java -XX:+UnlockCommercialFeatures -XX:+FlightRecorder -jar app.jar
# Java 11+ OpenJDK (right)
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=app.jfr -jar app.jar

# OUTPUT:
# the second form works in OpenJDK with no unlock flag

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Overhead is usually around 1 to 2 percent with the default profile (varies by workload).

  • Reduce events: raise thresholds, for example for file and socket I/O.
  • Disk: use maxsize.
  • Stack depth: the default stack depth is 64, and deeper stacks cost more.
  • Measure: compare latency with and without recording on your load.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 JFR.start name=low settings=default maxsize=100m
jcmd 4242 JFR.check

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# Recording 1: name=low maxsize=100.0MB (running)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: p99 latency spikes every few minutes.

  • Step 1: keep a rolling recording running.
  • Step 2: after a spike, dump the last 10 minutes.
  • Step 3: open it and compare the spike time with GC pauses, safepoints and lock waits.
  • Step 4: tune the cause: heap size, collector, or the contended lock.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 JFR.dump name=rolling filename=spike.jfr
jfr print --events jdk.GCPhasePause spike.jfr | head -8

# OUTPUT: (excerpt, varies)
# jdk.GCPhasePause { startTime = 10:15:02  duration = 145 ms  name = "GC Pause" }

beginner.content:
What is JMC?

Java Mission Control (JMC) is a free desktop GUI application for viewing and analyzing the data recorded by JFR (Java Flight Recorder). While JFR does the recording inside the JVM, JMC is the tool you use to actually look at that data - with charts, tables, and drill-down views instead of raw text.

Think of JFR as the "black box recorder" and JMC as the "playback software" investigators use to review it.

Getting JMC

JMC used to ship bundled with the JDK, but since Java 9 it's a separate free download maintained by the OpenJDK community (and also offered by vendors like Azul and Red Hat). You download and install it once, then point it at any .jfr recording file, or connect it live to a running JVM on your network.
codeExamples:
# Open a saved recording directly from the command line (once JMC is installed)
jmc -open recording.jfr

beginner.content:
Connecting JMC to a Live JVM

Besides opening saved .jfr files, JMC can connect directly to a running JVM (local or over the network, via JMX) to start/stop recordings and watch live data, without needing to manually use jcmd first.

Key Views in JMC

Once a recording is open, JMC organizes the data into tabs, the most important being:
• General - overview of the JVM, its version, flags, and system info during the recording.
• Memory - heap usage over time, garbage collection pauses and their causes.
• Code - "hot methods" - which methods consumed the most CPU time.
• Threads - thread activity, lock contention (which locks caused the most blocking).
• I/O - file and socket reads/writes, useful for spotting slow external calls.

Why Use JMC Instead of Reading Raw JFR Text?

While you can print raw event data with the jfr command-line tool, JMC's real value is visual correlation - seeing a CPU spike, a GC pause, and a lock-contention event all lined up on the same timeline, which makes cause-and-effect jump out in a way scrolling through text output never does.

Fresher Notes

  • JMC (JDK Mission Control) is a desktop tool to open and analyze .jfr files and monitor live JVMs.
  • Automated analysis: the rules page lists problems such as GC pauses and lock contention, with a score.
  • Separate download: JMC is not bundled with the JDK since version 9, so install it on its own.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Where to look:

  • Automated Analysis: first view.
  • Method Profiling: hot methods and flame graph.
  • Memory and GC: allocation, heap use and pauses.
  • Threads and Lock Instances: contention.
  • Environment: flags, system properties, container limits.

expert.content:
The Automated Analysis Engine

JMC includes a built-in Automated Analysis Results tab that runs a rule engine over the recording and automatically flags likely problems - similar in spirit to a linter, but for runtime behavior. It scores findings by severity (info / warning / severe) and explains them in plain language, for example:
• "Long garbage collection pauses detected"
• "Class loading is a significant contributor to total time"
• "Thread X spent a large percentage of the recording BLOCKED"

This is often the fastest way to get oriented in an unfamiliar recording before manually drilling into the Memory, Code, or Threads tabs.

Threads Page: Lock Contention Analysis

The Threads tab's "Lock Instances" view ranks every monitor/lock by total accumulated blocking time across all threads during the recording - directly answering "which lock is causing the most contention in production" without manually cross-referencing multiple thread dumps by hand.

Combined with the "Hot Methods" view under Code, you can typically go from "the app feels slow under load" to "this exact synchronized block in OrderService.reserveInventory() is the bottleneck" within a few minutes.

Memory Page: GC Pause Analysis

ChartWhat It ShowsWhat to Look For
Heap usage over timeLive heap size across the recording windowSteady sawtooth = healthy; a rising floor after each GC = possible leak
GC pause timesDuration of every individual GC pause, plotted over timeOccasional long pauses correlating with latency spike reports
Allocation by classWhich classes are allocated the most (by count and total size)Unexpectedly high allocation rate from a class you didn't expect (often a hidden autoboxing or string concatenation hot spot)

beginner.content:
What is jstack?

jstack is a command-line tool bundled with the JDK that prints a thread dump - a snapshot of every thread's state and stack trace - for a running Java process. It's the quickest way to check "what is my application's threads actually doing right now?" without adding any monitoring code.

Basic Usage

You first need the process ID (PID) of the running JVM, which you can get with jps (JVM Process Status), then pass it to jstack.
codeExamples:
# List running Java processes with their main class name
jps -l
# Sample output:
# 12345 com.myapp.Application
# 8820  sun.tools.jps.Jps

# Print a thread dump for process 12345 to the terminal
jstack 12345

# Save the thread dump to a file for later analysis
jstack 12345 > thread_dump.txt

beginner.content:
Reading a Basic jstack Entry

Each thread in the output looks like this - a header line with the thread's name/state, followed by its call stack from the current point of execution downward.
codeExamples:
"main" #1 prio=5 os_prio=0 tid=0x00007f8ab4009800 nid=0x1a03 waiting on condition [0x00007f8ab7]
   java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (sleeping)
        at java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Native Method)
        at com.myapp.Application.main(Application.java:15)

beginner.content:
What -l and -F Options Do

• jstack -l <pid> - adds extra information about ownable synchronizers (java.util.concurrent locks), not just built-in synchronized monitors. Useful if your app uses ReentrantLock.
• jstack -F <pid> - "force" mode; use this if the process is hung so badly that a normal dump request doesn't respond.
codeExamples:
# Include java.util.concurrent lock ownership details
jstack -l 12345

# Force a dump when the process isn't responding to a normal request
jstack -F 12345

beginner.content:
Why Every Java Developer Should Know jstack

When production support asks "why is the app frozen," a thread dump from jstack is usually the fastest and least invasive first step - it takes a fraction of a second, doesn't require restarting anything, and often immediately reveals the culprit (a deadlock, a stuck external call, or threads piling up on one lock).

Fresher Notes

  • jstack prints the thread stacks of a running Java process: jstack <pid>.
  • Find the pid with jps or jcmd with no arguments.
  • Same user: run it as the user that owns the Java process.

Worked Example 1

Count threads by state.
codeExamples:
jstack 4242 | grep "java.lang.Thread.State" | sort | uniq -c

# OUTPUT: (varies)
#      6 java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
#     31 java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (parking)
#     12 java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (on object monitor)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Windows count.
codeExamples:
jstack 4242 | findstr /C:"Thread.State" > states.txt
(Get-Content states.txt | Group-Object).Count

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 4 distinct state lines

beginner.content:

codeExamples:
jps -l
jstack 4242 > dump.txt
jstack -l 4242 | findstr /C:"deadlock"      # Windows
jstack -l 4242 | grep -i deadlock           # Linux

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 4242 com.shop.Main
# Found one Java-level deadlock:

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

jstack is an attach-based client.

  • Attach: the tool connects to the target JVM through a socket file in the temp directory.
  • Command: it asks the JVM to run the thread-print diagnostic command.
  • Output: the JVM writes the dump back to jstack, which prints it.
  • Same engine: that is why jcmd Thread.print gives identical text.
codeExamples:
jstack -l 4242 | head -4

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 2026-10-07 10:15:03
# Full thread dump OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM (21.0.2+13-58 mixed mode, sharing):
#
# Threads class SMR info:

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • jstack pid: stacks only.
  • jstack -l pid: with lock details.
  • jstack -e pid: extended info in older releases.
  • jstack -F pid: forced dump of a hung JVM, removed in recent JDKs.
  • jstack core: read a core file (older JDKs).
codeExamples:
jstack -l 4242 > dump.txt
jcmd 4242 Thread.print -l > dump2.txt

# OUTPUT:
# both files hold the same kind of data

expert.content:
Full Anatomy of a jstack Thread Entry

"http-nio-8080-exec-7" #52 daemon prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=340.10ms elapsed=612.44s tid=0x00007f allocated=48MB defined_classes=2
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
        at com.myapp.inventory.InventoryService.reserve(InventoryService.java:112)
        - waiting to lock <0x000000076bd12340> (a com.myapp.inventory.InventoryService)
        at com.myapp.order.OrderController.checkout(OrderController.java:58)
        at java.base/jdk.internal.reflect.NativeMethodAccessorImpl.invoke0(Native Method)

   Locked ownable synchronizers:
        - <0x000000076bc98a10> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync)
Key fields: daemon (whether it's a daemon thread, JVM won't wait for it to exit), cpu (total CPU time consumed), elapsed (wall-clock lifetime), and the Thread.State line which tells you exactly what category of wait/execution the thread is in.

jstack vs Alternatives

ToolOutputBest For
jstackPlain text thread dump, one-time snapshotFast, scriptable, works over SSH with no GUI
kill -3 (SIGQUIT)Same content, written to the app's own stdout/logWhen you don't have direct JDK tool access but can signal the process
jcmd <pid> Thread.printSame content, via the unified jcmd toolModern JDKs where jcmd is the preferred single entry point (see jcmd topic)
JFR thread/lock eventsContinuous data over a time window, not just an instantUnderstanding contention trends over time, not just "right now"

Scripting Repeated Dumps for Trend Analysis

A single dump is a snapshot; the real diagnostic power comes from taking several in quick succession and diffing which threads remain stuck at the same frame.
codeExamples:
#!/bin/bash
# Capture 6 thread dumps, 5 seconds apart, each timestamped
PID=12345
for i in $(seq 1 6); do
  jstack $PID > "dump_$(date +%H%M%S).txt"
  sleep 5
done

# Then compare which stack frames repeat across all files (candidates for "truly stuck")
grep -A1 "java.lang.Thread.State" dump_*.txt | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
jstack <pid> itself hangs and never prints outputThe target JVM is in a state (e.g. deep GC pause, or the target process is actually a different/zombie process) where it can't respond to the attach requestRetry with jstack -F <pid> (force mode) which reads process memory directly instead of requesting cooperation from the target JVMIf force mode also fails, the JVM may be completely wedged - consider a heap+thread dump via OS-level core dump instead
