Mid-Level Notes

  • Options: -l adds lock information, such as owned ownable synchronizers.
  • Save: redirect to a file, jstack -l 4242 > dump.txt, for later reading.
  • Deadlock: jstack reports Java-level deadlocks at the end of the output.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer jcmd: jcmd <pid> Thread.print does the same job and works with the other jcmd commands.
  • Hung JVM: if the attach fails, use kill -3 on Linux, because it needs no attach.
  • Safepoint: a dump stops the threads briefly, so avoid very frequent dumps on huge thread counts.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Different user: use sudo -u appuser jstack pid.
  • Different JDK version than the target: use the matching JDK.
  • Container: run it inside the container or share the pid namespace.
  • Reading the stdout of kill -3 in the wrong place: it goes to the application log.
codeExamples:
sudo -u appuser jstack 4242 > dump.txt
docker exec shop-app jcmd 1 Thread.print

# OUTPUT:
# 1:
# Full thread dump OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM ...

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Cost and care:

  • Pause: short, grows with thread count.
  • Frequency: one dump per few seconds is fine, many per second is not.
  • Size: huge thread counts produce large files, so compress them.
codeExamples:
jstack 4242 | gzip > dump.txt.gz
ls -l dump.txt.gz

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# -rw-r--r-- 1 app app 18432 Oct  7 10:16 dump.txt.gz

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: CPU is at 100 percent.

  • Step 1: top -H -p pid finds the busiest thread id.
  • Step 2: convert it to hex.
  • Step 3: find that nid in the dump and read its stack.
codeExamples:
top -H -p 4242 -b -n 1 | head -12
printf "%x\n" 15361
jstack 4242 | grep -A8 "nid=0x3c01"

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 3c01
# "pool-2-thread-4" ... nid=0x3c01 runnable
#         at com.shop.Report.loop(Report.java:57)

beginner.content:
What is jmap?

jmap is a command-line tool bundled with the JDK for inspecting a running JVM's memory - its heap. It can print a summary of memory usage, list the object types filling up the heap, and produce a full heap dump file for deeper analysis in a tool like Eclipse MAT.

Finding the Process to Inspect

Like other JDK diagnostic tools, jmap operates on a process ID (PID), which you find with jps.
codeExamples:
jps -l
# 12345 com.myapp.Application
# 8820  sun.tools.jps.Jps

beginner.content:
Quick Heap Summary with -heap

This gives you a fast overview of heap configuration and current usage per generation, without producing any large file.
codeExamples:
jmap -heap 12345

# Sample output (trimmed):
# Heap Configuration:
#    MinHeapFreeRatio = 40
#    MaxHeapSize      = 1073741824 (1024.0MB)
# Heap Usage:
# G1 Heap:
#    used     = 214748364 (204.8MB)
#    free     = 858993460 (819.2MB)
#    16.0% used

beginner.content:
Listing the Biggest Object Types with -histo

The histogram option lists every class currently in the heap, sorted by total memory used - a quick way to spot "what's eating all my memory" without opening a full heap dump.
codeExamples:
jmap -histo 12345 | head -10

# Sample output:
#  num     #instances         #bytes  class name
#    1:        420381       40196256  [C  (char array)
#    2:        180221       28835360  com.myapp.model.UserSession
#    3:        180221       11534144  java.util.HashMap$Node
#    4:         98211        7856880  java.lang.String

beginner.content:
Producing a Full Heap Dump with -dump

When a summary or histogram isn't enough and you need to inspect the actual object graph, jmap -dump writes a full .hprof heap dump file to disk - the same kind of file covered in the Heap Dumps topic.
codeExamples:
# Dump only live (reachable) objects, in binary format
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=myapp.hprof 12345

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • jmap inspects heap memory: jmap -histo <pid> lists classes by instance count and size.
  • Heap dump: jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid> writes an HPROF file.
  • Analyze the dump in Eclipse MAT, VisualVM or IntelliJ.

Worked Example 1

Dump on OutOfMemoryError.
codeExamples:
java -Xmx256m -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError ^
     -XX:HeapDumpPath=C:\dumps -jar app.jar

# OUTPUT:
# java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
# Dumping heap to C:\dumps\java_pid4242.hprof ...

beginner.content:

A leak that the histogram shows.

Practice Exercise 1

codeExamples:
jmap -histo:live 4242 | head -5
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof 4242

# OUTPUT: (varies)
#  num     #instances         #bytes  class name
#    1:        812340       64987200  [B

# Heap dump file created

Practice Exercise 2

Same with jcmd.
codeExamples:

jcmd 4242 GC.heap_dump C:\dumps\heap.hprof

# OUTPUT: (varies)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

jmap also attaches to the JVM.

  • Histogram: walks the heap and counts instances per class.
  • Dump: writes the heap in HPROF format at a safepoint, so the application pauses.
  • live: triggers a full GC before the walk.
  • Class names: [B means byte[], [C means char[], and [Ljava.lang.String; means String[].
codeExamples:
jmap -histo 4242 | head -4

# OUTPUT: (varies)
#  num     #instances         #bytes  class name (module)
#    1:        500112       40009600  [B (java.base@21.0.2)
#    2:        210554        5053296  java.lang.String (java.base@21.0.2)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • -histo: all objects.
  • -histo:live: reachable objects only.
  • -dump:live,format=b,file=f: HPROF.
  • -clstats / -finalizerinfo: classloader and finalizer data in older JDKs.
  • jcmd GC.heap_dump -all: keep unreachable objects too.
codeExamples:
jmap -dump:format=b,file=all.hprof 4242
jcmd 4242 GC.heap_dump -all all2.hprof

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# Heap dump file created

expert.content:
jmap -histo:live vs -histo

Adding :live forces a full garbage collection before generating the histogram, so only reachable objects are counted. This gives a more accurate view of "what's actually still needed" but the forced GC causes a pause, so it's best avoided on latency-sensitive production traffic during peak load.
codeExamples:
# Includes garbage not yet collected - no GC pause triggered
jmap -histo 12345

# Forces a full GC first, so only live/reachable objects appear - causes a pause
jmap -histo:live 12345

expert.content:
Comparing Two Histograms to Spot a Leak

A classic lightweight leak-hunting technique doesn't even require a full heap dump - just two histograms taken minutes apart, diffed for classes whose instance count keeps growing.
codeExamples:
jmap -histo:live 12345 > histo_t1.txt
sleep 600
jmap -histo:live 12345 > histo_t2.txt

diff histo_t1.txt histo_t2.txt | grep com.myapp

# Example diff output showing a suspicious grower:
# <    2:        180221       28835360  com.myapp.model.UserSession
# ---
# >    2:        512980       82076800  com.myapp.model.UserSession

expert.content:
jmap Options Reference

OptionPurposeCaution
-heapPrint heap configuration and generation usage summarySafe, negligible overhead
-histoPrint class histogram (instance count, bytes) of the current heapCan briefly pause the JVM while iterating the heap on some collectors
-histo:liveSame as -histo but forces a full GC firstCauses a real, sometimes multi-second stop-the-world pause on a large heap
-dump:live,format=b,file=...Write a full heap dump of live objectsForces full GC and can pause the app for seconds on large heaps; large output file
-clstatsPrint class loader statisticsUseful for diagnosing Metaspace/class-loader leaks (e.g. in app servers doing hot redeploys)

Sample -clstats Output for a Class Loader Leak

$ jmap -clstats 12345

class_loader    classes bytes   parent_loader       alive?  type

<bootstrap>      724     3841004                              live    <internal>
0x00000007a1b3  1204    5230112 0x00000007a0d2      dead    org.myapp.PluginClassLoader
0x00000007a1c9  1204    5230112 0x00000007a0d2      dead    org.myapp.PluginClassLoader
0x00000007a1d5  1204    5230112 0x00000007a0d2      dead    org.myapp.PluginClassLoader
...(37 more identical dead PluginClassLoader entries)...
Many "dead" class loaders of the same type still holding classes/bytes is the textbook signature of a classloader leak - typically caused by something (a static field, a ThreadLocal, or a registered shutdown hook) outside the loader still referencing one of its classes, preventing the whole loader and everything it defined from being collected.

Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
Metaspace usage keeps climbing after every hot-redeploy in an app serverOld class loaders from previous deployments are never freed because something still references their classesjmap -clstats <pid> shows growing numbers of "dead" class loaders of the same application type still holding bytesFind and remove the lingering reference (common culprits: ThreadLocal not cleared, static caches, unregistered JDBC drivers/shutdown hooks)
Running jmap -dump on a large production heap causes a multi-second outage-dump:live forces a full GC and heap dump generation is itself expensive on a multi-GB heapCompare heap size to typical dump duration; check if the app became unresponsive during the dump windowPrefer non-forced jmap -dump (no :live) if a full GC pause is unacceptable, or schedule dumps during low-traffic windows, or use JFR sampling first to narrow the investigation before a full dump
Histogram shows millions of char[]/String instances dominating memoryExcessive string creation/duplication - e.g. not using String interning for repeated values, or verbose logging building large strings unnecessarilyCross-reference the histogram with a heap dump's "Path to GC Roots" for a sample String to find where they're created/retainedIntern or deduplicate repeated strings, or reduce unnecessary string concatenation in hot paths

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is jmap used for?Inspecting a running JVM's heap - printing configuration/usage summaries, class histograms, or producing full heap dumps
What does jmap -histo:live do differently from jmap -histo?-histo:live forces a full GC first so only live/reachable objects are counted, giving a more accurate but pause-inducing snapshot
How do you generate a full heap dump with jmap?jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>
How can you spot a memory leak without taking a full heap dump?Take two jmap -histo:live snapshots minutes apart and diff them, looking for a class whose instance count/bytes keeps growing
What does jmap -clstats help diagnose?Class loader leaks - it lists class loaders, their classes/bytes, and whether they're still alive, revealing loaders that should have been collected but weren't
Why should jmap -dump:live be used carefully in production?It forces a full GC and heap iteration, which can pause a large-heap application for seconds, potentially causing a visible outage
What's the difference between jmap and jstack?jmap inspects heap/memory (histograms, heap dumps); jstack inspects threads (thread dumps, deadlock detection)

Mid-Level Notes

  • live in the dump option runs a full GC first and keeps only reachable objects.
  • Pause: a dump stops the application, and a big heap can take many seconds and as much disk.
  • OOM dump: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps writes a dump at the failure.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer jcmd: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump file and jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram replace jmap.
  • -histo:live triggers a full GC, so use it with care in production.
  • Sensitive data: a heap dump contains passwords and tokens, so store and share it with care.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Dump to a small disk: the file is about the heap size.
  • Dump on a busy node: remove it from the load balancer first.
  • Relative file path: the file goes where the target JVM runs, not where jmap runs.
  • Sharing a dump: it holds secrets.
  • Using histo to find a leak at one time: take two and compare the growth.
codeExamples:
jmap -histo:live 4242 > h1.txt
sleep 600
jmap -histo:live 4242 > h2.txt
diff <(head -20 h1.txt) <(head -20 h2.txt)

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# < 1: 100 100002400 [B
# > 1: 300 300002400 [B       <- growing class is the leak suspect

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and cost:

  • Pause scales with heap size, so a 16 GB heap can pause for a long time.

beginner.content:
What is OutOfMemoryError?

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError is thrown by the JVM when it cannot allocate an object because it has run out of memory in a particular area, and the Garbage Collector (GC) cannot free up enough space to continue.

It is an Error, not an Exception - it signals a serious problem that a normal application usually cannot recover from on its own.

There isn't just one kind of OutOfMemoryError - the JVM has several memory regions, and each can run out independently. The most common ones you will meet as a Java developer are:
• Java heap space - too many live objects for the configured heap
• Metaspace - too many loaded classes
• GC overhead limit exceeded - the GC is running constantly but reclaiming almost nothing

1. Heap Space OutOfMemoryError

The heap is where all your objects (new Foo(), ArrayList entries, Strings, etc.) live. If you keep creating objects and something keeps a reference to them (so GC can't collect them), the heap eventually fills up completely and the JVM gives up.

2. Metaspace OutOfMemoryError

Metaspace stores class metadata (the bytecode/definitions of classes, not objects). If your application (or a buggy framework) keeps generating and loading new classes at runtime without ever unloading them, Metaspace fills up.

3. GC Overhead Limit Exceeded

Sometimes the heap isn't 100% full, but the JVM notices it is spending almost all its CPU time running Garbage Collection while reclaiming very little memory each time (by default: more than 98% of time in GC, recovering less than 2% of the heap). Rather than let the app hang forever, the JVM throws this error early.

Common Causes and Quick Fixes

• Loading a huge file/dataset fully into memory - stream it instead (e.g. BufferedReader line by line) rather than reading it all into one giant String or List.
• Unbounded caches or collections - a static Map that keeps growing forever - use a bounded cache (e.g. Caffeine with a max size) or clear it periodically.
• Heap sized too small for the workload - increase -Xmx if the application genuinely needs more memory.
• Too many classes generated dynamically - increase -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize or fix the code/library that keeps generating classes.

Fresher Notes

  • OutOfMemoryError is an Error, not an exception: the JVM could not allocate memory and the message tells you which area ran out.
  • Java heap space means the heap is full of live objects; Metaspace means too many classes are loaded.
  • Heap size is set with -Xmx, and a bigger value only delays the failure if the code has a leak.

Worked Example 1

Production JVM flags.
codeExamples:
java -Xms512m -Xmx512m \
  -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=192m \
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps \
  -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -jar app.jar

// OUTPUT:
// no output until a failure; then the dump is written and the JVM exits with code 3

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The JVM throws OOM from several areas, and each has its own message.

  • Java heap space: an allocation failed after GC could not free enough.
  • GC overhead limit exceeded: the Parallel collector gives up when GC time is about 98 percent and recovery is under 2 percent.
  • Metaspace: class metadata lives in native memory, limited by -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
  • Direct buffer memory: ByteBuffer.allocateDirect exceeds -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize.
  • Unable to create native thread: the OS refused a thread or its stack.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful flags and tools:

  • -Xms / -Xmx: initial and maximum heap; equal values avoid resize pauses.
  • -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError: writes an hprof file when heap OOM occurs.
  • -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError: exits at the first OOM; -XX:+CrashOnOutOfMemoryError also writes a crash file.
  • -XX:OnOutOfMemoryError="cmd": runs a command, such as sending an alert.
  • -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary: then jcmd PID VM.native_memory summary.
  • -XX:MaxRAMPercentage: sizes the heap from the container limit.

expert.content:
How the JVM Decides "Out of Memory"

Before throwing OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space, the JVM does not give up after a single failed allocation. Modern collectors (G1, Parallel, ZGC) will:
• Trigger a full GC to try to reclaim space
• If a full GC barely reclaims anything and this keeps repeating, the collector estimates the "GC overhead" ratio
• Only after this threshold is repeatedly breached (or a single allocation genuinely cannot fit even after a full GC) does the JVM throw the error and, optionally, dump the heap

This is why OOM often correlates with a visible GC storm in monitoring dashboards just before the crash - CPU usage spikes because the collector is working overtime trying (and failing) to free space.

Reading the Full Error Message

The text after the colon in OutOfMemoryError tells you exactly which memory region failed - always read it carefully before jumping to conclusions. 
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
    -> The object heap itself is full. Classic memory leak or undersized heap.

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
    -> Class metadata region is full. Usually a ClassLoader leak (redeploys, dynamic proxies).

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded
    -> GC is thrashing: >98% time in GC, <2% heap reclaimed. App is effectively dying slowly.

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread
    -> Not heap at all - OS/process cannot allocate a new native thread stack.

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit
    -> A single array allocation is larger than the JVM/platform allows.

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory
    -> off-heap NIO DirectByteBuffer space (-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize) exhausted.

Diagnosing a Production Heap OOM

The standard production workflow when a service dies with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space:

1. Capture a heap dump - ideally automatically, using -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps so you get a .hprof file at the moment of the crash rather than trying to reproduce it later.
2. Open the dump in Eclipse MAT (Memory Analyzer Tool) or VisualVM and run the "Leak Suspects" report - it clusters retained objects by dominator and flags the largest retainers.
3. Follow the "retained size" (not just "shallow size") to find which single object graph is holding the most memory - this is usually the actual leak, e.g. a static Map<String, Session> with millions of stale entries.
4. Check the GC logs (-Xlog:gc*) leading up to the crash - if old-gen occupancy climbs steadily after every full GC instead of returning to baseline, that's the signature of a genuine leak versus just an undersized heap.

Symptom -> Root Cause -> Diagnosis -> Fix

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
App crashes after running fine for days/weeks with heap space OOMSlow memory leak - a static/long-lived collection grows unboundedHeap dump + MAT Leak Suspects; old-gen occupancy trending upward across multiple full GCsBound the collection (LRU/TTL cache), remove entries on cleanup, or use WeakReference where appropriate
OOM appears immediately under a specific request pattern (e.g. large file uploads)A single request loads an entire large payload into memory at onceCorrelate OOM timestamp with access logs / APM traces for that endpointStream the payload (chunked reads, InputStream processing) instead of buffering it fully
Metaspace OOM after repeated hot-redeploys in an app serverClassLoader leak - old web app's classes never get garbage collected because something still references them (ThreadLocal, static field, JDBC driver registration)Heap/class histogram shows duplicate classes across multiple classloader instancesDeregister JDBC drivers, clear ThreadLocals in a shutdown hook, avoid static references to app classes from container-level singletons

OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native threadNot heap - too many OS threads created (thread pool misconfiguration)jstack thread count vs OS ulimit -u; thread count climbing unboundedUse bounded thread pools, fix thread leak, raise ulimit only as a last resort

War Story: The Session Cache That Ate Production

A production order-processing service ran fine in staging but died with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space roughly every 9 days in production, always around peak traffic. The on-call team's first instinct was "just bump -Xmx" - which delayed the crash but didn't fix it.

A heap dump taken via -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError on the next crash showed a single static ConcurrentHashMap<String, UserSession> retaining 92% of the heap, with over 4 million entries - one for every user who had ever logged in since the last restart. The code added a session on login but only removed it on an explicit "logout" click; most mobile users simply closed the app, so their session objects (each holding a cached shopping cart and order history) never got removed.

Fix: replaced the unbounded map with a Caffeine cache configured with expireAfterAccess(30, TimeUnit.MINUTES) and a hard max size, so idle sessions are evicted automatically regardless of whether logout was ever called.

Prevention Checklist

• Always run production JVMs with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError so you capture evidence instead of just a restart.
• Set -Xmx deliberately based on measured working-set size plus headroom, not by copy-pasting a default.
• Prefer bounded caches (Caffeine, Guava CacheBuilder with maximumSize/expireAfter) over raw HashMap/ArrayList for anything that grows with user activity.
• Monitor old-gen occupancy after full GC over time (not just heap %) - a rising floor across GCs is the earliest reliable leak signal, well before an actual OOM.
• Use -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize explicitly in containerized environments so a classloader leak fails fast and visibly instead of silently eating host memory.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Only raising -Xmx: a leak just fails later; find the retaining path.
  • Catching OutOfMemoryError and continuing: state may be corrupt; log and exit.
  • No dump path space: the volume must hold a file as large as the heap.
  • Ignoring off-heap: heap looks fine while the container is killed.
  • Loading whole files or result sets: stream or page the data.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning to prevent OOM:

  • Measure live set: heap after Full GC times 2 to 3 is a sensible heap size.
  • Cap pools and queues: unbounded structures are the usual cause.
  • Page database reads: use setFetchSize and keyset paging.
  • Pre-size collections to avoid copy spikes during growth.
  • Leave headroom: container limit above heap by 25 to 40 percent for off-heap use.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Incident: a service restarts every few hours in Kubernetes with exit code 137.

  • Symptoms: pod status OOMKilled, latency spikes before each restart, no Java exception in logs.
  • Diagnosis: kubectl describe pod, then jcmd PID VM.native_memory summary and GC logs.
  • Root cause: heap was 90 percent of the container limit; Netty direct buffers and thread stacks pushed the process past it, so the kernel killed it before Java could throw OOM.
  • Fix: heap set with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65, -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m, alerts on container working set, and -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError for real heap OOM.

What is StackOverflowError?

Every time a method is called, the JVM pushes a new stack frame onto that thread's call stack, to remember local variables, parameters, and where to return to. Each thread's stack has a fixed maximum size.

java.lang.StackOverflowError is thrown when a thread's call stack grows beyond that limit - almost always because of a method calling itself (directly or indirectly) too many times without stopping, i.e. uncontrolled recursion.

Like OutOfMemoryError, it is a subclass of java.lang.Error, not Exception.

1. Infinite Recursion

The simplest way to trigger it: a method that calls itself with no base case (no stopping condition) at all.

2. A Base Case That's Wrong (Bug, Not Design)

More often in real code, the recursion does have a base case - but a bug means it's never actually reached for certain inputs.

3. Mutual (Indirect) Recursion

StackOverflowError doesn't require a method to call itself - two or more methods calling each other in a cycle produce the exact same problem.

Fixing It: Convert Recursion to Iteration

The most reliable fix for deep/unbounded recursion is to rewrite it as a loop, which uses a small, constant amount of stack space no matter how many "steps" are performed.

Fresher Notes

  • StackOverflowError happens when the call stack of a thread is full, most often because of recursion without a stop condition.
  • Each call adds a stack frame that holds local variables and the return address, and frames are freed on return.
  • Fix the base case first; the stack trace repeats the same few lines, which shows the loop.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Every thread has its own stack, created with a fixed size.

  • Frame: each call pushes a frame with locals, operand stack and a return address.
  • Limit: when the next frame does not fit, the JVM throws StackOverflowError at that call.
  • Frame size: methods with many locals use bigger frames, so the maximum depth varies.
  • JIT: compiled code can use smaller frames or inline calls, so depth differs between runs.
  • Heap: objects are not on the stack, only references.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options and variants:

  • -Xss: -Xss512k, -Xss2m; applies to new Java threads.
  • Thread constructor: the fourth argument sets a stack size hint for one thread.
  • -XX:ThreadStackSize: same effect in KB.
  • Trace length: the trace is capped by -XX:MaxJavaStackTraceDepth (default 1024).
  • Explicit stack: ArrayDeque for DFS, tree walks, flood fill.

expert.content:
Why Java Has No Guaranteed Tail-Call Optimization

In languages like Scala or Scheme, "tail-recursive" calls (where the recursive call is the very last operation, with nothing left to do after it returns) can be compiled into a loop by the compiler, reusing the same stack frame.

The JVM specification does not guarantee tail-call optimization, and the HotSpot JVM does not perform it (as of current mainstream JDKs). This means even a "clean" tail-recursive Java method still consumes one stack frame per call - so relying on deep recursion in Java is inherently risky, unlike in TCO languages.

Manually Simulating Tail-Call Style with an Explicit Stack

When a recursive algorithm is naturally elegant but might recurse too deep (e.g. traversing a very deep tree or long linked list), a common production technique is to replace the call stack with your own heap-allocated Deque, which has no fixed size limit (bounded only by heap memory, which can grow far larger than a thread stack).

Tuning Thread Stack Size with -Xss

The -Xss flag sets the stack size per thread (default is typically 512KB-1MB depending on OS and JDK version). Increasing it lets recursion go deeper before overflowing, but it is a trade-off, not a real fix: 

java -Xss4m RecursiveApp   # 4MB stack instead of default ~512KB-1MB

Trade-off:
  Larger -Xss  -> deeper recursion survives, BUT
                  each thread now reserves more memory,
                  so max thread count for a given RAM budget goes DOWN.

  1000 threads x 512KB = ~512MB reserved for stacks
  1000 threads x 4MB   = ~4GB reserved for stacks (may itself cause native OOM)
In server applications running hundreds of threads, bumping -Xss globally to fix one bad recursive path can quietly push the JVM toward OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread instead - so treat it as a stopgap, and fix the recursion (or convert it to iteration) as the real solution.

Reading a StackOverflowError Stack Trace

The key diagnostic signal is repetition: the same one or two method frames repeating hundreds or thousands of times is the fingerprint of runaway recursion, as opposed to a normal deep-but-varied call chain. 
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.StackOverflowError
    at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.applyRule(DiscountEngine.java:42)
    at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.applyRule(DiscountEngine.java:42)
    at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.applyRule(DiscountEngine.java:42)
    at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.applyRule(DiscountEngine.java:42)
    ... (repeats thousands of times) ...
    at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.applyRule(DiscountEngine.java:42)
    at com.shop.pricing.OrderService.calculateTotal(OrderService.java:88)
    at com.shop.web.CheckoutController.checkout(CheckoutController.java:31)
Line 42 in DiscountEngine.applyRule is where to look first - that's the recursive call site, and the bug is almost always in its base/stopping condition.

Symptom -> Root Cause -> Diagnosis -> Fix

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
StackOverflowError on a specific "rule engine" / tree-walking code path only for certain inputsRecursive base case never reached for those inputs (e.g. cyclic data structure, off-by-one termination bug)Trace repeating frame in the stack trace to find the exact recursive method and inspect its termination conditionFix the base case / add a cycle-detection guard (visited set) before recursing further

Two mutually-recursive methods (e.g. Parser/Evaluator) overflow on complex expressionsIndirect/mutual recursion with no depth limit, common in recursive-descent parsersLook for alternating method names in the repeating stack framesAdd an explicit maximum nesting-depth check, or rewrite using an explicit stack-based parser
Increasing -Xss "fixes" it temporarily, then OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread appears under loadLarger per-thread stacks multiplied across many concurrent threads exhaust native/process memoryCompare thread count x -Xss against available process memory; check ulimit -uRevert -Xss increase; fix the underlying unbounded recursion instead of masking it

War Story: The Self-Referencing Category Tree

An e-commerce catalog service exposed a "breadcrumb" feature that recursively walked up a product category's parent chain to build a path like Electronics > Laptops > Gaming Laptops. It had worked in production for two years.

A data-migration script introduced a bug that, under a rare merge-conflict scenario, set a category's parentId to point to one of its own descendants - creating a cycle. The very next time a customer viewed a product in that category, the breadcrumb-building recursion walked up the "parent" chain forever (A -> B -> C -> A -> B -> C ...) until StackOverflowError crashed that request thread. Because the cycle only affected one category, it looked like a random, hard-to-reproduce crash for days.

Fix: the recursive breadcrumb builder was rewritten iteratively with an explicit Set<Long> visitedIds, so that if a cycle is ever encountered again, the code detects it and throws a clear, catchable IllegalStateException("Cyclic category detected") instead of crashing the thread with StackOverflowError.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What causes StackOverflowError?A thread's call stack exceeds its maximum size, almost always due to recursion (direct, indirect, or via a cyclic data structure) without a properly reached base case
Is StackOverflowError an Exception or an Error?It is a java.lang.Error (subclass of Throwable, sibling of Exception) - it signals a serious JVM-level condition, not an ordinary recoverable exception
Does Java optimize tail-recursive calls into loops?No - the JVM spec does not require tail-call optimization and mainstream HotSpot JVMs do not perform it, so every recursive call, even tail-recursive ones, consumes a stack frame
How does -Xss relate to StackOverflowError?-Xss sets the per-thread stack size; increasing it lets recursion go deeper before overflowing, but increases memory reserved per thread, reducing how many threads a given memory budget supports
How would you fix a recursive method that risks StackOverflowError on deep input?Rewrite it iteratively using an explicit Deque/stack on the heap, since heap-based structures aren't bound by the fixed thread stack size
How do you recognize StackOverflowError from a stack trace at a glance?The same one or two method frames repeat an unusually large number of times consecutively, unlike a normal varied deep call chain
Can mutual recursion between two methods cause StackOverflowError?Yes - Method A calling Method B calling Method A in a cycle with no terminating condition overflows the stack exactly like direct self-recursion
Why is simply increasing -Xss risky as a fix in a high-concurrency server app?Multiplying a larger stack size across hundreds/thousands of threads can exhaust native process memory, potentially trading StackOverflowError for OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread

Mid-Level Notes

  • Stack size is set per thread with -Xss, for example -Xss1m; the default is usually 512 KB to 1 MB.
  • Hidden recursion hides in toString(), equals(), hashCode() and JPA bidirectional links that call each other.
  • Deep but valid recursion (big trees, long linked lists) is better rewritten with an explicit Deque loop.

Senior Notes

  • No tail call optimization exists in Java, so tail-recursive code still uses one frame per call.
  • Raising -Xss costs memory for every thread, so raise it only for a known deep workload or use a dedicated thread with a custom stack size.
  • Serialization and JSON libraries recurse on object graphs; a cycle gives a StackOverflowError, so break cycles with @JsonIgnore or @JsonManagedReference.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Missing base case: add and unit test the stop condition.
  • Base case never reached: for example the argument moves away from zero.
  • Cyclic data: track visited nodes in a Set.
  • Mutual toString/equals/hashCode: exclude the back reference.
  • Catching the Error: hides the bug; fix the cause.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning notes:

  • Memory cost: stack memory is reserved per thread, so 500 threads at 2 MB reserve about 1 GB virtual.
  • Shrink for many threads: lower -Xss only if you have measured the depth you need.
  • Memoize: dynamic programming turns deep recursion into loops.
  • Avoid deep recursion in request threads because the web container stack is small.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Incident: a JSON endpoint returns HTTP 500 for some customers only.

  • Symptoms: StackOverflowError with a repeating trace of BeanSerializer frames.
  • Diagnosis: read the repeating lines of the trace; they list Order.getCustomer then Customer.getOrders.
  • Root cause: a bidirectional JPA relation serialized directly; customers with orders loop forever.
  • Fix: return a DTO, or mark the back reference with @JsonIgnore or use @JsonManagedReference and @JsonBackReference; add a test with a linked pair.

What Does "High CPU" Mean for a Java App?

A Java process is said to have a "high CPU" problem when it consumes an unusually large, sustained share of the machine's CPU - often 100% of one or more cores - even though the actual useful work being done doesn't justify it.

This isn't a single exception you can catch. It's a symptom you observe from outside the JVM (via the OS) and then have to trace back inside the JVM to find which thread(s) and which line(s) of code are responsible.

Cause 1: A Busy (Spinning) Loop

The simplest way to cause high CPU is a loop that keeps running without ever pausing or blocking - e.g. waiting for a condition by spinning instead of using proper thread coordination.

Cause 2: Catastrophic Regex Backtracking

Certain regular expressions can take exponential time on specific "evil" inputs due to backtracking - a single matches() call can peg a CPU core for minutes on a moderately long string.

Cause 3: GC Thrashing

When the JVM is allocating objects faster than it can safely reclaim memory, the Garbage Collector runs almost continuously, consuming large amounts of CPU just to keep the app barely alive (see the "High GC" and "OutOfMemoryError" topics for the full picture).

How to Start Investigating High CPU

On any OS, the basic workflow is the same two-step process:
• Find which OS thread is hot - use top -H -p <pid> (Linux) or Task Manager's per-thread view to find the native thread ID (TID/LWP) consuming the most CPU.
• Map that OS thread to a Java thread - take a thread dump with jstack <pid> and match the hex-converted TID to the nid=0x... field in the dump to see exactly which Java method that thread is stuck executing.

Fresher Notes

  • High CPU means the process uses most cores; first decide whether the work is useful (real load) or wasted (spin loop, GC, regex).
  • top shows the busy process, and top -H -p PID shows the busy thread inside it.
  • Thread dump with jstack PID shows what the busy threads are executing.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

CPU time in a JVM is spent in a few places.

  • Application threads: your code and libraries.
  • GC threads: marking and copying; busy when memory is tight.
  • JIT compiler threads: compile hot methods; heavy at startup.
  • Safepoint and VM thread: pauses for GC and deopt.
  • Runnable but blocked in native I/O: shows RUNNABLE but uses little CPU, so confirm with top.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Diagnosis toolbox:

  • top -H -p PID: per-thread CPU.
  • jstack PID / jcmd PID Thread.print: thread dump with nid.
  • jcmd PID JFR.start duration=60s filename=a.jfr: Flight Recorder.
  • async-profiler: asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f flame.html PID.
  • jstat -gcutil: rules GC in or out.
  • ThreadMXBean: in-process per-thread CPU time.

expert.content:
The top -H + jstack Correlation Technique

This is the single most important production skill for high-CPU Java diagnosis - correlating an OS-level thread ID with a JVM-level stack trace.

1. Identify the process: top -p <pid> confirms the Java process itself is the CPU hog.
2. Break it down by thread: top -H -p <pid> shows individual native threads (LWPs) and their individual CPU%. Note the TID of the hottest thread(s), e.g. 18452.
3. Convert to hex: printf "%x\n" 18452 gives 4814.
4. Take a thread dump: jstack <pid> > dump.txt (or kill -3 <pid> to print it to stdout/log).
5. Search the dump for nid=0x4814 - that block of the dump is exactly what that hot native thread was executing in Java at that moment. 
"pool-3-thread-7" #47 prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=48213.45ms elapsed=612.09s tid=0x00007f2c productive
   nid=0x4814 runnable [0x00007f2b1a1fe000]
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
        at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.matchPromoCode(DiscountEngine.java:118)
        at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.applyRule(DiscountEngine.java:64)
        at com.shop.pricing.OrderService.calculateTotal(OrderService.java:88)
Taking 2-3 thread dumps a few seconds apart and seeing the same line repeatedly is strong evidence of a genuine hot loop (as opposed to normal, varying activity) at that exact line.

Async-Profiler / JFR for Flame Graphs

For CPU problems that are spread across many methods rather than one obvious hot loop, sampling profilers give a much clearer picture than manual thread-dump correlation:

• Java Flight Recorder (JFR) - built into the JDK, low overhead, can even be run continuously in production: java -XX:+FlightRecorder -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=recording.jfr MyApp, then open the recording in JDK Mission Control to see a flame graph of where CPU time was actually spent.
• async-profiler - an external agent that samples native + Java stacks with very low overhead, commonly attached on demand: ./profiler.sh -d 30 -e cpu -f flamegraph.html <pid>.

Flame graphs let you see, at a glance, which method call trees consume the widest share of total CPU samples - far faster than manually diffing multiple jstack dumps.

Symptom -> Root Cause -> Diagnosis -> Fix

War Story: The Promo Code Regex That Cost 40% of the Fleet

A retail checkout service began throwing timeouts across roughly 40% of instances during a flash sale, while the rest of the fleet looked healthy. CPU graphs showed the affected instances pinned at 100% on exactly one core each, while overall request rate hadn't grown dramatically.

Running top -H plus jstack on an affected instance repeatedly showed the same hot thread stuck inside DiscountEngine.matchPromoCode, which validated promo codes using a hand-written regex containing a nested quantifier: ^(PROMO-[A-Z0-9]+)+$. A marketing campaign had, that day, started generating promo codes with an unusual trailing suffix that didn't cleanly match - triggering catastrophic backtracking on every validation attempt for those specific codes, and each affected instance happened to be one that had recently received a request containing one of the problem codes.

Fix: the regex was replaced with a simple, linear-time manual prefix/character-class check (no nested quantifiers), and a CPU-time watchdog was added around promo validation as a safety net for future regex-related regressions.

Prevention Checklist

• Avoid regex patterns with nested or overlapping quantifiers on untrusted/variable-length input; test regexes against long adversarial strings before shipping.
• Never busy-wait; always use blocking coordination primitives (wait/notify, BlockingQueue, CompletableFuture, CountDownLatch).
• Bake top -H + jstack correlation (or an equivalent APM CPU profiler) into your standard incident runbook so responders don't waste time guessing.
• Run continuous low-overhead JFR recording in production so a CPU spike can be analyzed retroactively without needing to reproduce it live.
• Load-test with realistic, occasionally adversarial input data (not just "happy path" fixtures) to catch algorithmic complexity issues before production.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you diagnose which Java thread is causing high CPU on a server?Use "top -H -p <pid>" to find the hot native thread ID (TID), convert it to hex, then match it against the nid field in a jstack thread dump to see exactly what that thread was executing
What is a "busy-wait" loop and why is it bad?A loop that repeatedly checks a condition without blocking/sleeping, consuming 100% CPU on that core; it should be replaced with proper blocking coordination like wait/notify or a BlockingQueue
What is catastrophic regex backtracking?A regex with ambiguous nested/overlapping quantifiers can require exponential time to fail to match certain inputs, because the engine tries an exponential number of backtracking paths, pegging CPU
How can GC cause high CPU?If allocation rate is too high or the heap is undersized, the GC runs very frequently or continuously trying to reclaim space, consuming large amounts of CPU with little useful application progress
What's the difference between jstack and a profiler like async-profiler/JFR for CPU issues?jstack gives point-in-time snapshots useful for finding one obviously hot, repeating stack frame; a sampling profiler aggregates over time into a flame graph, better for CPU spread across many methods
Why might taking multiple jstack dumps a few seconds apart be more useful than just one?Seeing the same stack frame repeat across multiple dumps is strong evidence of a genuine hot loop, distinguishing it from normal varying thread activity captured in a single snapshot
Can high CPU happen right after a deployment even with no bug?Yes - JIT warm-up means new code runs interpreted/less-optimized initially, causing temporarily elevated CPU until hot methods are compiled by C2; this is usually benign and settles quickly

Mid-Level Notes

  • Hex conversion: the thread id in top is decimal, but jstack shows nid=0x..., so convert with printf "%x" TID.
  • Common causes: infinite loops, busy waiting without sleep, catastrophic regex backtracking, and a HashMap corrupted by threads.
  • GC threads can be the busy ones; check with jstat -gcutil before blaming application code.

Senior Notes

  • Sampling profiler: async-profiler or JFR gives hot methods with low overhead, which is safe in production.
  • Take 3 dumps a few seconds apart; a thread in the same frame each time is the suspect.
  • JIT compiler threads burn CPU during warm-up, so a spike right after start is often normal.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Guessing: changing code before taking a dump.
  • One dump only: a single sample can be unlucky; take three.
  • Spin on a flag: use a latch, a condition or a blocking queue.
  • Regex on user input: avoid nested quantifiers and bound input length.
  • Unsynchronized HashMap: concurrent resize can create a loop in old JDKs; use ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Logging in a hot loop: string formatting costs CPU even when the level is off, unless you use parameters.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning approach:

  • Profile first: optimize the top frame in the flame graph only.
  • Algorithm: a better data structure beats micro tuning.
  • Cache pure results with a bounded cache.
  • Batch work to reduce per-call overhead.
  • Size pools to cores for CPU-bound work: about availableProcessors() threads.
  • Warm-up: expect higher CPU for the first minutes while the JIT compiles.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Incident: CPU of one pod sits at 800 percent after a deployment, other pods are fine.

  • Symptoms: p99 latency up, load average high, no errors in the log.
  • Diagnosis: top -H shows 6 threads near 100 percent; converted ids match http-nio-exec threads; three dumps show the same Pattern.matcher frames.
  • Root cause: a new validation regex with nested quantifiers hit a long malformed input from one client.
  • Fix: rewrite the regex without nesting, limit input length to 256, use a timeout wrapper, and add a test with a hostile string.

What is "High GC"?

Garbage Collection (GC) is the JVM automatically reclaiming memory used by objects that are no longer reachable. Some GC activity is normal and healthy - it's how Java manages memory without manual free() calls.

"High GC" describes a situation where GC runs too often or takes too long relative to the actual work the application is doing - so much of the app's time is spent pausing for GC instead of serving requests. This shows up to users as slow response times, timeouts, or stutter, even though there's no crash (yet).

Simulating High GC Frequency

Allocating lots of short-lived objects very rapidly forces the JVM's young generation to fill up and collect over and over again, which you can literally watch happen with GC logging enabled.

Simulating Long, Painful GC Pauses

Filling the heap close to its limit with objects that survive (are retained) forces expensive, longer full GCs instead of quick young-gen collections.

Simple Fixes at the Beginner Level

• Reduce unnecessary allocation - avoid creating throwaway objects inside hot loops (e.g. building Strings with + in a loop instead of StringBuilder).
• Reuse objects/buffers where safe, instead of allocating a new one every call.
• Right-size the heap - a heap that's too small forces the JVM to collect constantly just to make room for normal traffic.

Fresher Notes

  • High GC means the JVM spends a large share of time collecting garbage, so the application slows down or pauses.
  • GC logs are switched on with -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log in Java 9 and later.
  • Young versus old: short-lived objects die in the young generation cheaply; objects that survive move to the old generation.

How the generational collectors work in outline.

  • Eden: new objects are allocated here by fast pointer bumping.
  • Young GC: live objects are copied to survivor spaces; dead ones cost nothing.
  • Promotion: objects that survive several collections move to the old generation.

Reading GC Logs Like an Engineer

Modern JVMs (9+) use unified logging (-Xlog:gc*). A single Young GC log line carries several important numbers worth learning to read at a glance: 
[12.451s][info][gc] GC(142) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 812M->210M(1024M) 45.223ms
   |          |     |                                         |     |      |
   timestamp  GC#   pause type / cause                     before after total-heap  duration

Key ratios to track over time, not just single lines:
  - Frequency:  how many GC(#) events per minute -> allocation rate proxy
  - Reclaim %:  (before - after) / before        -> how effective each GC is
  - Pause time: duration in ms                    -> user-facing latency impact
  - Post-GC floor: "after" value trending UP over successive GCs -> leak signal
A healthy young-gen GC reclaims 80-95% of the young generation in a few milliseconds. When reclaim percentage drops and pause duration climbs together, that's the classic signature of a heap under real memory pressure, not just routine collection.

Throughput vs Latency: Choosing (and Tuning) a Collector

"High GC" often isn't really about a bug - it's about a collector mismatched to the workload's goals.

• G1 GC (default since JDK 9) - balances throughput and pause time; tunable target pause via -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200. Good general-purpose default.
• Parallel GC - maximizes throughput, accepts longer/less predictable pauses; suited for batch jobs where total runtime matters more than individual pause length.
• ZGC / Shenandoah - designed for very low pause times (sub-millisecond to a few ms) even on huge heaps (100s of GB), at some throughput/CPU cost; ideal for latency-sensitive services with big heaps.

A common production mistake is running a latency-sensitive API on Parallel GC's default settings (tuned for throughput) and being surprised by occasional multi-second pauses under load - the fix is often just switching collector or its goals, not rewriting application code.

Symptom -> Root Cause -> Diagnosis -> Fix

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
Frequent short Young GC pauses (many per second) under normal loadHigh allocation rate - too many short-lived objects created per requestGC logs show high GC(#) frequency; profiler (JFR Allocation Profiling) shows top allocating call sitesReduce allocations in hot paths (avoid boxing, reuse buffers, use StringBuilder, avoid unnecessary intermediate collections)
Occasional very long Full GC pauses (seconds) causing request timeoutsOld generation filling up, forcing expensive Full/Mixed GC compactionGC logs show "Pause Full" events with large before->after deltas and long duration; correlate with request timeout spikesInvestigate for a leak first (see Memory Leak topic); if genuinely legitimate live-set, increase heap or switch to a low-pause collector (G1/ZGC) with tuned targets
Reclaim percentage steadily dropping across successive GCs over hoursSlow memory leak - live set growing, less to reclaim each cyclePlot post-GC heap occupancy over time; a rising floor (not returning to baseline) confirms a leak, not just loadHeap dump + MAT to find and fix the leak (see Memory Leak topic)

Latency-sensitive service has rare multi-second pause spikes despite low average GC timeWrong collector for the goal - e.g. Parallel/throughput-tuned GC used for a latency-critical APICheck configured collector (-XX flags) and its pause-time targets against SLA requirementsSwitch to G1 with -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, or ZGC/Shenandoah for very tight pause SLAs on large heaps

War Story: The Nightly Batch Job That Broke the Live API

An order-analytics service shared its JVM heap between two workloads: a customer-facing REST API and a nightly batch aggregation job. After a new "real-time trending" feature was added to the batch job, on-call started getting paged for API p99 latency spiking to 4-6 seconds every night at 2 AM - always exactly when the batch job ran.

GC logs during the incident window showed a burst of large "Pause Full" events instead of the usual quick Young GCs - the batch job's new trending logic built several large intermediate HashMaps that lived just long enough to get promoted into old generation, filling it and triggering expensive full compactions, which stopped-the-world for every thread including the ones serving live API traffic.

Fix: the batch workload was moved to a separate JVM process entirely (different heap, different GC tuning profile suited to throughput), fully isolating its allocation behavior from the latency-sensitive API process - a textbook case of "one JVM, two very different workloads" being the real root cause, not a code bug.

Prevention Checklist

• Enable GC logging permanently in production (-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=10,filesize=50m) - the overhead is negligible and the historical data is invaluable during incidents.
• Track GC pause time and frequency as first-class dashboard metrics (via JMX/Micrometer), not just heap percentage.
• Separate workloads with very different allocation profiles (batch vs. real-time) into different JVM processes/pods rather than sharing one heap.
• Choose the collector based on stated latency vs throughput goals, and revisit that choice as heap size or SLA requirements change.
• Load-test with production-realistic allocation patterns, not just request volume, since GC pressure depends on what each request allocates, not just how many requests arrive.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does "high GC" mean and what user-facing symptom does it usually cause?GC running too frequently or taking too long relative to actual work, causing elevated latency, timeouts, or throughput drops even without a crash
What's the difference between a Young GC pause and a Full GC pause?Young GC only collects the young generation (fast, frequent, usually a few ms); Full GC collects the entire heap including old gen (slower, less frequent, can pause for hundreds of ms to seconds)
How do you tell from GC logs whether you have a leak versus just high load?Track post-GC heap occupancy over time - if it returns to roughly the same baseline after each GC, it's load; if the floor keeps rising across successive GCs, it's a leak
What does -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis do?Sets a soft target maximum pause time for G1 GC; G1 adapts region sizing and collection scheduling to try to meet it, though it's a goal, not a hard guarantee
When would you choose ZGC or Shenandoah over G1?When the application needs very low, consistent pause times (sub-millisecond to a few ms) even with a very large heap, and can accept somewhat higher CPU/throughput overhead in exchange
Why might running a batch job and a latency-sensitive API in the same JVM cause GC problems?Their very different allocation patterns (large batch intermediate structures vs small request-scoped objects) share one heap, so the batch job's allocations can trigger costly full GCs that pause the API's threads too
What's the first thing to check if GC frequency suddenly increases after a deploy?What changed in allocation behavior - new code creating more objects per request, larger cached objects, or a new dependency with heavier allocation patterns

Mid-Level Notes

  • Allocation rate: creating many temporary objects (strings in loops, boxing) triggers frequent young collections.
  • Full GC that frees little means the live set is too big for the heap; this is a leak or an undersized heap.
  • jstat: jstat -gcutil PID 1000 prints occupancy and counts every second.

Senior Notes

  • Collector choice: G1 balances throughput and pauses; ZGC and Shenandoah give very short pauses on large heaps.
  • Pause target: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 is a goal for G1, not a guarantee.
  • Tune last: reduce allocation and fix leaks first, then size the heap, and only then change collector flags.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • System.gc() calls: forces a Full GC; remove or add -XX:+DisableExplicitGC.
  • Heap too small: frequent collections; raise -Xmx after measuring the live set.
  • Heap too large with default pauses: long Full GCs; consider ZGC.
  • Large temporary arrays: humongous allocations in G1; stream data.
  • Copying tuning flags from blogs: test each flag against your own GC log.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning order:

  • 1. Cut allocation: avoid boxing, reuse buffers, avoid needless copies.
  • 2. Fix leaks: a rising floor cannot be tuned away.
  • 3. Size the heap: about 2 to 3 times the live set.
  • 4. Pick a collector for the goal: throughput or latency.
  • 5. Compare pause p99 and GC time percentage before and after.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Incident: an API has 5 second pauses every few minutes.

  • Symptoms: timeouts in bursts, CPU spikes, GC pause metric high.
  • Diagnosis: GC log shows Pause Full (Allocation Failure) every 3 minutes; the heap after Full GC is 90 percent of 2 GB.
  • Root cause: a report job loaded a million rows into a list; the live set filled the heap.
  • Fix: stream rows with a fetch size, move the job off the API pod, set heap to 4 GB with a heap-usage alert, and watch the floor after Full GC.

Can Java Even Have Memory Leaks?

Java has automatic Garbage Collection (GC), so many beginners assume "memory leaks" are a C/C++ problem that simply can't happen in Java. That's not true.

A memory leak in Java happens when objects are no longer needed by the application, but something still holds a reference to them - so the GC considers them "reachable" and correctly refuses to collect them. The objects are technically alive but functionally garbage; over time they accumulate and can eventually cause OutOfMemoryError.

In short: Java prevents dangling pointer bugs, but it cannot prevent you from forgetting to let go of a reference you no longer need.

Cause 1: An Unbounded Static Collection

A static field lives for the entire lifetime of the application. If you keep adding to a static collection and never remove old entries, it grows forever.

Cause 2: Unclosed Resources

Streams, database connections, and file handles hold onto native/off-heap resources. Forgetting to close them leaks memory (and OS handles) even though the Java object itself is small.

Cause 3: Listener / Callback Leaks

Registering a listener (observer/callback) on a long-lived object, but never unregistering it, keeps the listener - and everything it references - alive forever, even after the "real" owner is done with it.

The Beginner-Level Fix Pattern

• Always pair "register" with "unregister", "open" with "close" (prefer try-with-resources).
• Don't put request-scoped or session-scoped data into static fields.
• If you need a cache, use one with a maximum size and/or expiry, never a plain growing List/Map.

Fresher Notes

  • Memory leak in Java means objects that are no longer needed are still reachable, so the GC cannot free them.
  • Symptom: heap use after each GC grows slowly until an OutOfMemoryError appears after hours or days.
  • Static collections such as a static Map used as a cache are the most common leak source.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The GC frees what is unreachable from GC roots, so a leak is a reachable but useless object.

  • GC roots: thread stacks, static fields, JNI references and class loaders.
  • Retained size: memory that would be freed if an object was removed.
  • Class loader leaks: in app servers, a leftover reference keeps the whole old webapp and its Metaspace.
  • Saw-tooth shape: heap use falls after each GC but the minimum rises, which is the leak signature.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools and commands:

  • jcmd PID GC.class_histogram: counts per class; run twice and compare.
  • jcmd PID GC.heap_dump: full dump for MAT or VisualVM.
  • JFR with OldObjectSample: finds leak candidates with low overhead.
  • jmap -histo:live PID: forces a GC then lists live objects.
  • Weak and soft references: WeakReference for listeners, SoftReference only for simple memory-sensitive caches.

The GC Roots Model: Why "Reachable" Isn't Always "Needed"

The JVM's GC works purely on reachability from a set of "GC Roots" (local variables on active stacks, static fields, JNI references, etc.) - not on whether a human thinks an object is "still useful." An object graph is kept alive as long as any chain of references connects it back to a GC root, no matter how irrelevant that chain has become to the application's actual logic. 
GC Roots (static fields, thread stacks, JNI refs)
        |
        v
  EventBus.listeners (static singleton, always reachable)
        |
        v
  Listener lambda  --references-->  Widget.this
                                          |
                                          v
                                    byte[1MB] bigData

Even though 'Widget' has gone completely out of scope in main(),
it is still reachable via EventBus -> listeners -> lambda -> Widget.this
so the GC correctly (but unhelpfully) keeps it alive forever.
This is the core mental model every "memory leak" investigation comes back to: find the unexpected path from a GC root to the object that shouldn't still be alive.

ThreadLocal Leaks in Pooled-Thread Environments

ThreadLocal is a particularly sneaky leak source in server applications that use thread pools (which is essentially all of them - servlet containers, executor services). Because pooled threads are reused indefinitely, a ThreadLocal value set during one request and never explicitly removed stays attached to that pooled thread and leaks into - or just wastes memory across - every future task that thread executes.

Diagnosing a Leak with a Heap Dump: Dominator Tree and Retained Size

The professional workflow for confirming and pinpointing a leak:

1. Capture two heap dumps some time apart under steady load (e.g. via jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=dump1.hprof <pid>), then compare object counts/sizes between them in Eclipse MAT's "Compare Basket" - classes whose instance count grows roughly linearly with time/traffic and never shrinks are your leak suspects.
2. Run the Leak Suspects report - MAT clusters the dominator tree and highlights the single biggest retained-size object graphs automatically.
3. Inspect "Path to GC Roots" on the suspect object, excluding weak/soft references - this shows you the exact reference chain (e.g. Thread -> ThreadLocalMap -> Entry -> YourObject) keeping it alive, which tells you precisely which piece of code to fix.
4. Distinguish shallow vs retained size - shallow size is just that one object; retained size is everything that would be freed if that object became unreachable. Sort by retained size, not shallow size, to find the real culprit.

War Story: The Executor Service That Remembered Every User

A support-ticketing platform started seeing gradual memory growth over about two weeks per deployment, always eventually requiring a restart. The team initially suspected the newest feature (file attachments) since memory growth "felt" proportional to ticket volume.

A heap dump comparison in MAT told a different story: the fastest-growing class was java.lang.ThreadLocal$ThreadLocalMap$Entry, retained by the application's fixed-size ExecutorService thread pool. A "current user" ThreadLocal, set at the start of each ticket-processing task to make the acting user's ID conveniently available deep in the call stack (avoiding having to pass it as a parameter everywhere), was never removed at the end of the task. Because the executor's threads were long-lived and reused for years, each thread's ThreadLocalMap silently accumulated stale entries - technically the map does replace the value on the next set() for the same ThreadLocal instance, but the real leak was several different ThreadLocal instances (one per feature team, added over years) each accumulating separately, and some of those held large per-user context objects that outlived their usefulness.

Fix: every ThreadLocal.set() in the codebase was audited and paired with a matching remove() in a finally block, and a code-review checklist item was added specifically for ThreadLocal usage going forward.

  • Listeners: registering a listener or callback and never removing it keeps the whole owner object alive.
  • ThreadLocal values in a thread pool stay for the life of the pooled thread unless you call remove() in a finally block.
  • Unclosed resources: streams, connections and executors that are not closed keep buffers and threads alive.

Senior Notes

  • Diagnose with two heap dumps (jcmd PID GC.heap_dump file.hprof) taken some time apart and compare the growing classes in MAT.
  • Dominator tree and path to GC roots show which static field or thread holds the memory.
  • Bounded caches: use Caffeine or a size-limited LinkedHashMap, and use WeakHashMap only when you understand its key semantics.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Cache without limit or TTL: use Caffeine with maximumSize and expireAfterWrite.
  • Mutable key without equals/hashCode: entries pile up.
  • Inner class holding the outer: a non-static inner class or lambda keeps this alive.
  • Not closing resources: use try-with-resources.
  • Not shutting down executors: idle pool threads keep class loaders alive.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and prevention:

  • Monitor the floor: alert on heap after GC trend, not on peak usage.
  • Load test long: leaks need hours; run a soak test.
  • Size limits everywhere: queues, caches, maps, sessions.
  • Prefer weak listeners or explicit unregister in lifecycle callbacks.
  • Dump on OOM: keep the flag always on.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Incident: heap grows 40 MB per hour and the service dies after 2 days.

  • Symptoms: old generation floor rises on every Full GC; OOM at the weekend.
  • Diagnosis: two class histograms 1 hour apart show com.shop.AuditEvent growing; MAT path to roots ends at a static List in AuditBuffer.
  • Root cause: the flusher thread died after a network error and the buffer was never drained.
  • Fix: use a bounded queue, restart the flusher on error, drop or spill oldest events when full, and alert on queue size.

What is Thread Exhaustion?

Every Java thread you create consumes real operating-system resources: a native memory stack (default roughly 512KB-1MB), kernel scheduling structures, and a slot against the OS's per-process thread limit.

Thread exhaustion happens when an application creates far more threads than it should (usually unintentionally) - either running out of memory to back them, or hitting the OS's hard limit on threads per process. Unlike heap OOM, this isn't about your objects; it's about the JVM itself running out of room to create new threads.

Cause 1: Creating a New Thread Per Task, Unbounded

The classic beginner mistake is calling new Thread(...).start() for every incoming task instead of using a bounded thread pool. Under enough load, this creates thousands of threads simultaneously.

Cause 2: An Unbounded Thread Pool (CachedThreadPool)

Executors.newCachedThreadPool() creates a new thread for every submitted task if none are idle, with no upper bound on pool size. If tasks arrive faster than they complete (e.g. they're all blocked waiting on something slow), the pool will keep growing without limit - same problem as Cause 1, just hidden behind an innocent-looking API.

The Beginner-Level Fix: Always Use a Bounded Pool

Use a thread pool with an explicit, sensible maximum size for the kind of work being done, instead of an unbounded pool or raw new Thread() per task.

Fresher Notes

  • Thread exhaustion means no thread is free (pool full) or the JVM cannot create more threads.
  • Platform threads are mapped to OS threads and each reserves a stack, so thousands of them are costly.
  • Symptom: requests wait in a queue, latency rises, and the log may show unable to create native thread.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Why threads run out.

  • Platform thread: a thin wrapper over an OS thread with its own stack (about 1 MB reserved).
  • Pool saturation: all workers are busy, new tasks wait in the queue or are rejected.
  • Blocking: threads waiting on slow I/O are not doing useful work but still occupy the pool.
  • Virtual thread: a JVM-managed thread that mounts on a carrier, and unmounts when it blocks.
  • Little's law: needed threads = request rate times average latency.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and options:

  • Fixed pool: newFixedThreadPool(n) with an unbounded queue; safe thread count, unsafe queue.
  • Cached pool: unbounded threads; risky under load.
  • ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, bounded queue and a rejection policy (AbortPolicy, CallerRunsPolicy).
  • Virtual threads: Thread.ofVirtual().start(r) or the per-task executor.
  • Tomcat: server.tomcat.threads.max.
  • Stack size: -Xss.

expert.content:
Anatomy of "unable to create new native thread"

This specific OutOfMemoryError message is misleading to newcomers because it says "OutOfMemoryError" but usually has nothing to do with the Java heap. It occurs when the JVM asks the OS to create a new native thread (via pthread_create on Linux) and the OS refuses. That refusal has two common underlying causes:

• Native memory exhaustion - each thread reserves a stack (-Xss, default ~512KB-1MB); with thousands of threads, that alone can exhaust available process/native memory, especially in a memory-constrained container.
• OS thread-count limits - Linux's ulimit -u (max user processes/threads) or /proc/sys/kernel/threads-max, and inside containers, resource limits (cgroups) can cap the number of threads far below what raw memory would allow. 

Exception in thread "pool-4-thread-8231" java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread
    at java.base/java.lang.Thread.start0(Native Method)
    at java.base/java.lang.Thread.start(Thread.java:803)
    at java.base/java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.addWorker(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:957)
    at java.base/java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.execute(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:1378)
    at java.base/java.util.concurrent.AbstractExecutorService.submit(AbstractExecutorService.java:145)
    at com.shop.orders.OrderNotifier.notifyAsync(OrderNotifier.java:52)

Diagnostic checklist:
  $ ps -eLf | grep  | wc -l        # actual current thread count for the process
  $ cat /proc//limits | grep processes    # ulimit -u as seen by the process
  $ jstack  | grep 'nid=' | wc -l         # cross-check via JVM's own thread list

Thread Pool Sizing: CPU-Bound vs I/O-Bound Work

Choosing a pool size isn't arbitrary - it should be driven by what the tasks actually spend their time doing:

• CPU-bound tasks (pure computation, no blocking) - optimal pool size is roughly number of CPU cores (+1). More threads than cores just adds context-switching overhead with no throughput gain.
• I/O-bound tasks (waiting on network calls, DB queries, disk) - threads spend most of their time blocked, not computing, so a much larger pool can improve throughput. A common starting formula: threads = cores x (1 + wait_time / compute_time) - e.g. if a task waits 90ms for every 10ms of actual CPU work, that's a wait/compute ratio of 9, suggesting roughly 10x the core count.

In practice, teams tune this empirically with load tests rather than trusting the formula blindly, but the formula gives a sane starting point instead of guessing "100 sounds fine."

Bounding Cached Pools and Rejecting Overload Gracefully

The real production fix for thread exhaustion is rarely "just use a fixed pool" alone - it's combining a bounded pool with a bounded queue and an explicit rejection policy, so the system fails predictably under overload instead of unboundedly consuming resources.

War Story: The Retry Storm That Multiplied Threads

A payments-notification service used Executors.newCachedThreadPool() to fire outbound webhook calls to merchant endpoints asynchronously - reasonable when merchant endpoints usually respond in under 200ms. During a partial outage of one large merchant's endpoint, its webhook URL started timing out after the client's default 60-second socket timeout instead of failing fast.

Because the cached pool has no upper bound, and webhook volume didn't slow down, the service kept spinning up a brand-new thread for every notification, each of which sat blocked for up to 60 seconds waiting on that one unresponsive merchant. Within about 12 minutes, the process had accumulated over 30,000 threads and crashed with OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread - taking down webhook delivery for every merchant, not just the one that was actually having problems.

Fix: the cached pool was replaced with a bounded ThreadPoolExecutor (max 200 threads, bounded queue, CallerRunsPolicy), and the HTTP client's socket timeout was reduced to 5 seconds with a per-merchant circuit breaker, so one slow merchant could no longer starve threads needed for everyone else.

Prevention Checklist

• Never use Executors.newCachedThreadPool() or raw new Thread() per task in production code that handles untrusted/variable load - always define an explicit maximum.
• Pair a bounded pool with a bounded queue and a deliberate rejection policy ( CallerRunsPolicy, AbortPolicy with monitoring, or a custom handler) so overload is handled predictably.
• Set aggressive timeouts on any blocking call made from within a pooled task - a thread blocked forever on a downstream dependency is a thread that can never be reused.
• Monitor thread count (via JMX/Micrometer jvm.threads.live) as a first-class metric with alerting, the same way you'd monitor heap usage.
• Size pools deliberately using the CPU-bound vs I/O-bound distinction, and validate under realistic load tests rather than trusting a guessed constant.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer

Why is Executors.newCachedThreadPool() dangerous in production?It has no maximum pool size, so if tasks arrive faster than they complete (e.g. they block on a slow dependency), it will keep creating new threads without bound, risking thread exhaustion
How do you size a thread pool for CPU-bound work versus I/O-bound work?CPU-bound: roughly the number of CPU cores (+1); I/O-bound: a larger pool since threads spend most time blocked, often estimated as cores x (1 + wait_time/compute_time)
What's the role of a bounded queue and rejection policy in a ThreadPoolExecutor?They provide backpressure - once the pool and queue are both saturated, the rejection policy (e.g. CallerRunsPolicy) determines what happens next instead of letting the pool grow unboundedly or silently dropping work
How would you diagnose which threads are causing thread exhaustion in a running process?Compare ps -eLf thread count and /proc/<pid>/limits against expectations, then use jstack to see what the accumulated threads are doing (often BLOCKED/WAITING on the same downstream call)
Why can a slow downstream dependency cause thread exhaustion even with reasonable traffic volume?If each task blocks waiting on the slow dependency for a long time, worker threads accumulate faster than they're freed, especially with an unbounded pool, eventually exhausting native thread capacity
What's the trade-off of reducing -Xss to allow more threads within the same memory budget?Smaller per-thread stacks let more threads fit in a given memory budget, but increase the risk of StackOverflowError for any code with deep recursion or large stack frames

Mid-Level Notes

  • Pool sizing: an unbounded Executors.newCachedThreadPool() can create thousands of threads under load.
  • Blocking calls: threads waiting for a slow database or HTTP call are held, so a slow dependency exhausts the pool.
  • Thread dump shows many threads in the same WAITING or BLOCKED frame, which names the bottleneck.

Senior Notes

  • OS limits: check ulimit -u, /proc/sys/kernel/threads-max and container pid limits; each thread also uses -Xss of native memory.
  • Virtual threads (Java 21) are cheap and block without holding an OS thread, so use Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() for blocking I/O.
  • Protect dependencies with timeouts, bulkheads and bounded queues, and limit concurrency with a Semaphore when a downstream cannot take more.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Pool per request: creating an executor in each call leaks threads; share one and shut it down.
  • Forgetting shutdown: non-daemon workers keep the JVM alive.
  • Waiting for a task in the same pool (nested submit and get) causes deadlock.
  • No timeouts: a hung dependency holds threads forever.
  • Huge ThreadLocals with virtual threads: millions of copies; prefer scoped values or pass parameters.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • CPU-bound: pool near the core count.
  • I/O-bound: more threads, or virtual threads, sized by the downstream limit.
  • Bulkheads: separate pools per dependency so one slow service cannot take all threads.
  • Timeouts everywhere: connect, read and queue wait.
  • Lower -Xss only after measuring depth.
  • Monitor: active threads, queue size and rejection count.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Incident: the checkout API stops answering although CPU is near zero.

  • Symptoms: requests time out, load balancer marks pods unhealthy, CPU 3 percent.
  • Diagnosis: jstack shows all 200 http-nio-exec threads in SocketInputStream.socketRead0 inside the payment client; ls /proc/PID/task | wc -l shows 260 threads.
  • Root cause: the payment provider became slow and the HTTP client had no read timeout, so every Tomcat thread waited.
  • Fix: 2 second read timeout, a separate bounded pool with a circuit breaker for payments, return a clear error when full; consider virtual threads for the blocking calls.
